questions.q: Which is the best sociological definition of social class?
o: A group of people sharing similar economic position and life chances
Correct: Social class is a group sharing a similar economic position and life chances, such as access to education, health, and opportunity.
A group defined only by shared ancestry
Shared ancestry alone describes ethnicity, not class.
A rank in an organization
A rank in an organization describes hierarchy within an institution.
A category defined by occupation prestige alone
Occupational prestige alone is Weber's status dimension, not the full class concept.
questions.x: Social class is a group sharing a similar economic position and life chances, such as access to education, health, and opportunity. Trap: Defining class only by income.

questions.q: Compared with income, wealth is:
o: Annual earnings
Annual earnings are income.
Wages from employment
Wages from employment are a form of income.
Net worth, including assets minus debts
Correct: Wealth is net worth, meaning accumulated assets minus debts, whereas income is a flow over time.
Government transfers
Government transfers are also income, not accumulated net worth.
questions.x: Wealth is net worth, meaning accumulated assets minus debts, whereas income is a flow over time. Trap: Using income and wealth interchangeably.

questions.q: A country's Gini coefficient rises from 0.30 to 0.45. This indicates:
o: Decreased income inequality
Decreased inequality would require a falling Gini.
Increased income inequality
Correct: The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality), so a rise from 0.30 to 0.45 means greater inequality.
Increased poverty only
Gini measures distribution of income, not the level of poverty.
Unchanged inequality
The value changed, so inequality did not stay the same.
questions.x: The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality), so a rise from 0.30 to 0.45 means greater inequality. Trap: Thinking a higher Gini means greater equality.

questions.q: On a Lorenz curve, the further the curve bows from the line of equality:
o: The less the inequality
Less inequality would put the curve closer to the line.
The higher the average income
Average income is not shown by the curve's distance from equality.
The lower the poverty line
The poverty line is not represented by the bowing.
The greater the inequality
Correct: The farther a Lorenz curve bows below the line of equality, the larger the area between them and the greater the inequality, which underlies the Gini.
questions.x: The farther a Lorenz curve bows below the line of equality, the larger the area between them and the greater the inequality, which underlies the Gini. Trap: Reading the line of equality as average income.

questions.q: A family lacks the income necessary to afford basic necessities such as food and shelter. This is:
o: Relative poverty
Relative poverty is falling below a societal standard while having basic needs met.
Social exclusion
Social exclusion is being shut out of participation in society.
Underclass
Underclass refers to a persistently disadvantaged group, not the lack of basic needs.
Absolute poverty
Correct: Absolute poverty is lacking the resources for basic needs such as food and shelter.
questions.x: Absolute poverty is lacking the resources for basic needs such as food and shelter. Trap: Equating poverty with low rank.

questions.q: A household has enough food and housing but cannot afford what is typical in its society. This is:
o: Absolute poverty
Absolute poverty means lacking basic needs, which this household does not.
Relative poverty
Correct: Relative poverty means resources fall short of what is typical in society even when basic needs are met.
Anomie
Anomie is normlessness, not an economic condition.
Social mobility
Social mobility is movement between class positions.
questions.x: Relative poverty means resources fall short of what is typical in society even when basic needs are met. Trap: Thinking relative poverty is not real poverty.

questions.q: A child of factory workers becomes a physician. This is:
o: Upward intergenerational mobility
Correct: Intergenerational mobility compares class position across generations, and a factory worker's child becoming a physician is an upward move.
Intragenerational mobility
Intragenerational mobility is change within one person's lifetime.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility is a move within the same class level.
Structural mobility
Structural mobility results from economic shifts, not an individual comparison to parents.
questions.x: Intergenerational mobility compares class position across generations, and a factory worker's child becoming a physician is an upward move. Trap: Confusing intergenerational with intragenerational.

questions.q: A clerk becomes a company manager after 15 years. This is:
o: Intergenerational mobility
Intergenerational mobility compares parent and child.
Downward mobility
Downward mobility would be a decline in position.
Intragenerational upward mobility
Correct: Intragenerational mobility is change in position within one person's career, and clerk to manager is upward.
Caste mobility
Caste mobility is not possible within a closed ascribed system.
questions.x: Intragenerational mobility is change in position within one person's career, and clerk to manager is upward. Trap: Reading the example as comparing parent and child.

questions.q: Large numbers of people move up as a result of economic expansion creating new professional jobs. This is:
o: Structural mobility
Correct: Structural mobility results from changes in the economy and occupational structure that move many people up at once.
Exchange mobility
Exchange mobility is individuals trading places with no net change.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility is a move within the same level.
Caste mobility
Caste mobility is not possible in a closed system.
questions.x: Structural mobility results from changes in the economy and occupational structure that move many people up at once. Trap: Attributing structural change to individual effort.

questions.q: A system in which social position is determined by individual talent and effort is:
o: Caste system
A caste system assigns position by birth.
Aristocracy
Aristocracy assigns position by lineage and nobility.
Meritocracy
Correct: Meritocracy allocates position and rewards by individual talent and effort.
Oligarchy
Oligarchy is rule by a small elite.
questions.x: Meritocracy allocates position and rewards by individual talent and effort. Trap: Assuming real societies are purely meritocratic.

questions.q: In a caste system, social position is primarily:
o: Achieved by merit
Achieved by merit describes an open class system.
Ascribed at birth and rigid
Correct: A caste system is closed, with position ascribed at birth and rigid across a lifetime.
Fluid
Fluid describes open class systems with movement.
Based on education
Education-based placement describes a class or meritocratic system.
questions.x: A caste system is closed, with position ascribed at birth and rigid across a lifetime. Trap: Thinking caste systems allow movement.

questions.q: Marx described the class that owns the means of production as the:
o: Proletariat
The proletariat sells its labor and does not own capital.
Petite bourgeoisie
The petite bourgeoisie are small-scale owners who work their own businesses.
Lumpenproletariat
The lumpenproletariat is the lowest, non-working underclass.
Bourgeoisie
Correct: Marx called the owners of the means of production the bourgeoisie and the wage laborers the proletariat.
questions.x: Marx called the owners of the means of production the bourgeoisie and the wage laborers the proletariat. Trap: Swapping bourgeoisie and proletariat.

questions.q: Workers who believe their interests align with their employer's despite exploitation exhibit:
o: Class consciousness
Class consciousness is awareness of shared class interests.
Anomie
Anomie is normlessness.
Cultural capital
Cultural capital is non-financial knowledge that confers advantage.
False consciousness
Correct: False consciousness means failing to recognize one's class position and exploitation, so workers identify with employer interests.
questions.x: False consciousness means failing to recognize one's class position and exploitation, so workers identify with employer interests. Trap: Confusing with class consciousness.

questions.q: Weber argued that stratification involves:
o: Class only
Class only is Marx's emphasis.
Class, status, and party
Correct: Weber described three dimensions of stratification: class (wealth), status (prestige), and party (power).
Culture and religion only
Culture and religion only omits Weber's economic, prestige, and power dimensions.
Economic production alone
Economic production alone is Marx's materialist focus.
questions.x: Weber described three dimensions of stratification: class (wealth), status (prestige), and party (power). Trap: Attributing Weber's three-part model to Marx.

questions.q: The Davis-Moore thesis holds that stratification:
o: Is functional by motivating talented people to fill important roles
Correct: The Davis-Moore thesis is a functionalist view that unequal rewards motivate talented people to fill the most important positions.
Is harmful and unnecessary
Calling stratification harmful and unnecessary is a conflict-theory critique.
Results from conflict between classes
Stratification resulting from class conflict is the Marxist view.
Is produced by labeling
Labeling theory explains deviance, not the function of stratification.
questions.x: The Davis-Moore thesis is a functionalist view that unequal rewards motivate talented people to fill the most important positions. Trap: Assuming it asserts inequality is fair.

questions.q: Bourdieu argued that elite families pass advantage by transmitting:
o: Only financial capital
Financial capital alone is too narrow; Bourdieu stressed non-economic forms.
Only genetics
Genetics alone is not Bourdieu's mechanism.
Cultural and social capital
Correct: Bourdieu argued that elite families reproduce advantage by transmitting cultural and social capital, not just money.
Only occupational skill
Occupational skill alone omits the cultural tastes and networks he emphasized.
questions.x: Bourdieu argued that elite families reproduce advantage by transmitting cultural and social capital, not just money. Trap: Thinking advantage is only monetary.

questions.q: Intersectionality emphasizes that:
o: Overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class produce distinct experiences of oppression
Correct: Intersectionality (Crenshaw) holds that overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class interact to produce distinct experiences of oppression.
Each form of inequality operates independently
Independent operation of each inequality denies the interaction central to the concept.
Inequality is mainly economic
Inequality being mainly economic ignores multiple interacting categories.
Race is biologically determined
Race being biologically determined contradicts the social-construction view.
questions.x: Intersectionality (Crenshaw) holds that overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class interact to produce distinct experiences of oppression. Trap: Treating each category as additive.

questions.q: A hiring manager who holds negative attitudes about a group but treats all applicants equally shows:
o: Discrimination without prejudice
Discrimination without prejudice would mean unequal treatment without negative attitudes.
Both
Both is wrong because the manager treats applicants equally, so no discrimination occurs.
Prejudice without discrimination
Correct: Prejudice is a negative attitude and discrimination is behavior, so holding negative attitudes while treating all applicants equally is prejudice without discrimination.
Neither
Neither is wrong because the manager does hold negative attitudes.
questions.x: Prejudice is a negative attitude and discrimination is behavior, so holding negative attitudes while treating all applicants equally is prejudice without discrimination. Trap: Assuming prejudice always leads to discrimination.

questions.q: Lending policies that appear neutral but systematically deny mortgages in certain neighborhoods exemplify:
o: Individual discrimination
Individual discrimination is unequal treatment by persons, not systemic policy.
Institutional discrimination
Correct: Institutional discrimination is built into policies and practices, such as neutral-looking lending rules that systematically deny mortgages, regardless of intent.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is performance anxiety about confirming a stereotype.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
Self-fulfilling prophecy is a false belief that becomes true through behavior.
questions.x: Institutional discrimination is built into policies and practices, such as neutral-looking lending rules that systematically deny mortgages, regardless of intent. Trap: Requiring discriminatory intent.

questions.q: A student performs worse on a test after being reminded of a negative stereotype about their group. This is:
o: Self-serving bias
Self-serving bias is attributing success to self and failure to external factors.
Halo effect
Halo effect is letting one positive trait color overall judgment.
Cultural lag
Cultural lag is nonmaterial culture adapting slowly to material change.
Stereotype threat
Correct: Stereotype threat is anxiety about confirming a negative group stereotype, which can impair performance.
questions.x: Stereotype threat is anxiety about confirming a negative group stereotype, which can impair performance. Trap: Thinking it reflects ability differences.

questions.q: Women and minorities blocked from top executive positions by invisible barriers face:
o: Glass escalator
The glass escalator describes men advancing quickly in female-dominated occupations.
Trickle-down effect
Trickle-down effect is an economic theory about wealth flowing downward.
Tokenism
Tokenism is symbolic inclusion of a few members, not an invisible barrier.
The glass ceiling
Correct: The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier preventing women and minorities from reaching top positions.
questions.x: The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier preventing women and minorities from reaching top positions. Trap: Mixing glass ceiling and escalator.

questions.q: The 'feminization of poverty' refers to:
o: Women being less likely to work
Women being less likely to work is not the meaning of the term.
Women, especially single mothers, being disproportionately poor
Correct: Feminization of poverty describes the over-representation of women, especially single mothers, among the poor.
Poverty being caused by women
Claiming women cause poverty reverses the causal structure the term describes.
Men earning less
Men earning less is not what the term refers to.
questions.x: Feminization of poverty describes the over-representation of women, especially single mothers, among the poor. Trap: Reading the phrase as claiming women cause poverty rather than being over-represented among the poor.

questions.q: Placing hazardous waste facilities disproportionately in minority neighborhoods illustrates:
o: Environmental racism
Correct: Environmental racism is the disproportionate placement of hazards, like waste facilities, in minority communities.
Gentrification
Gentrification is wealthier residents displacing lower-income residents.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is evaluating cultures on their own terms.
Anomie
Anomie is normlessness.
questions.x: Environmental racism is the disproportionate placement of hazards, like waste facilities, in minority communities. Trap: Assuming hazard siting is random rather than a pattern linked to race and political power.

questions.q: Compared with higher-SES groups, lower-SES groups typically show:
o: Equal life expectancy
Equal life expectancy contradicts the SES health gradient.
Better access to care
Lower-SES groups typically have worse, not better, access to care.
Higher morbidity and mortality
Correct: Socioeconomic gradients show lower-SES groups with higher morbidity and mortality due to exposure, stress, and limited resources.
Lower stress
Lower-SES groups generally experience more stress, not less.
questions.x: Socioeconomic gradients show lower-SES groups with higher morbidity and mortality due to exposure, stress, and limited resources. Trap: Assuming differences stem only from health behaviors.

questions.q: Social exclusion refers to:
o: Processes that prevent groups from fully participating in society
Correct: Social exclusion is the systematic processes and barriers that prevent groups from fully participating in society.
Voluntary withdrawal
Voluntary withdrawal is a choice, not imposed barriers.
Residential segregation only
Residential segregation only is one form, not the full concept.
Free-market competition
Free-market competition is not exclusion by itself.
questions.x: Social exclusion is the systematic processes and barriers that prevent groups from fully participating in society. Trap: Equating social exclusion with homelessness alone rather than broad barriers to participation.

questions.q: Neighborhoods concentrated with poverty, poor schools, and limited services illustrate:
o: Mechanical solidarity
Mechanical solidarity is cohesion from similarity.
Social mobility
Social mobility is movement between class positions.
Spatial inequality
Correct: Spatial inequality is the unequal distribution of resources and opportunities by place, as in concentrated poverty neighborhoods.
Primary socialization
Primary socialization is early learning in the family.
questions.x: Spatial inequality is the unequal distribution of resources and opportunities by place, as in concentrated poverty neighborhoods. Trap: Overlooking that where one lives shapes access to schools and services independent of individual traits.

questions.q: Unequal access to internet and computers across income groups is called:
o: Cultural lag
Cultural lag is nonmaterial culture adapting slowly to technology.
The digital divide
Correct: The digital divide is unequal access to internet and computers across groups such as income levels.
Structural mobility
Structural mobility is movement caused by economic change.
Technological determinism
Technological determinism is the idea that technology drives society.
questions.x: The digital divide is unequal access to internet and computers across groups such as income levels. Trap: Assuming the divide only concerns hardware.

questions.q: C. Wright Mills's 'power elite' refers to:
o: Voting majority
Voting majority reflects pluralist democratic power.
Union leaders
Union leaders are not the elite Mills described.
Religious leaders
Religious leaders are not one of his three elite institutions.
A small group of leaders in military, corporate, and political institutions
Correct: Mills's power elite is a small group of leaders in military, corporate, and political institutions who hold concentrated power.
questions.x: Mills's power elite is a small group of leaders in military, corporate, and political institutions who hold concentrated power. Trap: Thinking pluralism describes Mills.

questions.q: The 'culture of poverty' thesis is criticized because it:
o: Ignores culture
It does emphasize culture, so ignoring culture is not the criticism.
Over-emphasizes inequality
It underplays rather than over-emphasizes inequality.
Rejects mobility
The thesis claims poverty persists across generations, so it doesn't reject mobility as the main critique.
Blames the poor's values instead of structural conditions
Correct: The culture of poverty thesis is criticized for blaming the poor's values and ignoring structural conditions.
questions.x: The culture of poverty thesis is criticized for blaming the poor's values and ignoring structural conditions. Trap: Treating poverty as the product of the poor's chosen values rather than structure.

questions.q: Placing students into different academic tracks based on early performance often:
o: Eliminates inequality
Eliminating inequality contradicts the evidence on tracking.
Reinforces existing class differences
Correct: Tracking sorts students early by performance and tends to reinforce existing class differences through unequal resources and expectations.
Increases mobility
Increased mobility is not what research finds; tracking tends to limit it.
Has no effect
No effect ignores documented reproduction of inequality.
questions.x: Tracking sorts students early by performance and tends to reinforce existing class differences through unequal resources and expectations. Trap: Assuming tracking by early performance is neutral when it often reinforces class differences.

questions.q: Mandatory retirement based on age, regardless of ability, exemplifies:
o: Ageism
Correct: Ageism is prejudice or discrimination based on age, as with forced retirement regardless of ability.
Sexism
Sexism is discrimination based on sex or gender.
Racism
Racism is discrimination based on race.
Credentialism
Credentialism is overreliance on diplomas as qualifications.
questions.x: Ageism is prejudice or discrimination based on age, as with forced retirement regardless of ability. Trap: Treating mandatory age-based retirement as neutral policy rather than discrimination based on age.

questions.q: Women's lower average earnings than men's, even after similar education, is:
o: Gender socialization
Gender socialization is learning gender roles, not unequal resources.
Role conflict
Role conflict is tension between roles of different statuses.
Gender stratification
Correct: Gender stratification is the unequal distribution of resources, such as pay, by gender, even with equal education.
Role strain
Role strain is tension within one role.
questions.x: Gender stratification is the unequal distribution of resources, such as pay, by gender, even with equal education. Trap: Reducing the pay gap to individual choices instead of structural gender stratification.

questions.q: When workers recognize shared interests and unite against owners, they have developed:
o: Class consciousness
Correct: Class consciousness is workers' awareness of shared class interests and willingness to unite against owners.
False consciousness
False consciousness is failing to recognize one's class interests, the opposite.
Anomie
Anomie is normlessness.
Alienation
Alienation is estrangement from work and others, not collective awareness.
questions.x: Class consciousness is workers' awareness of shared class interests and willingness to unite against owners. Trap: Confusing class consciousness with false consciousness, its conceptual opposite.

questions.q: Marx's concept of alienation describes workers' estrangement from:
o: Their families
Families are not the focus of Marx's alienation.
Their government
Government is not what workers are alienated from in his concept.
Their labor, products, and fellow workers
Correct: Marx's alienation describes workers' estrangement from their labor, the products they make, fellow workers, and their human potential, from lack of control over work.
Cultural norms
Cultural norms estrangement is closer to anomie.
questions.x: Marx's alienation describes workers' estrangement from their labor, the products they make, fellow workers, and their human potential, from lack of control over work. Trap: Treating alienation as a purely psychological mood rather than a result of the economic structure of work.

questions.q: People who work full time yet earn below the poverty line are:
o: The underclass
The underclass is persistently unemployed or marginal.
The working poor
Correct: The working poor are people who work full time yet earn below the poverty line.
The petite bourgeoisie
The petite bourgeoisie are small business owners.
The power elite
The power elite is a small group of leaders holding concentrated power.
questions.x: The working poor are people who work full time yet earn below the poverty line. Trap: Assuming poverty implies not working.

questions.q: Putnam's concept of social capital emphasizes the value of:
o: Accumulated financial assets
Accumulated financial assets are economic capital.
Educational credentials and skills
Educational credentials and skills are human capital.
Ownership of physical property
Ownership of physical property is physical capital.
Resources and trust embedded in social networks
Correct: Putnam's social capital is the value of resources, trust, and reciprocity embedded in social networks.
questions.x: Putnam's social capital is the value of resources, trust, and reciprocity embedded in social networks. Trap: Equating social capital with money or credentials rather than relationships.

questions.q: Which factor best explains class-based gaps in educational achievement according to most sociologists?
o: Fixed differences in innate ability between classes
Class-linked innate ability is not supported by evidence.
Lower value placed on education by poor families
Poor families do value education, so lower valuation is not supported.
Differences in the age at which children start school
School start age does not explain class-based gaps.
Unequal school funding and family resources
Correct: Unequal school funding and family resources create structural advantages that most sociologists see as the main source of class gaps in achievement.
questions.x: Unequal school funding and family resources create structural advantages that most sociologists see as the main source of class gaps in achievement. Trap: Blaming individual or cultural deficits rather than structural resource differences.

questions.q: Racial wealth gaps in the U.S. are often explained by:
o: Income differences alone
Income differences alone ignore accumulated assets.
Historical discrimination in housing and lending compounding across generations
Correct: Historical discrimination in housing and lending compounds across generations through inherited assets, producing racial wealth gaps.
Differences in saving only
Saving differences only miss structural barriers.
Education differences only
Education differences only omit asset inheritance and discrimination.
questions.x: Historical discrimination in housing and lending compounds across generations through inherited assets, producing racial wealth gaps. Trap: Equating wealth gaps with income gaps and ignoring accumulated assets across generations.

questions.q: Countries with high income inequality tend to have:
o: Lower intergenerational mobility
Correct: The Great Gatsby curve shows high-inequality countries tend to have lower intergenerational mobility.
Higher intergenerational mobility
Higher mobility contradicts the observed relationship.
No effect
No effect conflicts with cross-country data.
More meritocracy
More meritocracy is not associated with high inequality; unequal origins limit merit-based advancement.
questions.x: The Great Gatsby curve shows high-inequality countries tend to have lower intergenerational mobility. Trap: Assuming inequality fosters mobility.

questions.q: Hiring a single minority employee to appear inclusive without changing practices is:
o: Affirmative action
Affirmative action is a policy to increase opportunities for underrepresented groups, with genuine practice changes.
Segregation
Segregation is separation of groups.
Tokenism
Correct: Tokenism is symbolic inclusion of one or few minority members to appear inclusive without changing practices.
Assimilation
Assimilation is absorption into the dominant culture.
questions.x: Tokenism is symbolic inclusion of one or few minority members to appear inclusive without changing practices. Trap: Confusing with affirmative action.

questions.q: Glycine has pKa values of 2.3 (carboxyl) and 9.6 (amino). What is the approximate isoelectric point of glycine?
o: Correct: The pI of an amino acid with a nonionizable side chain is the average of its two pKa values: (2.3 + 9.6)/2 = 5.95, about 6.0.
4.0 matches no combination of the pKa values and is not the midpoint of anything relevant.
7.9 is not the midpoint of 2.3 and 9.6 (it would require other pKa values).
11.9 is the sum 2.3 + 9.6 rather than the average.
questions.x: The pI of an amino acid with a nonionizable side chain is the average of its two pKa values: (2.3 + 9.6)/2 = 5.95, about 6.0. Trap: Adding the pKa values instead of averaging them, or picking one pKa.

questions.q: Aspartate has pKa values of 2.0 (alpha-carboxyl), 3.9 (side chain), and 9.9 (amino). What is its approximate pI?
o: 6.0 is roughly the average of the alpha-carboxyl and amino pKa values as for a neutral amino acid, ignoring the acidic side chain.
6.9 averages the side-chain (3.9) and amino (9.9) pKa values, which flank a net -1 species rather than the neutral one.
9.9 is simply the amino-group pKa, not a pI.
Correct: The net-zero zwitterion lies between the two lowest pKa values (the two carboxyl groups): (2.0 + 3.9)/2 = 2.95, about 3.0.
questions.x: The net-zero zwitterion lies between the two lowest pKa values (the two carboxyl groups): (2.0 + 3.9)/2 = 2.95, about 3.0. Trap: Averaging the carboxyl and amino pKa values as with a neutral amino acid, ignoring the acidic side chain.

questions.q: Rotation about the C-N bond of a peptide linkage is restricted. What best explains this?
o: The nitrogen is sp3 hybridized and bulky
The amide nitrogen is effectively planar (sp2-like) because of resonance, not a bulky sp3 center.
Hydrogen bonding between adjacent residues locks the bond
Hydrogen bonds between residues stabilize secondary structure but do not cause the restricted rotation within the bond itself.
The bond is an ionic linkage between the carbonyl carbon and nitrogen
The C-N bond is a covalent amide bond, not an ionic linkage.
Resonance gives the bond partial double-bond character
Correct: Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character, making the amide group planar and rigid.
questions.x: Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character, making the amide group planar and rigid. Trap: Thinking a peptide bond is a single bond that rotates freely like other C-N single bonds.

questions.q: Which standard amino acid is NOT optically active?
o: Alanine
Alanine has four different groups (H, NH3+, COO-, CH3) on the alpha carbon, so it is chiral.
Proline
Proline is chiral; its ring links the side chain to the nitrogen but the alpha carbon still has four different groups.
Glycine
Correct: Glycine's side chain is H, so its alpha carbon has two identical substituents and is not a stereocenter.
Cysteine
Cysteine is chiral (it is R by CIP priorities only because sulfur raises the CH2SH priority).
questions.x: Glycine's side chain is H, so its alpha carbon has two identical substituents and is not a stereocenter. Trap: Assuming proline's ring or cysteine's R designation makes it achiral.

questions.q: Disulfide bonds are common in secreted proteins but rare in cytosolic proteins. What is the best explanation?
o: The cytosol is a reducing environment that keeps cysteines as free thiols
Correct: Disulfide formation is an oxidation; the cytosol is rich in glutathione and other reducing agents, whereas the ER and extracellular space are oxidizing.
Cysteine is absent from cytosolic proteins
Cytosolic proteins do contain cysteines, which stay as free thiols.
Disulfide bonds can only form between two different polypeptide chains
Disulfide bonds form both within a chain (tertiary) and between chains, so this is not a restriction to interchain bonds.
The cytosol has a much lower pH that protonates sulfur irreversibly
Cytosolic pH is near neutral, and protonation of sulfur is not what prevents disulfide formation.
questions.x: Disulfide formation is an oxidation; the cytosol is rich in glutathione and other reducing agents, whereas the ER and extracellular space are oxidizing. Trap: Believing disulfide bonds only join separate chains, so confusing them with quaternary-only structure.

questions.q: In an alpha helix, which interaction stabilizes the structure?
o: Hydrogen bonds between side chains of residues i and i+4
Side chains point outward from the helix and do not form the repeating i to i+4 hydrogen-bond pattern; this describes side chains instead of backbone atoms.
Hydrogen bonds between the backbone C=O of residue i and N-H of residue i+4
Correct: The helix is held by backbone hydrogen bonds between the C=O of residue i and the N-H of residue i+4, running parallel to the helix axis.
Disulfide bonds between cysteine residues along the helix
Disulfide bonds are covalent tertiary-structure links, not what stabilizes a helix.
Ionic bonds between the N- and C-termini of the polypeptide
Interactions between the termini are not the stabilizing force of a helix.
questions.x: The helix is held by backbone hydrogen bonds between the C=O of residue i and the N-H of residue i+4, running parallel to the helix axis. Trap: Attributing secondary structure to side-chain interactions, which define tertiary structure.

questions.q: Proline is often found at turns and is called a helix breaker. Why?
o: It is highly negatively charged and repels the helix
Proline is uncharged, so there is no charge repulsion with the helix.
It is too hydrophobic to remain in the helix interior
Hydrophobicity does not disrupt helices (leucine is common in helices).
It forms disulfide bonds that kink the backbone
Proline has no sulfur and cannot form disulfide bonds.
Its amide nitrogen has no hydrogen to donate and its ring restricts the phi angle
Correct: Proline's backbone N is bonded to its ring and so cannot donate an H-bond, and the ring locks the phi angle, kinking the chain.
questions.x: Proline's backbone N is bonded to its ring and so cannot donate an H-bond, and the ring locks the phi angle, kinking the chain. Trap: Blaming charge or hydrophobicity rather than backbone geometry and loss of the N-H donor.

questions.q: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, two lines with and without an inhibitor intersect on the y-axis. Which inhibitor type is this?
o: Competitive
Correct: Lines that share a y-intercept (1/Vmax) mean Vmax is unchanged while apparent Km increases, characteristic of competitive inhibition.
Noncompetitive
Noncompetitive inhibition gives lines that intersect on the x-axis (Vmax falls, Km unchanged).
Uncompetitive
Uncompetitive inhibition gives parallel lines (both Vmax and Km fall).
Irreversible covalent
Irreversible covalent inhibitors permanently remove active enzyme, lowering Vmax like noncompetitive inhibitors, so the y-intercept would change.
questions.x: Lines that share a y-intercept (1/Vmax) mean Vmax is unchanged while apparent Km increases, characteristic of competitive inhibition. Trap: Mixing up which intercept stays constant for competitive versus noncompetitive inhibition.

questions.q: A protein is treated with 8 M urea and loses its activity. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Noncovalent interactions are disrupted while the primary structure remains intact
Correct: Urea disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions, unfolding secondary through quaternary structure while leaving covalent peptide bonds intact.
Peptide bonds are hydrolyzed
Peptide bond hydrolysis requires strong acid with heat or proteases, not urea.
The amino acid sequence is rearranged
The amino acid sequence is covalently fixed and cannot rearrange.
Only the quaternary structure is affected
Urea also unfolds tertiary and secondary structure, not just quaternary.
questions.x: Urea disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions, unfolding secondary through quaternary structure while leaving covalent peptide bonds intact. Trap: Equating denaturation with breaking the peptide backbone, so assuming it is irreversible by definition.

questions.q: A protein is a heterodimer of 40 kDa and 25 kDa subunits joined by a disulfide bond. SDS-PAGE is run in the presence of beta-mercaptoethanol. What bands appear?
o: One band at 65 kDa
A single 65 kDa band would appear only without a reducing agent, since the disulfide would hold the dimer together.
Two bands, at 40 kDa and 25 kDa
Correct: SDS denatures the protein and coats it with uniform negative charge, and beta-mercaptoethanol reduces the disulfide, so the 40 and 25 kDa subunits separate by mass.
One band at about 32.5 kDa
32.5 kDa is an arithmetic average that has no physical basis.
Three bands at 65, 40, and 25 kDa
Three bands (65, 40, 25) would require incomplete reduction, which excess beta-mercaptoethanol avoids.
questions.x: SDS denatures the protein and coats it with uniform negative charge, and beta-mercaptoethanol reduces the disulfide, so the 40 and 25 kDa subunits separate by mass. Trap: Forgetting that a reducing agent breaks disulfides, leaving subunits as separate bands.

questions.q: A protein with pI 8.5 is placed in a native gel at pH 7.4. Toward which electrode does it migrate?
o: The cathode, because it is net positively charged
Correct: When pH < pI the protein is protonated and net positive, so it migrates toward the negative electrode (cathode).
The anode, because it is net positively charged
A net positive species does not move to the anode (the positive electrode).
The cathode, because it is net negatively charged
Negative charge would require pH above the pI, but 7.4 is below 8.5.
It does not migrate because its pI is above 7
Only pH equal to the pI gives no net migration; the pI being above 7 does not stop movement.
questions.x: When pH < pI the protein is protonated and net positive, so it migrates toward the negative electrode (cathode). Trap: Reversing the relation between pH, pI, and net charge.

questions.q: An enzyme has Vmax of 100 umol/min and Km of 2 mM. What is the initial velocity at [S] = 6 mM?
o: 50 umol/min
50 umol/min would occur at [S] = Km, not at 6 mM.
67 umol/min
67 results from using a denominator of 9 (Km + [S] mistakenly summed as 3 + 6).
75 umol/min
Correct: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) = 100(6)/(2 + 6) = 75 umol/min.
86 umol/min
86 results from using a denominator of 7.
questions.x: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) = 100(6)/(2 + 6) = 75 umol/min. Trap: Assuming velocity is Vmax/2 whenever substrate exceeds Km, or mis-adding in the denominator.

questions.q: In exercising muscle, pH falls and CO2 rises. How does this affect hemoglobin?
o: The curve shifts left, increasing O2 affinity
A left shift would mean greater affinity and less unloading, the opposite of the Bohr effect.
Hemoglobin changes to a hyperbolic curve like myoglobin
A hyperbolic curve reflects a monomer like myoglobin; hemoglobin stays sigmoidal.
The oxygen-binding curve shifts right, increasing O2 release
Correct: Lower pH and higher CO2 stabilize the T state (Bohr effect), decreasing O2 affinity and shifting the curve right, so more O2 is released to the muscle.
P50 decreases so more oxygen is unloaded
A lower P50 means higher affinity, whereas the Bohr effect raises P50.
questions.x: Lower pH and higher CO2 stabilize the T state (Bohr effect), decreasing O2 affinity and shifting the curve right, so more O2 is released to the muscle. Trap: Confusing a right shift with higher affinity.

questions.q: Which statement about an enzyme-catalyzed reaction is correct?
o: The enzyme makes an endergonic reaction spontaneous
An enzyme cannot make an endergonic reaction spontaneous because it does not change delta G.
The enzyme shifts the equilibrium toward products
An enzyme does not shift the equilibrium, since it speeds forward and reverse reactions equally.
The enzyme raises the energy of the transition state
Enzymes lower, not raise, the transition-state energy.
The enzyme lowers the activation energy without changing the overall delta G
Correct: Catalysts stabilize the transition state, lowering the activation energy, but do not alter delta G or the equilibrium constant.
questions.x: Catalysts stabilize the transition state, lowering the activation energy, but do not alter delta G or the equilibrium constant. Trap: Thinking catalysts change thermodynamics instead of only kinetics.

questions.q: Trypsinogen is secreted by the pancreas and activated by enteropeptidase in the duodenum. What is the main advantage of this arrangement?
o: It prevents the protease from digesting pancreatic tissue before reaching the intestine
Correct: Secreting an inactive zymogen that is cleaved only at its site of action (the duodenum) protects the producing pancreatic tissue from self-digestion.
It increases the Vmax of trypsin
Activation by cleavage does not change Vmax relative to the mature enzyme.
It allows trypsin to act as an allosteric activator of lipases
Trypsin is a protease and is not an allosteric activator of lipases.
It converts trypsinogen to a competitive inhibitor
The zymogen is not converted into a competitive inhibitor.
questions.x: Secreting an inactive zymogen that is cleaved only at its site of action (the duodenum) protects the producing pancreatic tissue from self-digestion. Trap: Believing zymogens are activated by phosphorylation like many signaling enzymes.

questions.q: Phosphorylation of a serine residue can alter a protein's conformation primarily because it
o: converts serine to a hydrophobic residue
Phosphoserine is more polar and charged, not more hydrophobic.
adds negative charge that can create or disrupt electrostatic interactions
Correct: The phosphate group carries about two negative charges at physiological pH, forming new salt bridges or repelling nearby negative groups.
creates a new peptide bond
Phosphorylation forms a phosphoester, not a new peptide bond.
removes the hydroxyl group as water
The hydroxyl oxygen is esterified to phosphate rather than lost as water.
questions.x: The phosphate group carries about two negative charges at physiological pH, forming new salt bridges or repelling nearby negative groups. Trap: Overlooking that charge, not hydrophobicity, drives the conformational change.

questions.q: A DNA-binding protein needs surface residues to interact with the phosphate backbone. Which pair would be most favorable?
o: Aspartate and glutamate
Aspartate and glutamate are negatively charged and would repel phosphates.
Leucine and valine
Leucine and valine are hydrophobic and cannot form electrostatic contacts.
Serine and alanine
Serine and alanine lack a charge for interacting with phosphates.
Lysine and arginine
Correct: Lysine and arginine are protonated and positively charged at physiological pH, forming electrostatic contacts with the negatively charged phosphate backbone.
questions.x: Lysine and arginine are protonated and positively charged at physiological pH, forming electrostatic contacts with the negatively charged phosphate backbone. Trap: Choosing negatively charged residues because DNA is an acid.

questions.q: A transmembrane segment of an integral protein spans the lipid bilayer as an alpha helix. Which residues most likely compose it?
o: Lysine, arginine, and histidine
Lysine, arginine, and histidine are basic and charged, which is energetically unfavorable inside the bilayer core.
Aspartate, glutamate, and serine
Aspartate, glutamate, and serine are acidic or polar and would be unfavorable inside the bilayer core.
Leucine, isoleucine, valine, and phenylalanine
Correct: Nonpolar side chains interact favorably with the hydrophobic fatty acid tails of the bilayer core.
Glutamine, asparagine, and threonine
Glutamine, asparagine, and threonine are polar uncharged residues that do not suit the hydrophobic core.
questions.x: Nonpolar side chains interact favorably with the hydrophobic fatty acid tails of the bilayer core. Trap: Choosing polar residues to satisfy backbone hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: Alanine has a carboxyl pKa of 2.3. At pH 2.3, what is the ratio of the fully protonated form to the zwitterion?
o: 10:1 would occur at a pH one unit below the pKa.
Correct: By Henderson-Hasselbalch, when pH = pKa the protonated and deprotonated forms are present in equal amounts, a 1:1 ratio.
1:10 would occur at a pH one unit above the pKa.
1:100 would occur at a pH two units above the pKa.
questions.x: By Henderson-Hasselbalch, when pH = pKa the protonated and deprotonated forms are present in equal amounts, a 1:1 ratio. Trap: Forgetting pH = pKa gives equal concentrations.

questions.q: Myoglobin's oxygen-binding curve is hyperbolic whereas hemoglobin's is sigmoidal. Which is the best explanation?
o: Myoglobin binds O2 less tightly than hemoglobin
Myoglobin has higher, not lower, O2 affinity than hemoglobin.
Myoglobin is a monomer lacking subunit cooperativity
Correct: Cooperativity requires multiple interacting subunits; hemoglobin's tetramer undergoes T-to-R transitions while myoglobin, a monomer, binds a single O2 independently.
Myoglobin has four heme groups that interact allosterically
Myoglobin has a single heme and therefore cannot interact allosterically.
Hemoglobin lacks a heme group
Hemoglobin contains four heme groups.
questions.x: Cooperativity requires multiple interacting subunits; hemoglobin's tetramer undergoes T-to-R transitions while myoglobin, a monomer, binds a single O2 independently. Trap: Assuming hyperbolic curves mean lower affinity.

questions.q: Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable, yet proteins are stable in water for long periods. Why?
o: The reaction has a positive delta G
Delta G of peptide hydrolysis is negative, not positive.
Water does not contact the peptide bond
Water does contact exposed peptide bonds, so access is not the issue.
The reaction has a high activation energy and is kinetically slow
Correct: Spontaneity (negative delta G) says nothing about rate; the uncatalyzed reaction has a large activation barrier and is kinetically slow.
Proteins are stabilized by a negative entropy of hydrolysis
Entropy increases on cleavage, so it does not stabilize the intact protein.
questions.x: Spontaneity (negative delta G) says nothing about rate; the uncatalyzed reaction has a large activation barrier and is kinetically slow. Trap: Equating thermodynamic spontaneity with rapid reaction.

questions.q: An inhibitor binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex. How does it affect Vmax and apparent Km?
o: Vmax unchanged, Km increases
Vmax unchanged with a higher Km describes competitive inhibition.
Both decrease
Correct: Uncompetitive inhibition removes ES complex, lowering Vmax; it also pulls the equilibrium toward ES, increasing apparent affinity so apparent Km falls.
Vmax decreases, Km unchanged
Vmax decreasing with unchanged Km describes noncompetitive inhibition.
Vmax increases, Km decreases
Vmax cannot increase in the presence of an inhibitor.
questions.x: Uncompetitive inhibition removes ES complex, lowering Vmax; it also pulls the equilibrium toward ES, increasing apparent affinity so apparent Km falls. Trap: Treating all non-competitive-type inhibitors as leaving Km unchanged.

questions.q: A template DNA strand reads 3'-TACGGATTC-5'. What is the mRNA transcribed from it?
o: 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'
Correct: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template, with U replacing T: 3'-TACGGATTC-5' gives 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'.
5'-UACGGAUUC-3'
5'-UACGGAUUC-3' simply copies the template sequence with U in place of T instead of its complement.
3'-AUGCCUAAG-5'
3'-AUGCCUAAG-5' has the correct bases but the wrong polarity.
5'-ATGCCTAAG-3'
5'-ATGCCTAAG-3' contains T instead of U, which is DNA, not RNA.
questions.x: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template, with U replacing T: 3'-TACGGATTC-5' gives 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'. Trap: Writing the complement without reversing polarity or leaving thymine in RNA.

questions.q: The mRNA codon 5'-AUG-3' pairs with which tRNA anticodon?
o: Correct: The anticodon is complementary and antiparallel to the codon: 3'-UAC-5', which written 5' to 3' is 5'-CAU-3'.
5'-UAC-3' is the complement of the codon written without reversing polarity.
3'-GUA-5' is the codon sequence itself read backwards (identical to 5'-AUG-3'), not its complement.
5'-GUA-3' is not complementary to AUG.
questions.x: The anticodon is complementary and antiparallel to the codon: 3'-UAC-5', which written 5' to 3' is 5'-CAU-3'. Trap: Reading the anticodon 5' to 3' as UAC.

questions.q: There are 61 sense codons but fewer than 61 distinct tRNAs. What explains this?
o: tRNAs read two codon positions at once
TRNAs read all three codon positions, not two at once.
Flexible pairing at the third codon position
Correct: Wobble pairing at the third codon position lets one anticodon recognize several codons differing at that base.
Ribosomes read mRNA in both directions
Ribosomes read mRNA only 5' to 3'.
Some codons are read by rRNA instead of tRNA
TRNAs, not rRNA, decode all sense codons.
questions.x: Wobble pairing at the third codon position lets one anticodon recognize several codons differing at that base. Trap: Believing the genetic code is unambiguous per tRNA.

questions.q: A point mutation changes a codon from GAA to GAG, both coding for glutamate. This is
o: missense
Missense would change the amino acid.
nonsense
Nonsense would create a stop codon.
silent
Correct: Because the code is degenerate, GAA and GAG both specify glutamate, so the amino acid is unchanged (a silent mutation).
frameshift
Frameshift is an insertion or deletion not divisible by three, not a substitution.
questions.x: Because the code is degenerate, GAA and GAG both specify glutamate, so the amino acid is unchanged (a silent mutation). Trap: Assuming any base substitution alters the protein.

questions.q: Deletion of three consecutive nucleotides within the coding region would most likely
o: shift the reading frame for all downstream codons
A frameshift requires a deletion that is not a multiple of three.
remove one amino acid while preserving the downstream reading frame
Correct: Three nucleotides equal one codon, so the reading frame is maintained and a single amino acid is lost (or one is changed).
always create a premature stop codon
A premature stop is not guaranteed, since the deleted codon is usually a sense codon.
have no effect on the protein
The protein length changes by one residue, so it is not without effect.
questions.x: Three nucleotides equal one codon, so the reading frame is maintained and a single amino acid is lost (or one is changed). Trap: Assuming all deletions cause frameshifts.

questions.q: A mutation changes the conserved GU at a 5' splice donor site. What is the most likely outcome?
o: Failure of 5' capping
5' capping occurs at the transcript's start and uses different signals.
Abnormal splicing such as exon skipping or intron retention
Correct: The spliceosome recognizes the conserved GU at the 5' donor site; disrupting it produces aberrant mRNA, often with exon skipping or intron retention.
Premature poly-A addition
Polyadenylation uses an AAUAAA signal at the 3' end, not the splice donor.
Loss of the promoter
The promoter lies upstream of the gene and is unaffected by an intronic splice site.
questions.x: The spliceosome recognizes the conserved GU at the 5' donor site; disrupting it produces aberrant mRNA, often with exon skipping or intron retention. Trap: Thinking exons are spliced out and introns are retained.

questions.q: Which function is provided by the 5' cap and poly-A tail of eukaryotic mRNA?
o: Template for reverse transcription
Reverse transcription templating is not a function of the cap or tail.
Signal for splicing of introns
Splicing uses internal consensus sequences, not the cap or tail.
Binding site for RNA polymerase
RNA polymerase binds promoters in DNA, not the mRNA cap.
Protection from exonuclease degradation and enhanced translation
Correct: The cap and poly-A tail protect mRNA from exonucleases and help ribosome recruitment and export, enhancing translation.
questions.x: The cap and poly-A tail protect mRNA from exonucleases and help ribosome recruitment and export, enhancing translation. Trap: Thinking processing elements are encoded in DNA templates.

questions.q: Cells are treated with alpha-amanitin at a concentration that inhibits RNA polymerase II but not I or III. Which is most directly reduced?
o: mRNA synthesis
Correct: Pol II transcribes protein-coding genes, so inhibiting it most directly reduces mRNA synthesis.
Ribosomal RNA (28S) synthesis
28S rRNA is made by Pol I, which is unaffected.
tRNA synthesis
TRNA is made by Pol III, which is unaffected.
All rRNA and tRNA synthesis
RRNA and tRNA are made by Pol I and Pol III, so synthesis continues.
questions.x: Pol II transcribes protein-coding genes, so inhibiting it most directly reduces mRNA synthesis. Trap: Mixing up which polymerase makes which RNA.

questions.q: E. coli is grown with lactose but no glucose. Which describes the lac operon?
o: Repressor remains bound and cAMP is low
A bound repressor would block transcription, and cAMP is high, not low, without glucose.
Repressor binds allolactose and cAMP is low
Allolactose releases the repressor rather than helping it bind, and low cAMP gives little transcription.
Allolactose inactivates the repressor and CAP-cAMP enhances transcription
Correct: Lactose yields allolactose, which inactivates the repressor, and low glucose raises cAMP, which binds CAP and enhances transcription.
Glucose binds CAP to activate transcription
Glucose lowers cAMP and does not bind CAP to activate transcription.
questions.x: Lactose yields allolactose, which inactivates the repressor, and low glucose raises cAMP, which binds CAP and enhances transcription. Trap: Forgetting that cAMP rises when glucose is absent.

questions.q: A mutation in the lac operator prevents repressor binding. What is the likely phenotype in a haploid cell?
o: No expression even with lactose
An operator mutation removes repression, so it cannot block expression.
Expression only when glucose is present
Glucose still reduces CAP-cAMP activation but does not restore repression.
Normal regulation
Regulation is lost, since the repressor can no longer bind.
Constitutive expression of lac genes even without lactose
Correct: Without repressor binding at the operator, RNA polymerase transcribes the lac genes freely, giving constitutive expression.
questions.x: Without repressor binding at the operator, RNA polymerase transcribes the lac genes freely, giving constitutive expression. Trap: Confusing an operator mutation with a mutation that makes a super-repressor.

questions.q: A cell has defective DNA ligase. Which is expected to accumulate?
o: Unwound DNA with no primers
Unwinding and primer synthesis depend on helicase and primase, which are unaffected.
Long leading strand fragments
The leading strand is synthesized continuously and needs no ligation of fragments.
Unjoined Okazaki fragments with nicks in the lagging strand
Correct: Ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments after the RNA primer is replaced with DNA, so without it unjoined fragments accumulate.
RNA primers with no DNA
Primers are replaced by DNA polymerase, which is unaffected.
questions.x: Ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments after the RNA primer is replaced with DNA, so without it unjoined fragments accumulate. Trap: Assigning ligase function to helicase or primase.

questions.q: Telomerase solves which problem?
o: Supercoiling ahead of the replication fork
Supercoiling ahead of the fork is relieved by topoisomerase.
Shortening of linear chromosome ends because the lagging strand cannot be fully replicated
Correct: Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template that extends telomeres, countering shortening of linear chromosome ends.
Mismatch repair after replication
Mismatch repair is a separate pathway.
Separating the two DNA strands
Strand separation is performed by helicase.
questions.x: Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template that extends telomeres, countering shortening of linear chromosome ends. Trap: Forgetting telomerase carries its own RNA template.

questions.q: Which activity of DNA polymerase III allows proofreading?
o: 3' to 5' exonuclease activity
Correct: Pol III's 3' to 5' exonuclease activity removes a mismatched nucleotide just added, which is proofreading.
5' to 3' polymerase activity
5' to 3' polymerase activity adds nucleotides rather than removing errors.
5' to 3' exonuclease activity
5' to 3' exonuclease activity removes RNA primers (Pol I).
Helicase activity
Helicase unwinds the duplex and does not remove mismatches.
questions.x: Pol III's 3' to 5' exonuclease activity removes a mismatched nucleotide just added, which is proofreading. Trap: Confusing proofreading with primer removal.

questions.q: Xeroderma pigmentosum patients are hypersensitive to UV light because they lack
o: base excision repair for uracil
Base excision repair fixes single damaged bases such as uracil, not bulky dimers.
nucleotide excision repair
Correct: UV light causes thymine dimers, which are repaired by nucleotide excision repair; XP patients lack this pathway.
telomere maintenance
Telomere maintenance is unrelated to UV damage repair.
spliceosome function
Spliceosome function is unrelated to UV damage repair.
questions.x: UV light causes thymine dimers, which are repaired by nucleotide excision repair; XP patients lack this pathway. Trap: Mixing up NER and mismatch repair.

questions.q: A eukaryotic mRNA lacks the 5' cap. Which is the most likely effect?
o: Increased splicing
Splicing is a separate process and would not be increased by losing the cap.
No effect
Capping matters for translation and stability, so the effect is not nil.
Premature termination at the poly-A tail
Termination depends on stop codons, not the poly-A tail.
Decreased translation initiation and stability
Correct: The 5' cap recruits initiation factors and the small subunit, which scans to the AUG, and it protects the mRNA, so loss decreases initiation and stability.
questions.x: The 5' cap recruits initiation factors and the small subunit, which scans to the AUG, and it protects the mRNA, so loss decreases initiation and stability. Trap: Applying prokaryotic Shine-Dalgarno logic to eukaryotes.

questions.q: Which catalyzes peptide bond formation on the ribosome?
o: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNAs with amino acids.
The rRNA of the large subunit
Correct: Peptidyl transferase activity resides in the large-subunit rRNA, making the ribosome a ribozyme.
Elongation factor Tu
EF-Tu delivers aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site.
The small subunit proteins
The small subunit proteins help decode mRNA and do not form the peptide bond.
questions.x: Peptidyl transferase activity resides in the large-subunit rRNA, making the ribosome a ribozyme. Trap: Assuming enzymes are always proteins.

questions.q: About how many high-energy phosphate bonds are consumed to add one amino acid to a growing chain?
o: 1 counts only a single step.
2 counts only the charging step.
6 overcounts the steps.
Correct: Charging uses 2 high-energy bonds (ATP to AMP + PPi), delivery uses 1 GTP, and translocation uses 1 GTP: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.
questions.x: Charging uses 2 high-energy bonds (ATP to AMP + PPi), delivery uses 1 GTP, and translocation uses 1 GTP: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Trap: Counting only the two GTP steps and forgetting the ATP spent charging the tRNA.

questions.q: Histone acetylation generally
o: tightens chromatin and decreases transcription
Tightening chromatin and decreasing transcription describes deacetylation.
removes histones from DNA permanently
Histones are not permanently removed by acetylation.
loosens chromatin and increases transcription
Correct: Acetyl groups neutralize lysine's positive charge, weakening histone-DNA binding, loosening chromatin and increasing transcription.
methylates DNA cytosines
Methylating DNA cytosines is a separate process.
questions.x: Acetyl groups neutralize lysine's positive charge, weakening histone-DNA binding, loosening chromatin and increasing transcription. Trap: Reversing acetylation and methylation effects.

questions.q: Methylation of CpG islands in a gene promoter typically results in
o: gene silencing
Correct: Methylated CpG islands recruit proteins that compact chromatin, silencing the gene.
increased transcription
Increased transcription would follow demethylation.
increased mRNA stability
MRNA stability is not affected by promoter methylation.
loss of introns
Introns are unaffected by promoter methylation.
questions.x: Methylated CpG islands recruit proteins that compact chromatin, silencing the gene. Trap: Assuming methylation activates genes.

questions.q: A nascent polypeptide with an N-terminal signal sequence is recognized by SRP. Where does translation continue?
o: In the nucleus
Nuclear proteins are targeted by an NLS, not an SRP signal sequence.
On free cytosolic ribosomes
Free cytosolic ribosomes make cytosolic proteins lacking a signal sequence.
In the mitochondrial matrix
Mitochondrial proteins are imported post-translationally.
On the rough ER, with the protein entering the lumen
Correct: SRP directs the ribosome to the ER translocon, so translation continues on the rough ER with cotranslational import into the lumen.
questions.x: SRP directs the ribosome to the ER translocon, so translation continues on the rough ER with cotranslational import into the lumen. Trap: Confusing SRP-dependent targeting with nuclear localization.

questions.q: In E. coli, translation can begin before transcription of an mRNA is complete because
o: there is no nuclear envelope separating transcription and translation
Correct: Prokaryotes lack a nuclear envelope, so ribosomes can bind the mRNA while it is still being transcribed.
prokaryotic mRNA is spliced
Prokaryotic mRNA is not spliced because it lacks introns.
ribosomes bind the 5' cap
Prokaryotic ribosomes bind a Shine-Dalgarno sequence, not a 5' cap.
prokaryotic mRNA has a poly-A tail
Prokaryotic mRNA lacks a poly-A tail.
questions.x: Prokaryotes lack a nuclear envelope, so ribosomes can bind the mRNA while it is still being transcribed. Trap: Applying eukaryotic processing to bacteria.

questions.q: A coding region (excluding stop codon) is 1,200 nucleotides long. How many amino acids does it encode?
o: 1,200 ignores that codons are triplets.
600 divides by 2 rather than 3.
Correct: Three nucleotides encode one amino acid, so 1,200/3 = 400.
3,600 multiplies rather than divides.
questions.x: Three nucleotides encode one amino acid, so 1,200/3 = 400. Trap: Forgetting that three nucleotides specify each amino acid (the triplet code).

questions.q: Which event of meiosis is responsible for reducing the chromosome number from diploid to haploid?
o: Separation of sister chromatids during anaphase II
Sister chromatid separation in anaphase II leaves ploidy unchanged (haploid to haploid).
Replication of DNA during the S phase preceding meiosis
DNA replication in S phase doubles DNA content and does not alter chromosome number.
Exchange of segments between homologs during prophase I
Crossing over rearranges alleles between homologs without changing chromosome number.
Separation of homologous chromosomes during anaphase I
Correct: In anaphase I each homolog (still two chromatids) moves to an opposite pole, so each daughter cell receives one chromosome of each pair, halving ploidy.
questions.x: In anaphase I each homolog (still two chromatids) moves to an opposite pole, so each daughter cell receives one chromosome of each pair, halving ploidy. Trap: Thinking that sister chromatid separation, the step that resembles mitosis, is what halves ploidy.

questions.q: Crossing over generates new allele combinations on a single chromosome. Between which structures and during which phase does it occur?
o: Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, in prophase I
Correct: Homologs pair (synapsis) in prophase I to form tetrads, and chiasmata mark exchange between non-sister chromatids.
Sister chromatids of the same chromosome, in prophase II
Sister chromatids are genetically identical, so exchange between them creates no new combinations, and prophase II has no paired homologs.
Non-homologous chromosomes, in metaphase I
Non-homologous chromosomes do not pair or exchange segments.
Sister chromatids, in the S phase before meiosis
Homologs are not paired in S phase, and sister-chromatid exchange creates no new allele combinations.
questions.x: Homologs pair (synapsis) in prophase I to form tetrads, and chiasmata mark exchange between non-sister chromatids. Trap: Believing recombination occurs between sister chromatids, which are identical copies.

questions.q: Failure of one homologous pair to separate during meiosis I (and no other errors) is expected to produce which set of gametes from that cell?
o: Four aneuploid gametes: two with n+1 and two with n-1
Correct: Both homologs move to one pole in meiosis I, so both secondary cells are abnormal and all four products are aneuploid (two n+1, two n-1).
Two normal gametes and two aneuploid gametes
Two normal and two aneuploid gametes is the result of nondisjunction in meiosis II, where only one secondary cell is affected.
Four normal haploid gametes
All four gametes normal would need no error at all.
Two n+1 gametes and two normal gametes
N-1 gametes also form, so two n+1 and two normal is incomplete and wrong.
questions.x: Both homologs move to one pole in meiosis I, so both secondary cells are abnormal and all four products are aneuploid (two n+1, two n-1). Trap: Confusing the outcomes of meiosis I and meiosis II nondisjunction.

questions.q: A diploid organism has 2n = 6. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically distinct gametes can it produce through independent assortment?
o: 3 is the haploid number of chromosomes, not the number of combinations.
Correct: Each of the 3 homologous pairs orients independently, so 2^3 = 8 combinations.
6 is the diploid number, not the number of combinations.
64 is 2^6, wrongly using the diploid number as the exponent.
questions.x: Each of the 3 homologous pairs orients independently, so 2^3 = 8 combinations. Trap: Using 2n rather than the number of homolog pairs (n) in the exponent.

questions.q: In a trihybrid cross AaBbCc x AaBbCc with independent assortment and complete dominance, what fraction of offspring have the genotype pattern aa, B_ , cc (homozygous recessive for A and C, at least one dominant B allele)?
o: 1/64 is the probability of aabbcc, treating B_ as 1/4.
9/64 is (3/4)^2 x 1/4, treating two loci as dominant-phenotype classes instead of only B_.
Correct: Multiply independent probabilities: aa = 1/4, B_ = 3/4, cc = 1/4, so 3/64.
1/16 equals 4/64 and does not equal the product 1/4 x 3/4 x 1/4.
questions.x: Multiply independent probabilities: aa = 1/4, B_ = 3/4, cc = 1/4, so 3/64. Trap: Treating the dominant phenotype class (B_) as 1/4 instead of 3/4.

questions.q: A recessive autosomal disorder affects 1 in 10,000 people in a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. About what fraction of the population are carriers?
o: 1 in 50
Correct: q^2 = 0.0001, so q = 0.01 and p is about 0.99; carriers = 2pq = about 0.0198, roughly 1 in 50.
1 in 100 is the allele frequency q, not the carrier frequency.
1 in 5,000 would be q^2/2 and does not follow from the Hardy-Weinberg equation.
1 in 10,000 is q^2, the affected frequency, not the carrier frequency.
questions.x: q^2 = 0.0001, so q = 0.01 and p is about 0.99; carriers = 2pq = about 0.0198, roughly 1 in 50. Trap: Reporting q (allele frequency) instead of 2pq (heterozygote frequency).

questions.q: Which scenario most clearly violates the assumptions needed for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
o: The population is very large
A very large population is a required condition for equilibrium, not a violation.
Individuals preferentially mate with partners of similar phenotype
Correct: Non-random (assortative) mating shifts genotype frequencies away from p^2, 2pq, q^2 even if allele frequencies stay the same.
There is no net mutation at the locus
No net mutation is a required condition for equilibrium, not a violation.
There is no migration into or out of the population
No migration is a required condition for equilibrium, not a violation.
questions.x: Non-random (assortative) mating shifts genotype frequencies away from p^2, 2pq, q^2 even if allele frequencies stay the same. Trap: Mistaking the required conditions for the violations.

questions.q: A small group of birds colonizes an island, and a rare allele that was uncommon on the mainland becomes common among their descendants. This best illustrates
o: the founder effect
Correct: A new population established by a few individuals carries only a sample of the source gene pool, so allele frequencies shift by chance.
gene flow
Gene flow requires ongoing migration between populations, not a one-time colonization.
directional selection
Directional selection requires a fitness difference favoring the allele, which is not described.
the bottleneck effect
A bottleneck is a drastic reduction of an existing population, not colonization of a new site.
questions.x: A new population established by a few individuals carries only a sample of the source gene pool, so allele frequencies shift by chance. Trap: Confusing founder effect (colonization) with bottleneck (population crash).

questions.q: A mother who is a carrier of an X-linked recessive allele and an unaffected father have a child. What is the probability that the child is an affected male?
o: 1/2 is the probability among sons only, not among all children.
1/8 does not match the cross and would halve the answer again.
0 is wrong because sons can inherit the mutant X from the carrier mother.
Correct: Half of children are male (1/2) and half of the sons inherit the mutant X (1/2): 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
questions.x: Half of children are male (1/2) and half of the sons inherit the mutant X (1/2): 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. Trap: Reporting the risk for a son (1/2) when the question asks about a child of unknown sex.

questions.q: A testcross of a dihybrid yields 440 parental-type and 60 recombinant offspring. What is the map distance between the two genes?
o: 6 map units (cM)
6 map units halves the correct value.
14 map units (cM)
14 map units results from dividing recombinants by parental types (60/440).
12 map units (cM)
Correct: Recombination frequency = 60/500 = 12 percent = 12 cM.
88 map units (cM)
88 map units is the parental percentage, not the recombinant percentage.
questions.x: Recombination frequency = 60/500 = 12 percent = 12 cM. Trap: Dividing recombinants by parentals rather than by total offspring.

questions.q: Two genes are 50 cM apart on the same chromosome. How are their alleles expected to assort?
o: As if they were completely linked
Complete linkage would mean 0 percent recombination.
As if they were unlinked
Correct: A recombination frequency of 50 percent is the maximum and matches independent assortment, so the genes assort as if unlinked.
With 100 percent recombination
100 percent recombination is impossible because multiple crossovers cancel, capping frequency at 50 percent.
With no crossovers between them
No crossovers between them would also mean complete linkage.
questions.x: A recombination frequency of 50 percent is the maximum and matches independent assortment, so the genes assort as if unlinked. Trap: Thinking tightly linked genes cannot be 50 cM apart or that recombination can exceed 50 percent.

questions.q: A parent has genotype AB/ab and the genes show 20 percent recombination. What fraction of its gametes are Ab?
o: 20 percent
20 percent is the total of both recombinant types, not of Ab alone.
40 percent
40 percent is the frequency of each parental type (AB or ab), not of Ab.
10 percent
Correct: Recombinant gametes (Ab and aB) total 20 percent and are formed equally, so each is 10 percent.
5 percent
5 percent halves the correct value again.
questions.x: Recombinant gametes (Ab and aB) total 20 percent and are formed equally, so each is 10 percent. Trap: Assigning the total recombination frequency to one recombinant class.

questions.q: Crossing red-flowered snapdragons with white-flowered ones gives pink F1 plants (incomplete dominance). What is the expected phenotypic ratio in the F2?
o: 3 red : 1 white
3 red : 1 white applies to complete dominance.
1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
Correct: With incomplete dominance heterozygotes are intermediate, so the 1:2:1 genotype ratio of the F2 is also the phenotype ratio (1 red : 2 pink : 1 white).
1 pink : 1 white
1 pink : 1 white would come from a testcross-like backcross, not an F1 x F1 cross.
9:3:3:1 is a dihybrid ratio, but only one gene is involved here.
questions.x: With incomplete dominance heterozygotes are intermediate, so the 1:2:1 genotype ratio of the F2 is also the phenotype ratio (1 red : 2 pink : 1 white). Trap: Applying a complete-dominance 3:1 ratio to an incomplete-dominance trait.

questions.q: A mother with blood type A (genotype IAi) and a father with blood type B (genotype IBi) have a child. What is the probability that the child has type O?
o: 0 ignores that both parents carry the recessive i allele.
Correct: Type O requires genotype ii; each heterozygous parent passes i with probability 1/2, so 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
1/2 overstates the chance, since both parents must pass i.
3/4 is the probability of a non-O child, not of type O.
questions.x: Type O requires genotype ii; each heterozygous parent passes i with probability 1/2, so 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. Trap: Forgetting that type A and B parents can be heterozygous and carry i.

questions.q: A person carries a dominant disease allele but shows no signs of the disease, while a sibling with the same allele is severely affected. The first person's lack of phenotype is an example of
o: variable expressivity
Variable expressivity concerns differing severity among individuals who all show the trait, which does not describe a person with no signs.
codominance
Codominance describes two alleles both expressed in a heterozygote, not a missing phenotype.
epistasis
Epistasis describes one gene masking another, which is not given here.
incomplete penetrance
Correct: Penetrance is the fraction of individuals with a genotype who show any phenotype; carrying the allele with no signs reflects incomplete (reduced) penetrance.
questions.x: Penetrance is the fraction of individuals with a genotype who show any phenotype; carrying the allele with no signs reflects incomplete (reduced) penetrance. Trap: Mixing up penetrance (whether) and expressivity (how much).

questions.q: A father has a disease caused by a mutation in mitochondrial DNA. What proportion of his children is expected to inherit the mutation?
o: None of them
Correct: Mitochondria are inherited essentially from the egg cytoplasm, so mitochondrial mutations pass only through the mother and a father transmits none.
All of his sons
All his sons would inherit it only with paternal transmission, but sperm mitochondria do not contribute.
All of his daughters
All his daughters would inherit it only with paternal transmission, but sperm mitochondria do not contribute.
Half of his children
Half of his children would inherit it only with Mendelian paternal transmission, which does not apply to mtDNA.
questions.x: Mitochondria are inherited essentially from the egg cytoplasm, so mitochondrial mutations pass only through the mother and a father transmits none. Trap: Treating mitochondrial inheritance as sex-linked through the father.

questions.q: Loss of functional p53 in a cell with DNA damage would most likely result in
o: progression through the G1/S checkpoint with damaged DNA
Correct: p53 normally halts the cycle (via p21) or triggers apoptosis after damage; without it, damaged cells pass the G1/S checkpoint and keep dividing.
arrest in G2 with no possibility of progression
Loss of p53 removes arrest, so cells would not stay permanently arrested in G2.
accelerated apoptosis
Apoptosis would be reduced, not accelerated, without p53.
lengthening of telomeres
Telomere lengthening requires telomerase and is not directly caused by p53 loss.
questions.x: p53 normally halts the cycle (via p21) or triggers apoptosis after damage; without it, damaged cells pass the G1/S checkpoint and keep dividing. Trap: Thinking p53 promotes proliferation, as an oncogene would.

questions.q: A mutation that locks the Ras protein in its active GTP-bound state is best described as
o: a loss-of-function mutation of a tumor suppressor
Tumor suppressors typically require loss of both alleles, and Ras is not a tumor suppressor.
a silent mutation
The mutation changes protein function, so it is not silent.
a gain-of-function mutation of a proto-oncogene
Correct: Constitutively active Ras drives proliferation; a single mutated allele is enough, so this is a gain-of-function mutation of a proto-oncogene.
a frameshift mutation in a DNA repair gene
The effect is a hyperactive signaling protein, not a frameshift in a repair gene.
questions.x: Constitutively active Ras drives proliferation; a single mutated allele is enough, so this is a gain-of-function mutation of a proto-oncogene. Trap: Treating oncogene mutations as recessive loss-of-function events.

questions.q: Colchicine prevents microtubule polymerization. Dividing cells treated with it would be arrested at which point?
o: Telophase, because the nuclear envelope cannot reform
Telophase occurs after chromosome separation, which the drug prevents from happening.
Metaphase, because the spindle cannot form and attach to chromosomes
Correct: Without a spindle, chromosomes cannot align or be pulled apart, so cells halt before anaphase (in practice at prometaphase/metaphase, used for karyotyping).
S phase, because DNA cannot replicate
S phase replication does not depend on microtubules.
Prophase, because chromosomes cannot condense
Chromosome condensation in prophase occurs without a spindle.
questions.x: Without a spindle, chromosomes cannot align or be pulled apart, so cells halt before anaphase (in practice at prometaphase/metaphase, used for karyotyping). Trap: Choosing an interphase or later stage that does not depend on microtubules.

questions.q: A diploid G1 cell contains an amount of DNA X. How much DNA does a secondary spermatocyte contain?
o: 2X
2X is the DNA content of the primary spermatocyte.
X/2 is reached only after meiosis II (spermatid).
4X
4X would require another round of replication.
X
Correct: After replication the cell has 2X; meiosis I halves chromosome number but each chromosome still has two chromatids, so a secondary spermatocyte has X.
questions.x: After replication the cell has 2X; meiosis I halves chromosome number but each chromosome still has two chromatids, so a secondary spermatocyte has X. Trap: Thinking meiosis I reduces DNA content to haploid (X/2).

questions.q: At which stage are primary oocytes arrested from fetal life until puberty?
o: Metaphase II
Metaphase II arrest applies to the secondary oocyte after ovulation.
Anaphase I
Anaphase I is not an arrest point.
G1 of interphase
G1 of interphase is not an arrest point for primary oocytes.
Prophase I
Correct: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I from before birth until ovulation; the secondary oocyte then arrests in metaphase II until fertilization.
questions.x: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I from before birth until ovulation; the secondary oocyte then arrests in metaphase II until fertilization. Trap: Swapping the prophase I arrest with the metaphase II arrest.

questions.q: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) could arise from which event?
o: Fertilization by a sperm lacking sex chromosomes
A sperm with no sex chromosome plus an X egg gives 45,X (Turner syndrome).
Loss of one X in an early embryonic cell
Losing an X in an early embryonic cell gives mosaicism rather than 47,XXY.
Fertilization of an XX egg by a Y-bearing sperm
