Correct: Nondisjunction in the mother can give an XX egg, and a Y-bearing sperm then produces 47,XXY.
Fertilization of a normal egg by two sperm
Fertilization by two sperm (dispermy) gives triploidy, not 47,XXY.
questions.x: Nondisjunction in the mother can give an XX egg, and a Y-bearing sperm then produces 47,XXY. Trap: Remembering only paternal nondisjunction as the cause.

questions.q: Calico coat color in cats occurs almost exclusively in females because
o: the Y chromosome carries a color-suppressing gene
Males normally have one X and a Y that does not suppress color.
males inactivate their only X chromosome
Males do not inactivate their only X, since that would be lethal.
random X inactivation in each cell produces patches expressing different X-linked alleles
Correct: Female cells randomly silence one X early in development, and descendant cells keep that choice, creating mosaic patches expressing different X-linked color alleles.
each cell inactivates the same X in every patch
If the same X were silenced everywhere there would be no mosaic patches.
questions.x: Female cells randomly silence one X early in development, and descendant cells keep that choice, creating mosaic patches expressing different X-linked color alleles. Trap: Assuming X inactivation always silences the same (paternal) X.

questions.q: A bacteriophage packages a fragment of host bacterial DNA and delivers it to a second bacterium. This process is
o: transformation
Transformation is uptake of free DNA from the environment, with no phage.
transduction
Correct: Phage-mediated transfer of bacterial DNA to another bacterium is transduction.
conjugation
Conjugation requires cell-to-cell contact via a pilus.
binary fission
Binary fission is asexual division, not DNA transfer.
questions.x: Phage-mediated transfer of bacterial DNA to another bacterium is transduction. Trap: Confusing the three horizontal gene transfer mechanisms.

questions.q: An Hfr bacterium conjugates with an F- cell. What is the usual result?
o: The recipient becomes F+
The recipient does not become F+ because the F factor rarely reaches it.
The recipient becomes Hfr
The recipient does not become Hfr because the integrated F factor is not transferred.
The donor loses its entire chromosome
The donor retains its chromosome, since only a copy is transferred.
The recipient remains F- but may receive part of the donor chromosome

Correct: In Hfr cells the F factor is integrated in the chromosome and transferred last, so mating is usually interrupted before it enters and the recipient stays F- with part of the donor chromosome.
questions.x: In Hfr cells the F factor is integrated in the chromosome and transferred last, so mating is usually interrupted before it enters and the recipient stays F- with part of the donor chromosome. Trap: Treating Hfr like an F+ cell that transfers the F plasmid.

questions.q: Heterozygous carriers of the sickle cell allele are more resistant to severe malaria. Which outcome does this best explain?
o: Maintenance of the HbS allele in malaria-endemic regions
Correct: Heterozygote advantage maintains both alleles at intermediate frequency, since homozygotes for either allele have lower fitness, explaining persistence of HbS in malaria regions.
Fixation of the HbS allele in all populations
Fixation fails because homozygous sickle cell disease has reduced fitness.
Rapid elimination of the HbS allele
Rapid elimination fails because heterozygotes have higher fitness.
Evolution by drift alone
Drift alone does not explain it, since the allele persists because of selection.
questions.x: Heterozygote advantage maintains both alleles at intermediate frequency, since homozygotes for either allele have lower fitness, explaining persistence of HbS in malaria regions. Trap: Assuming deleterious alleles must be eliminated.

questions.q: Two closely related frog species breed at different times of the year and therefore rarely interbreed. This is an example of
o: a postzygotic barrier
Postzygotic barriers act after fertilization, which is not described.
hybrid sterility
Hybrid sterility is a postzygotic barrier, and no hybrids are mentioned.
geographic (allopatric) isolation
Geographic isolation involves physical separation of ranges, whereas these frogs differ in breeding season.
a prezygotic barrier
Correct: Temporal isolation prevents mating or fertilization before a zygote forms, which is a prezygotic barrier.
questions.x: Temporal isolation prevents mating or fertilization before a zygote forms, which is a prezygotic barrier. Trap: Misclassifying temporal isolation as postzygotic.

questions.q: A mule (horse 2n = 64, donkey 2n = 62) is usually sterile. What is the best explanation?
o: Its 63 chromosomes cannot pair normally during meiosis
Correct: Horse and donkey chromosomes differ in number and structure, so the mule's 63 chromosomes cannot synapse properly in meiosis and viable gametes rarely form.
It lacks an X chromosome
Mules have both sex chromosomes and are not lacking an X.
It is triploid
Mules are diploid hybrids, not triploid.
Its mitochondria cannot divide
Mitochondrial division is not the cause of sterility.
questions.x: Horse and donkey chromosomes differ in number and structure, so the mule's 63 chromosomes cannot synapse properly in meiosis and viable gametes rarely form. Trap: Believing sterility means the hybrid lacks a sex chromosome or is triploid rather than failing to pair homologs in meiosis.

questions.q: According to Hamilton's rule, an altruistic act is favored when rB > C. If the act costs the actor 3 units of fitness and benefits a full sibling (r = 0.5), what benefit is needed for the act to be favored?
o: More than 1.5 units
1.5 multiplies the cost by r instead of dividing by r.
More than 3 units
3 ignores relatedness (it would be correct only for r = 1).
More than 6 units
Correct: 0.5 x B > 3 requires B > 6.
More than 12 units
12 divides by r twice or otherwise overshoots.
questions.x: 0.5 x B > 3 requires B > 6. Trap: Ignoring relatedness (r) when applying Hamilton's rule.

questions.q: The forelimbs of a bat and of a human have similar bone arrangements but different functions. These structures are
o: homologous
Correct: Similar structures inherited from a shared ancestor are homologous, even when used for different functions.
analogous
Analogous structures share function but not ancestry (as bird versus insect wings), which is not true of bat and human limbs.
vestigial
Vestigial structures are reduced and functionless, not functional limbs.
convergent adaptations
Convergent adaptations would share function without shared bone plan, but these share ancestry.
questions.x: Similar structures inherited from a shared ancestor are homologous, even when used for different functions. Trap: Equating similar function with common ancestry.

questions.q: In a population of 500 at equilibrium, 45 individuals show a recessive trait. About how many are heterozygous carriers?
o: 90 is double the number of recessive homozygotes (2 x 45), not the carrier count.
105 does not follow from the allele frequencies (it would be 0.21 x 500).
300 (0.6 x 500) does not correspond to p, q, or 2pq for these frequencies.
questions.x: q^2 = 45/500 = 0.09, so q = 0.3, p = 0.7, and 2pq = 0.42; 0.42 x 500 = 210. Trap: Using q^2 or q instead of 2pq to count heterozygotes.

questions.q: A purple-flowered plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a white-flowered (recessive) plant and all progeny are purple. The unknown plant is most likely
o: heterozygous
A heterozygote gives a 1:1 purple:white ratio, not all purple.
homozygous dominant
Correct: A heterozygote would produce about half white offspring in a testcross, so all-purple progeny point to a homozygous dominant parent.
homozygous recessive
A homozygous recessive plant crossed with white would give all white.
codominant
Codominance would not give all purple offspring from a purple and white cross.
questions.x: A heterozygote would produce about half white offspring in a testcross, so all-purple progeny point to a homozygous dominant parent. Trap: Not applying the testcross logic that heterozygotes give recessive progeny.

questions.q: In Labrador retrievers, B (black) is dominant to b (brown), but ee prevents pigment deposition, giving yellow regardless of B genotype. A BbEe x BbEe cross yields what phenotypic ratio?
o: 9 black : 3 brown : 3 yellow : 1 other
The 9:3:3:1 split does not combine the ee classes, which both look yellow.
12 black : 3 brown : 1 yellow
12:3:1 describes dominant epistasis.
9 black : 3 brown : 4 yellow
Correct: B_E_ gives 9 black, bbE_ gives 3 brown, and all ee (3 + 1) give 4 yellow, a 9:3:4 recessive epistasis ratio.
9 black : 7 yellow
9:7 describes complementary gene action.
questions.x: B_E_ gives 9 black, bbE_ gives 3 brown, and all ee (3 + 1) give 4 yellow, a 9:3:4 recessive epistasis ratio. Trap: Applying the plain 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio when one gene masks another.

questions.q: A colorblind man (X-linked recessive) and a woman with normal vision whose father was colorblind have a daughter. What is the probability that the daughter is colorblind?
o: 0 would ignore the mother's carrier status.
Correct: The woman must be a carrier; the daughter always gets her father's affected X and gets the mother's affected X with probability 1/2.
1/4 would halve the correct value, as if the father contributed an affected X only half the time.
1 would require a homozygous affected mother.
questions.x: The woman must be a carrier; the daughter always gets her father's affected X and gets the mother's affected X with probability 1/2. Trap: Forgetting that a daughter always inherits her father's X.

questions.q: Two unaffected parents have a child with an autosomal recessive disease. What is the probability that an unaffected sibling is a carrier?
o: 1/2 ignores that the aa outcome is excluded from the denominator.
1/4 is the chance of an affected child, not of a carrier.
1 would mean all unaffected siblings are carriers, which ignores AA.
Correct: Unaffected offspring are AA (1/4) or Aa (2/4); carrier probability = (2/4)/(3/4) = 2/3.
questions.x: Unaffected offspring are AA (1/4) or Aa (2/4); carrier probability = (2/4)/(3/4) = 2/3. Trap: Failing to remove the affected class from the denominator.

questions.q: The Philadelphia chromosome seen in chronic myelogenous leukemia results from
o: trisomy of chromosome 21
Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome.
a deletion on chromosome 5
A chromosome 5 deletion causes cri-du-chat.
a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22
Correct: The t(9;22) reciprocal translocation creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity.
inactivation of one X chromosome
X inactivation is a normal process in females and not a cause of CML.
questions.x: The t(9;22) reciprocal translocation creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity. Trap: Confusing translocations with aneuploidies.

questions.q: The risk of having a child with Down syndrome increases with maternal age. Which factor best explains this?
o: Sperm quality declines with age
Sperm quality is not the cause of a maternal-age effect.
Mitochondrial DNA mutations accumulate in the egg
Accumulated mitochondrial mutations are not the mechanism of trisomy 21.
X inactivation becomes incomplete
X inactivation changes are not the mechanism of trisomy 21.
Oocytes remain arrested in prophase I for decades
Correct: Prolonged arrest of oocytes in prophase I raises the chance of chromosome segregation errors when meiosis resumes decades later.
questions.x: Prolonged arrest of oocytes in prophase I raises the chance of chromosome segregation errors when meiosis resumes decades later. Trap: Blaming paternal factors for a maternal-age effect.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes anaphase I of meiosis?
o: Homologous chromosomes separate, with each chromosome still composed of two sister chromatids
Correct: Anaphase I segregates homologs, each still composed of two sister chromatids; sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
Sister chromatid separation occurs in anaphase II (and mitosis), not anaphase I.
Chromosomes align as pairs at the metaphase plate
Aligned pairs at the plate describe metaphase I.
Nuclear envelopes reform around four haploid nuclei
Nuclear envelopes reforming around four haploid nuclei describe the end of meiosis II (telophase II).
questions.x: Anaphase I segregates homologs, each still composed of two sister chromatids; sister chromatids separate in anaphase II. Trap: Confusing which structures separate in anaphase I versus anaphase II.

questions.q: Two heterozygous carriers of an autosomal recessive disease have three children. What is the probability that none of the three is affected?
o: 9/16 is (3/4)^2, the answer for two children.
3/4 is the probability for a single child.
1/64 is the probability that all three are affected.
Correct: Each child is unaffected with probability 3/4, so (3/4)^3 = 27/64.
questions.x: Each child is unaffected with probability 3/4, so (3/4)^3 = 27/64. Trap: Using the single-child probability or the wrong number of children.

questions.q: Compared with isolated populations, populations that exchange migrants (gene flow) will tend to
o: diverge genetically faster
Divergence is favored by isolation, not gene flow.
experience more mutation
Gene flow does not raise the mutation rate.
become genetically more similar
Correct: Migration moves alleles between populations and homogenizes allele frequencies, so they become more similar.
speciate more rapidly
Speciation is favored by isolation, whereas gene flow counteracts it.
questions.x: Migration moves alleles between populations and homogenizes allele frequencies, so they become more similar. Trap: Confusing gene flow, which homogenizes, with drift, which diverges.

questions.q: A reaction has a positive standard free energy change, yet it proceeds spontaneously in the cell. Which statement best explains this?
o: The enzyme lowers the standard free energy change
Enzymes change the rate, not the standard free energy change.
The cell temperature changes the sign of delta G0'
Temperature changes in cells are small and cannot flip the sign of delta G0'.
Cellular conditions equal standard conditions
Cells are not at standard 1 M concentrations, so actual delta G differs from delta G0'.
The reaction quotient Q is low enough that the actual delta G is negative
Correct: delta G = delta G0' + RT ln Q; a low Q (products kept scarce) can make the actual delta G negative even when delta G0' is positive.
questions.x: delta G = delta G0' + RT ln Q; a low Q (products kept scarce) can make the actual delta G negative even when delta G0' is positive. Trap: Equating standard and actual free energy change.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of ATP has delta G0' = -30.5 kJ/mol. It is coupled to a reaction with delta G0' = +20 kJ/mol. What is the net delta G0'?
o: +50.5 kJ/mol
+50.5 comes from subtracting the ATP term as if it were positive (30.5 + 20).
-50.5 kJ/mol
-50.5 adds the magnitudes (30.5 + 20) and gives them the negative sign.
-10.5 kJ/mol
Correct: Free energy changes of coupled reactions add: -30.5 + 20 = -10.5 kJ/mol, so the coupled process is favorable.
+10.5 kJ/mol
+10.5 has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign.
questions.x: Free energy changes of coupled reactions add: -30.5 + 20 = -10.5 kJ/mol, so the coupled process is favorable. Trap: Sign errors when summing free energy changes.

questions.q: What is the net ATP produced by substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis per glucose?
o: 4 is the gross yield before subtracting the 2 ATP invested.
1 is not a result of the pathway.
36 is the approximate aerobic yield of complete glucose oxidation, not glycolysis alone.
Correct: Glycolysis invests 2 ATP and produces 4 by substrate-level phosphorylation, for a net of 2.
questions.x: Glycolysis invests 2 ATP and produces 4 by substrate-level phosphorylation, for a net of 2. Trap: Reporting gross rather than net ATP.

questions.q: High cytosolic citrate would be expected to
o: inhibit phosphofructokinase-1
Correct: Citrate signals abundant energy and biosynthetic precursors and inhibits PFK-1, the main regulated step of glycolysis.
activate phosphofructokinase-1
Activating PFK-1 would increase glycolysis despite high energy supply, which is the opposite of the signal.
activate pyruvate kinase
Pyruvate kinase is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, not by citrate.
directly inhibit hexokinase
Hexokinase is inhibited by its product glucose-6-phosphate, not directly by citrate.
questions.x: Citrate signals abundant energy and biosynthetic precursors and inhibits PFK-1, the main regulated step of glycolysis. Trap: Reversing the direction of regulation.

questions.q: In anaerobic muscle, conversion of pyruvate to lactate is important primarily because it
o: regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue
Correct: Lactate dehydrogenase oxidizes NADH to NAD+, sustaining glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and therefore glycolysis when oxygen is limiting.
produces additional ATP
The LDH reaction itself makes no ATP.
generates glucose for the brain
Glucose for the brain is made by the liver, not by this step.
produces NADH
NADH is consumed by the LDH reaction, not produced.
questions.x: Lactate dehydrogenase oxidizes NADH to NAD+, sustaining glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and therefore glycolysis when oxygen is limiting. Trap: Thinking the lactate step generates ATP.

questions.q: A thiamine-deficient patient develops lactic acidosis. This is best explained by impaired
o: pyruvate dehydrogenase, which requires thiamine pyrophosphate
Correct: PDH requires thiamine pyrophosphate; reduced PDH activity diverts pyruvate to lactate, causing lactic acidosis.
glycolysis, which requires thiamine
Glycolysis does not require thiamine.
complex IV of the electron transport chain
Complex IV is not thiamine dependent.
lactate dehydrogenase, which uses thiamine
LDH uses NADH, not thiamine.
questions.x: PDH requires thiamine pyrophosphate; reduced PDH activity diverts pyruvate to lactate, causing lactic acidosis. Trap: Not recalling cofactors of PDH (thiamine, lipoate, FAD, NAD+, CoA).

questions.q: How many NADH are produced by the citric acid cycle itself (not counting PDH) per molecule of glucose?
o: Correct: Each acetyl-CoA yields 3 NADH in the cycle, and one glucose gives 2 acetyl-CoA: 3 x 2 = 6.
3 is the yield per turn, not per glucose.
8 adds NADH from other steps such as PDH to the cycle total.
10 adds NADH from other pathways such as glycolysis and PDH.
questions.x: Each acetyl-CoA yields 3 NADH in the cycle, and one glucose gives 2 acetyl-CoA: 3 x 2 = 6. Trap: Counting a single turn instead of two per glucose.

questions.q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol is a protonophore that carries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Which effect is expected?
o: Decreased oxygen consumption and increased ATP synthesis
Oxygen use rises, not falls, and ATP synthesis falls rather than rises.
Increased oxygen consumption, decreased ATP synthesis, and increased heat
Correct: Dissipating the gradient removes back-pressure so the chain runs faster and consumes more O2, but energy is released as heat rather than captured in ATP.
Blocked electron flow at complex IV
The electron transport chain is not blocked at complex IV; DNP acts on the gradient.
Increased proton gradient
DNP collapses the proton gradient rather than increasing it.
questions.x: Dissipating the gradient removes back-pressure so the chain runs faster and consumes more O2, but energy is released as heat rather than captured in ATP. Trap: Thinking a dissipated gradient slows oxygen consumption.

questions.q: Cyanide binds cytochrome oxidase (complex IV). Which immediate effect is expected?
o: Complex I becomes more oxidized
Complex I becomes more reduced, not more oxidized, because electrons back up behind the block.
Electron carriers upstream become more reduced and ATP synthesis falls
Correct: Cyanide blocks electron transfer to oxygen, so upstream carriers remain reduced and the proton gradient and ATP synthesis collapse.
ATP synthesis increases
ATP synthesis falls rather than increases.
Oxygen consumption increases
Oxygen consumption falls rather than rises, since oxygen is no longer reduced.
questions.x: Cyanide blocks electron transfer to oxygen, so upstream carriers remain reduced and the proton gradient and ATP synthesis collapse. Trap: Thinking blocking the last step oxidizes upstream carriers.

questions.q: Oxidation of FADH2 yields less ATP than oxidation of NADH primarily because FADH2
o: has lower reduction potential than O2
FADH2 does pass electrons through the chain to oxygen, so its reduction potential relative to O2 is not the reason.
donates electrons to complex IV directly
FADH2 feeds complex II, not complex IV directly.
donates electrons at complex II, bypassing complex I proton pumping
Correct: FADH2 donates electrons at complex II, which does not pump protons, so fewer protons are pumped per electron pair and less ATP is made.
is only found in the cytosol
FADH2 in this pathway is found in the mitochondrial inner membrane/matrix, not only in the cytosol.
questions.x: FADH2 donates electrons at complex II, which does not pump protons, so fewer protons are pumped per electron pair and less ATP is made. Trap: Assuming both carriers yield the same ATP.

questions.q: Muscle glycogen cannot be used to raise blood glucose because muscle cells lack
o: glycogen phosphorylase
Muscle has glycogen phosphorylase and uses it to break down glycogen.
glucose-6-phosphatase
Correct: Without glucose-6-phosphatase, glucose-6-phosphate stays trapped in the muscle cell and enters glycolysis instead of being released into blood.
hexokinase
Muscle has hexokinase to phosphorylate glucose.
glycogen synthase
Muscle has glycogen synthase and makes glycogen.
questions.x: Without glucose-6-phosphatase, glucose-6-phosphate stays trapped in the muscle cell and enters glycolysis instead of being released into blood. Trap: Assuming muscle lacks phosphorylase or hexokinase because it does not export glucose, rather than lacking glucose-6-phosphatase.

questions.q: Which enzyme is unique to gluconeogenesis (not used in glycolysis)?
o: Phosphofructokinase-1
Phosphofructokinase-1 is a glycolytic irreversible enzyme.
Pyruvate kinase
Pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic irreversible enzyme.
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
Correct: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase bypasses the PFK-1 step and is one of the enzymes unique to gluconeogenesis.
Phosphoglycerate kinase
Phosphoglycerate kinase catalyzes a reversible step used in both pathways.
questions.x: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase bypasses the PFK-1 step and is one of the enzymes unique to gluconeogenesis. Trap: Choosing a glycolytic enzyme because the question mentions a glucose-pathway bypass.

questions.q: Complete beta-oxidation of one molecule of palmitic acid (16 carbons) yields how many acetyl-CoA?
o: 7 is the number of cycles, not the number of acetyl-CoA.
Correct: Each beta-oxidation cycle removes two carbons as acetyl-CoA; 7 cycles produce 8 acetyl-CoA because the last cycle cleaves a 4-carbon chain into two.
16 is the number of carbons, not the number of 2-carbon units.
14 does not match 2-carbon units (it would be the carbons released after 7 cycles).
questions.x: Each beta-oxidation cycle removes two carbons as acetyl-CoA; 7 cycles produce 8 acetyl-CoA because the last cycle cleaves a 4-carbon chain into two. Trap: Confusing number of cycles with number of acetyl-CoA.

questions.q: Malonyl-CoA inhibits which enzyme, preventing simultaneous fatty acid synthesis and oxidation?
o: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase produces malonyl-CoA rather than being the inhibited target.
Carnitine acyltransferase I (CPT-I)
Correct: Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, blocking entry of fatty acyl groups into mitochondria while synthesis is active.
Hormone-sensitive lipase
Hormone-sensitive lipase mobilizes stored fat and is regulated by hormones.
Fatty acid synthase
Fatty acid synthase uses malonyl-CoA as a substrate.
questions.x: Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, blocking entry of fatty acyl groups into mitochondria while synthesis is active. Trap: Reversing producer and inhibited enzyme.

questions.q: During prolonged fasting, ketone bodies are
o: synthesized by erythrocytes
Erythrocytes lack mitochondria and cannot make ketone bodies.
used as fuel by the liver
The liver cannot use ketones as fuel.
synthesized by the liver and used as fuel by the brain and muscle
Correct: The liver makes ketone bodies from acetyl-CoA but lacks the enzyme to use them, so the brain and muscle use them as fuel.
synthesized from glucose
Ketone bodies come from fatty acid-derived acetyl-CoA, not from glucose.
questions.x: The liver makes ketone bodies from acetyl-CoA but lacks the enzyme to use them, so the brain and muscle use them as fuel. Trap: Assuming the liver, which produces ketones, also burns them.

questions.q: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causes hemolysis during oxidative stress because red cells cannot
o: generate ATP by glycolysis
Glycolysis still works and supplies ATP in G6PD deficiency.
bind oxygen
Hemoglobin still binds oxygen.
synthesize 2,3-BPG
2,3-BPG production is not the issue.
regenerate NADPH to maintain reduced glutathione
Correct: The pentose phosphate pathway is the main NADPH source in erythrocytes, and NADPH keeps glutathione reduced against oxidative stress.
questions.x: The pentose phosphate pathway is the main NADPH source in erythrocytes, and NADPH keeps glutathione reduced against oxidative stress. Trap: Attributing the problem to ATP production.

questions.q: In the fed state after a carbohydrate meal, insulin
o: increases hepatic gluconeogenesis
Gluconeogenesis is stimulated by glucagon and fasting, not insulin.
stimulates glycogenolysis
Glycogenolysis is stimulated by glucagon and epinephrine, not insulin.
increases glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue via GLUT4
Correct: Insulin is anabolic: it promotes GLUT4 translocation to the membrane, glucose uptake in muscle and fat, and glycogen and fat synthesis.
increases ketogenesis
Ketogenesis is a fasting-state process suppressed by insulin.
questions.x: Insulin is anabolic: it promotes GLUT4 translocation to the membrane, glucose uptake in muscle and fat, and glycogen and fat synthesis. Trap: Mixing the effects of insulin and glucagon.

questions.q: Which description of the Cori cycle is correct?
o: Lactate from liver goes to muscle for oxidation
This reverses the organs, since lactate comes from muscle to the liver.
Glucose is converted to fat in adipose
Glucose conversion to fat in adipose is lipogenesis, not the Cori cycle.
Ketones are converted to glucose in the liver
Ketones are not converted to glucose in the liver.
Lactate from muscle is converted to glucose in the liver and returned to muscle
Correct: The Cori cycle sends muscle lactate to the liver, which converts it to glucose and returns it to muscle, transferring the metabolic cost of gluconeogenesis to the liver.
questions.x: The Cori cycle sends muscle lactate to the liver, which converts it to glucose and returns it to muscle, transferring the metabolic cost of gluconeogenesis to the liver. Trap: Thinking lactate travels from liver to muscle, reversing which organ makes lactate and which makes glucose.

questions.q: Transamination reactions require which cofactor and transfer the amino group to which acceptor?
o: Thiamine pyrophosphate; pyruvate
Thiamine pyrophosphate is for decarboxylations, and pyruvate is not the standard acceptor.
Pyridoxal phosphate; alpha-ketoglutarate
Correct: Aminotransferases use pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) and typically move amino groups to alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate.
Biotin; oxaloacetate
Biotin is a carboxylation cofactor, not used in transamination.
NAD+ only; glutamate
NAD+ is used in oxidative deamination, and glutamate is the product rather than the acceptor.
questions.x: Aminotransferases use pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) and typically move amino groups to alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate. Trap: Mixing up which vitamin-derived cofactor serves transamination versus decarboxylation or carboxylation.

questions.q: Which reaction is an example of substrate-level phosphorylation?
o: PEP to pyruvate catalyzed by pyruvate kinase
Correct: PEP donates its phosphate directly to ADP via pyruvate kinase, without needing the proton gradient.
NADH oxidation by complex I
NADH oxidation by complex I is part of the electron transport chain.
ATP synthesis by ATP synthase
ATP synthase makes ATP by chemiosmosis, which is oxidative phosphorylation.
FADH2 oxidation by complex II
FADH2 oxidation by complex II is part of the electron transport chain.
questions.x: PEP donates its phosphate directly to ADP via pyruvate kinase, without needing the proton gradient. Trap: Mistaking oxidative phosphorylation for substrate-level.

questions.q: A person oxidizing predominantly fat has a respiratory quotient (CO2 produced / O2 consumed) of about
o: Correct: Fat has few oxygens, so oxidation consumes more O2 per CO2 produced, giving an RQ of about 0.7.
1.0 is the RQ for carbohydrate oxidation.
1.3 is seen in net lipogenesis, not fat oxidation.
0.5 is below the range seen physiologically.
questions.x: Fat has few oxygens, so oxidation consumes more O2 per CO2 produced, giving an RQ of about 0.7. Trap: Associating an RQ of 1.0 with fat, when that value belongs to carbohydrate oxidation.

questions.q: NADH has E0' = -0.32 V and O2/H2O has E0' = +0.82 V. What is the free energy change for transfer of 2 electrons (F = 96.5 kJ/V mol)?
o: +220 kJ/mol
+220 has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign.
-110 kJ/mol
-110 uses n = 1 instead of 2.
-440 kJ/mol
-440 uses n = 4 instead of 2.
-220 kJ/mol
Correct: delta G = -nF delta E = -2(96.5)(1.14) = about -220 kJ/mol.
questions.x: delta G = -nF delta E = -2(96.5)(1.14) = about -220 kJ/mol. Trap: Sign or electron-count errors in delta G = -nF delta E.

questions.q: Cold-adapted organisms often have membrane phospholipids enriched in
o: saturated fatty acids
Saturated fatty acids are straight and pack tightly, making the membrane less fluid in the cold.
unsaturated fatty acids
Correct: Cis double bonds kink the fatty acid chains, preventing tight packing and maintaining membrane fluidity at low temperature.
long saturated hydrocarbon chains
Long saturated hydrocarbon chains pack even more tightly and reduce fluidity.
a higher cholesterol-to-phospholipid ratio at high temperature only
Cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer at high temperature, so a ratio raised at high temperature only does not address cold adaptation.
questions.x: Cis double bonds kink the fatty acid chains, preventing tight packing and maintaining membrane fluidity at low temperature. Trap: Confusing saturated with unsaturated packing effects.

questions.q: The rate of glucose uptake into a cell plateaus as extracellular glucose concentration is increased. This is most consistent with
o: simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
Simple diffusion through the bilayer increases linearly with concentration and does not saturate.
osmosis
Osmosis is movement of water, not glucose.
carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion
Correct: Saturation of uptake rate at high substrate concentration indicates a limited number of transporters, as in carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion.
bulk exocytosis
Bulk exocytosis exports material rather than taking glucose into the cell.
questions.x: Saturation of uptake rate at high substrate concentration indicates a limited number of transporters, as in carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion. Trap: Not recognizing saturation as evidence for carriers.

questions.q: Ouabain inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase. How would the intestinal Na+-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) be affected?
o: Reduced, because the Na+ gradient dissipates
Correct: SGLT relies on the Na+ gradient set up by the Na+/K+ ATPase; without the pump the gradient dissipates and glucose uptake falls.
Increased, because more Na+ is available
More Na+ is not available for cotransport, since the gradient collapses and uptake falls.
Unchanged, because SGLT uses ATP directly
SGLT is secondary active transport that uses the Na+ gradient, not ATP directly.
Reversed, because glucose moves down its gradient
SGLT does not reverse; the loss of the gradient reduces uptake rather than reversing flow.
questions.x: SGLT relies on the Na+ gradient set up by the Na+/K+ ATPase; without the pump the gradient dissipates and glucose uptake falls. Trap: Thinking cotransporters use ATP directly.

questions.q: Which solution has the highest osmotic pressure at the same temperature (assume complete dissociation of salts)?
o: 0.2 M glucose
0.2 M glucose gives only 0.20 osmol/L because it does not dissociate.
0.12 M NaCl
0.12 M NaCl gives 2 x 0.12 = 0.24 osmol/L.
0.25 M sucrose
0.25 M sucrose gives only 0.25 osmol/L because it does not dissociate.
0.1 M CaCl2
Correct: Osmolarity = iM: CaCl2 gives 3 x 0.1 = 0.30 osmol/L, the highest of the four.
questions.x: Osmolarity = iM: CaCl2 gives 3 x 0.1 = 0.30 osmol/L, the highest of the four. Trap: Ignoring the van't Hoff factor.

questions.q: In an axon, kinesin carries vesicles along microtubules toward the
o: minus end, at the cell body
Minus end at the cell body describes dynein-type (retrograde) direction and is the wrong polarity for kinesin.
plus end, at the axon terminal
Correct: Kinesin moves toward microtubule plus ends, which point away from the cell body toward the axon terminal (anterograde transport).
plus end, at the cell body
Plus end at the cell body places the plus end in the wrong location; plus ends point to the terminal.
minus end, at the axon terminal
Minus end at the axon terminal mismatches polarity and location, since minus ends lie at the cell body.
questions.x: Kinesin moves toward microtubule plus ends, which point away from the cell body toward the axon terminal (anterograde transport). Trap: Swapping kinesin and dynein directions.

questions.q: The contractile ring that pinches an animal cell in two during cytokinesis is composed mainly of
o: tubulin and kinesin
Tubulin and kinesin form and move along the spindle, not the contractile ring.
keratin
Keratin is an intermediate filament that provides mechanical strength.
actin and myosin
Correct: Actin microfilaments and myosin II contract to form the cleavage furrow during cytokinesis.
lamins
Lamins support the nuclear envelope.
questions.x: Actin microfilaments and myosin II contract to form the cleavage furrow during cytokinesis. Trap: Choosing microtubules because the spindle is involved.

questions.q: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) results in immotile cilia due to defective
o: actin filaments
Actin filaments do not form the axoneme.
keratin filaments
Keratin filaments are structural intermediate filaments and do not form the axoneme.
kinesin motors
Kinesin transports cargo along microtubules and does not drive ciliary bending.
dynein arms
Correct: Axonemal dynein arms generate sliding between microtubule doublets, which bends cilia; defective dynein causes immotile cilia.
questions.x: Axonemal dynein arms generate sliding between microtubule doublets, which bends cilia; defective dynein causes immotile cilia. Trap: Confusing dynein (ciliary bending) with kinesin (vesicle transport) or with actin-based motors.

questions.q: Rapid electrical coupling between cardiac muscle cells is mainly due to
o: gap junctions
Correct: Gap junctions contain connexons that allow ions to flow between adjacent cells, giving rapid electrical coupling.
tight junctions
Tight junctions seal the space between cells and do not conduct current.
desmosomes
Desmosomes give mechanical strength and are prominent in the heart but do not conduct current.
hemidesmosomes
Hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basement membrane.
questions.x: Gap junctions contain connexons that allow ions to flow between adjacent cells, giving rapid electrical coupling. Trap: Choosing desmosomes, which are prominent in the heart but do not conduct current.

questions.q: In intestinal epithelium, tight junctions primarily
o: allow cytoplasm to be shared
Sharing cytoplasm describes gap junctions.
limit paracellular leakage and maintain apical-basolateral polarity
Correct: Tight junctions seal the space between adjacent cells, limiting paracellular leakage and maintaining apical-basolateral polarity.
anchor cells to the basement membrane
Anchoring cells to the basement membrane describes hemidesmosomes.
form pores for ion conduction
Forming pores for ion conduction describes gap junctions.
questions.x: Tight junctions seal the space between adjacent cells, limiting paracellular leakage and maintaining apical-basolateral polarity. Trap: Mixing up tight junctions (sealing) with gap junctions (communication) or hemidesmosomes (anchoring).

questions.q: A secreted protein follows which route?
o: Rough ER, Golgi, secretory vesicle, plasma membrane
Correct: Synthesis on the rough ER is followed by Golgi processing, packaging into secretory vesicles, and exocytosis at the plasma membrane.
Golgi, rough ER, lysosome, plasma membrane
Golgi before rough ER reverses the order, and lysosomes are not on the secretory route.
Nucleus, smooth ER, Golgi, lysosome
A secreted protein is not made in the nucleus, and the route ends in lysosomes rather than at the plasma membrane.
Smooth ER, Golgi, peroxisome
The smooth ER does not synthesize secreted proteins, and peroxisomes are not on the secretory route.
questions.x: Synthesis on the rough ER is followed by Golgi processing, packaging into secretory vesicles, and exocytosis at the plasma membrane. Trap: Placing the Golgi before the rough ER or routing a secreted protein through lysosomes or peroxisomes.

questions.q: If lysosomal hydrolases leak into the cytosol, they usually cause limited damage because they
o: are destroyed in the cytosol
The hydrolases are not instantly destroyed in the cytosol.
require ATP
They do not require ATP to function.
are inactive at cytosolic pH
Correct: Lysosomal acid hydrolases work best at pH about 5 and are poorly active at the cytosolic pH of about 7.2, limiting damage.
cannot hydrolyze proteins
They can hydrolyze proteins, so that is not why damage is limited.
questions.x: Lysosomal acid hydrolases work best at pH about 5 and are poorly active at the cytosolic pH of about 7.2, limiting damage. Trap: Assuming lysosomal enzymes are always destructive.

questions.q: Which function is characteristic of peroxisomes?
o: ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation
ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation is mitochondrial.
Synthesis of secreted proteins
Synthesis of secreted proteins occurs on the rough ER.
Degradation of proteins by acid hydrolases
Protein degradation by acid hydrolases is lysosomal.
Oxidation of very long chain fatty acids and breakdown of hydrogen peroxide by catalase
Correct: Peroxisomes oxidize very long chain fatty acids and break down hydrogen peroxide with catalase.
questions.x: Peroxisomes oxidize very long chain fatty acids and break down hydrogen peroxide with catalase. Trap: Confusing peroxisomes with lysosomes.

questions.q: Which observation provides the strongest support for the bacterial origin of mitochondria?
o: A nuclear envelope
A nuclear envelope is a eukaryotic feature, not bacterial.
Presence of membrane proteins
Membrane proteins are found in all cells and say nothing about origin.
Linear chromosomes
Linear chromosomes are eukaryotic, whereas bacteria have circular chromosomes.
A circular genome and ribosomes resembling those of bacteria
Correct: Mitochondria have a circular genome and 70S-type ribosomes resembling those of bacteria, and divide by fission, supporting endosymbiosis.
questions.x: Mitochondria have a circular genome and 70S-type ribosomes resembling those of bacteria, and divide by fission, supporting endosymbiosis. Trap: Choosing a feature that eukaryotic cells share.

questions.q: The nucleolus is the site of
o: mRNA splicing
MRNA splicing occurs in the nucleoplasm.
DNA replication
DNA replication occurs throughout the nucleus, not specifically in the nucleolus.
rRNA synthesis and ribosomal subunit assembly
Correct: RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNA genes in the nucleolus, where ribosomal subunits are assembled.
protein translation
Protein translation occurs in the cytoplasm.
questions.x: RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNA genes in the nucleolus, where ribosomal subunits are assembled. Trap: Assigning mRNA processing to the nucleolus.

questions.q: Hepatocytes chronically exposed to phenobarbital show proliferation of
o: smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: Smooth ER contains cytochrome P450 enzymes used in drug detoxification, so it proliferates with chronic phenobarbital exposure.
rough endoplasmic reticulum
Rough ER synthesizes proteins and is not the primary site of drug metabolism.
lysosomes
Lysosomes degrade material and are not the primary site of drug metabolism.
the Golgi apparatus
The Golgi modifies and sorts proteins and is not the primary site of drug metabolism.
questions.x: Smooth ER contains cytochrome P450 enzymes used in drug detoxification, so it proliferates with chronic phenobarbital exposure. Trap: Choosing rough ER because it is the better-known ER type, instead of the detoxifying smooth ER.

questions.q: Scurvy weakens connective tissue because vitamin C is required for
o: synthesis of elastin
Elastin synthesis is not vitamin C dependent in the way collagen hydroxylation is.
hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen
Correct: Vitamin C is a cofactor for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen, which is needed for stable collagen triple helices.
glycosylation of fibronectin
Glycosylation of fibronectin is not vitamin C dependent.
integrin binding to the cytoskeleton
Integrin binding to the cytoskeleton is not vitamin C dependent.
questions.x: Vitamin C is a cofactor for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen, which is needed for stable collagen triple helices. Trap: Not linking vitamin C to hydroxylation of collagen proline and lysine, and picking elastin or integrins instead.

questions.q: Which epithelium is best suited for rapid gas exchange in the alveoli?
o: Stratified squamous epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium is thick and protective, like skin, which slows diffusion.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines airways to move mucus and is too thick for exchange.
Simple squamous epithelium
Correct: A thin single layer of flat cells minimizes diffusion distance, so simple squamous epithelium suits rapid gas exchange.
Simple columnar epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium is taller and suited to absorption and secretion, so diffusion distance is greater.
questions.x: A thin single layer of flat cells minimizes diffusion distance, so simple squamous epithelium suits rapid gas exchange. Trap: Choosing the protective epithelium of the skin.

questions.q: Cartilage heals slowly after injury mainly because it is
o: rich in osteoblasts
Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells and are not abundant in cartilage.
avascular
Correct: Cartilage is avascular, so limited nutrient delivery slows cell repair after injury.
highly vascular
Cartilage is avascular, not highly vascular (vascularity describes bone).
composed mostly of cells
Cartilage is mostly extracellular matrix, not mostly cells.
questions.x: Cartilage is avascular, so limited nutrient delivery slows cell repair after injury. Trap: Confusing cartilage with bone and assuming it is vascular and rich in osteoblasts.

questions.q: Removing calcium from the medium causes a tissue to dissociate into single cells because
o: cadherins require Ca2+ to mediate cell-cell adhesion
Correct: Cadherins are Ca2+-dependent adhesion proteins, so removing calcium disrupts cell-cell adhesion and the tissue dissociates.
integrins require Ca2+ to bind collagen
Integrins bind the extracellular matrix, so they do not explain cell-cell dissociation.
gap junctions require Ca2+ to open
Gap junction closure would not separate cells.
collagen fibers dissolve without Ca2+
Collagen fibers are not dissolved by loss of calcium.
questions.x: Cadherins are Ca2+-dependent adhesion proteins, so removing calcium disrupts cell-cell adhesion and the tissue dissociates. Trap: Choosing integrins or gap junctions instead of Ca2+-dependent cadherins as the cell-cell adhesion molecule.

questions.q: Defective LDL receptors cause high plasma LDL because
o: cells cannot take up LDL by receptor-mediated endocytosis
Correct: LDL is cleared from plasma by receptor-mediated endocytosis, so defective receptors leave LDL in the blood.
liver cells overproduce LDL
Liver overproduction of LDL is not the mechanism in receptor defects.
lysosomes rupture
Lysosome rupture does not explain high plasma LDL.
Na+/K+ ATPase is defective
A Na+/K+ ATPase defect does not explain failure to clear LDL.
questions.x: LDL is cleared from plasma by receptor-mediated endocytosis, so defective receptors leave LDL in the blood. Trap: Assuming high plasma LDL means overproduction rather than failed receptor-mediated clearance.

questions.q: Which treatment removes peripheral membrane proteins but leaves integral membrane proteins in the membrane?
o: Treating with a detergent
Detergent solubilizes the bilayer and extracts integral proteins too.
Heating to 90 C
Heating to 90 C denatures proteins in general rather than selectively removing peripheral ones.
Treating with phospholipase
Phospholipase degrades membrane lipids and would not selectively strip peripheral proteins.
Washing with a high-salt solution
Correct: Peripheral proteins bind through ionic interactions that high salt disrupts, while integral proteins stay embedded in the bilayer.
questions.x: Peripheral proteins bind through ionic interactions that high salt disrupts, while integral proteins stay embedded in the bilayer. Trap: Assuming detergent, heat, or lipases remove only peripheral proteins when they also disrupt integral proteins or lipids.

questions.q: Gram-positive bacteria stain purple after the Gram procedure primarily because they have:
o: a thick peptidoglycan layer that retains the crystal violet-iodine complex
Correct: A thick peptidoglycan wall resists alcohol decolorization and holds the crystal violet-iodine complex, so the cell stays purple.
an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide that binds the crystal violet
Describes the LPS-containing outer membrane of gram-negative cells, which is lost or disrupted by alcohol so those cells decolorize.
no cell wall, so the dye accumulates in the cytoplasm
Describes a wall-less cell; lacking a wall would not retain the dye complex during decolorization.
a thin peptidoglycan layer that traps safranin more efficiently
A thin peptidoglycan layer is characteristic of gram-negative cells, and safranin is the pink counterstain, not what makes cells purple.
questions.x: A thick peptidoglycan wall resists alcohol decolorization and holds the crystal violet-iodine complex, so the cell stays purple. Trap: Confusing the outer membrane of gram-negative cells with the structure that retains stain; the thick wall of gram-positive cells is what holds crystal violet.

questions.q: A culture begins with 500 bacterial cells and the doubling time is 30 minutes. Assuming exponential growth with no lag phase, approximately how many cells are present after 3 hours?
o: 3,000 treats growth as linear (500 x 6) rather than exponential.
Correct: 3 hours = 180 min / 30 min = 6 doublings, so N = 500 x 2^6 = 500 x 64 = 32,000.
16,000 is 500 x 2^5, using only 5 doublings.
64,000 is 2^6 alone (or 500 x 2^7), either dropping the initial 500 or using 7 doublings.
questions.x: 3 hours = 180 min / 30 min = 6 doublings, so N = 500 x 2^6 = 500 x 64 = 32,000. Trap: Multiplying by the number of doublings instead of raising 2 to that power, or miscounting the doublings (3 h / 0.5 h = 6).

questions.q: During bacterial conjugation, which of the following is typically transferred from the F+ donor to the F- recipient?
o: The entire bacterial chromosome in double-stranded form
Transfer of the whole chromosome occurs only in rare Hfr cells, is usually incomplete, and is single-stranded, not double-stranded.
Naked DNA fragments taken up from the surrounding medium
Uptake of naked DNA from the medium is transformation, not conjugation.
A single strand of the F plasmid DNA through the sex pilus-mediated cell contact
Correct: Conjugation moves a single strand of the F plasmid through a pilus-formed bridge, and the recipient synthesizes the complementary strand.
Bacterial DNA packaged inside a phage capsid
DNA packaged in a phage capsid is transduction.
questions.x: Conjugation moves a single strand of the F plasmid through a pilus-formed bridge, and the recipient synthesizes the complementary strand. Trap: Mixing up conjugation, transformation, and transduction; conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact and moves plasmid DNA.

questions.q: A bacteriophage that infected a donor bacterium later infects a recipient and delivers donor bacterial genes to it. This process is best described as:
o: transformation
Transformation is uptake of free DNA from the environment, with no phage involved.
conjugation
Conjugation requires direct pilus contact between cells and does not involve a phage.
binary fission
Binary fission is asexual division of one cell and transfers no genes between cells.
transduction
Correct: Phage-mediated transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another is transduction.
questions.x: Phage-mediated transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another is transduction. Trap: Assuming any gene transfer in bacteria is conjugation; the viral vector is the key clue for transduction.

questions.q: A bacterium inoculated into a tube of thioglycolate broth grows throughout the tube but is densest near the top. The organism is most likely a:
o: facultative anaerobe
Correct: Growth throughout the tube with heaviest growth at the oxygen-rich top shows the organism prefers oxygen (aerobic respiration) but can still ferment without it, i.e., a facultative anaerobe.
obligate aerobe
An obligate aerobe would grow only at the top, not throughout the tube.
obligate anaerobe
An obligate anaerobe would grow only at the bottom where oxygen is absent.
aerotolerant anaerobe that grows evenly regardless of oxygen
An aerotolerant anaerobe grows evenly throughout, since oxygen does not change its metabolism, which does not match the denser top growth.
questions.x: Growth throughout the tube with heaviest growth at the oxygen-rich top shows the organism prefers oxygen (aerobic respiration) but can still ferment without it, i.e., a facultative anaerobe. Trap: Choosing obligate aerobe because growth is heaviest at the top, ignoring growth lower in the tube.

questions.q: A bacterium has a mutation in lacI that produces a repressor unable to bind the operator. Which phenotype is expected?
o: Lac operon genes are never expressed, even with lactose
Never being expressed would result from a superrepressor that cannot bind allolactose or a promoter mutation, not from a repressor that cannot bind DNA.
Lac operon genes are expressed constitutively, even without lactose
Correct: A repressor that cannot bind the operator cannot block RNA polymerase, so lacZYA are transcribed constitutively regardless of lactose.
Lac operon genes are expressed only when lactose and glucose are both present
Requiring both lactose and glucose is not the logic here; glucose lowers CAP-cAMP activation but does not restore repression.
Expression is normal because the operator is not needed for repression
The operator is the repressor's binding site and is required for repression, so loss of binding is not normal.
questions.x: A repressor that cannot bind the operator cannot block RNA polymerase, so lacZYA are transcribed constitutively regardless of lactose. Trap: Confusing a repressor that cannot bind DNA (constitutive expression) with one that cannot bind allolactose (never induced).

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a prophage in the lysogenic cycle?
o: Viral DNA free in the cytoplasm that is rapidly translated to produce capsids
Free viral DNA rapidly directing capsid synthesis describes the lytic cycle.
Viral RNA that is reverse transcribed in the host cytoplasm
Viral RNA that is reverse transcribed is a retroviral feature, not a prophage.
Viral DNA integrated into the host chromosome and replicated along with it during cell division
Correct: A prophage is phage DNA integrated into the host chromosome and replicated with it at each cell division during lysogeny.
A completely assembled virion that is released by lysis
A completely assembled virion released by lysis is the end product of the lytic cycle.
questions.x: A prophage is phage DNA integrated into the host chromosome and replicated with it at each cell division during lysogeny. Trap: Thinking lysogeny kills the host immediately; the prophage is dormant until induced.

questions.q: Which enzyme must be carried in the virion of HIV because the host cell does not possess it?
o: DNA ligase
DNA ligase is supplied by the host cell.
RNA polymerase II
RNA polymerase II is the host's own transcription enzyme, used to transcribe the integrated provirus.
Peptidyl transferase
Peptidyl transferase is ribosomal rRNA activity supplied by the host.
Reverse transcriptase
Correct: HIV's RNA genome must be copied into DNA by viral reverse transcriptase, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity that human cells lack.
questions.x: HIV's RNA genome must be copied into DNA by viral reverse transcriptase, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity that human cells lack. Trap: Assuming every viral enzyme must be viral; only activities absent from the host need to be carried in.

questions.q: Which feature is characteristic of an enveloped virus as opposed to a naked virus?
o: A lipid bilayer derived from host membrane surrounding the capsid
Correct: Enveloped viruses bud from the host and acquire a host-derived lipid bilayer studded with viral glycoproteins around the capsid.
A peptidoglycan wall surrounding the capsid
Viruses have no peptidoglycan; that is a bacterial cell wall component.
Ribosomes for synthesizing viral proteins
Viruses lack ribosomes and use host ribosomes for translation.
A nucleoid region with histones
A nucleoid with histones describes cellular organization (eukaryote-like chromatin) that viruses lack.
questions.x: Enveloped viruses bud from the host and acquire a host-derived lipid bilayer studded with viral glycoproteins around the capsid. Trap: Attributing cellular components such as ribosomes to viruses; viruses are acellular.

questions.q: Bacillus species form endospores primarily in response to:
o: abundant nutrients, as a reproductive form that increases cell number
Abundant nutrients favor vegetative growth, and one cell makes one spore, so spores do not increase cell number.
nutrient depletion, producing a dormant structure highly resistant to heat and desiccation
Correct: Sporulation is a survival response to nutrient depletion that yields a dormant endospore resistant to heat and desiccation.
antibiotic exposure, to transfer resistance genes to neighbors
Antibiotic exposure does not trigger sporulation, and spores do not transfer resistance genes.
phage infection, to deliver DNA to other cells
Phage infection does not trigger sporulation, and spores do not deliver DNA to other cells.
questions.x: Sporulation is a survival response to nutrient depletion that yields a dormant endospore resistant to heat and desiccation. Trap: Treating endospores as reproductive spores; each vegetative cell forms just one.

questions.q: Streptomycin can treat bacterial infections with little harm to human cells because it binds to:
o: the 60S ribosomal subunit shared by all cells
The 60S subunit is eukaryotic and not a streptomycin target in bacteria.
the bacterial nucleus, which humans lack
Bacteria lack a nucleus, so there is no bacterial nucleus to bind.
the 30S ribosomal subunit, which differs from the eukaryotic 40S subunit
Correct: Streptomycin binds the bacterial 30S subunit of the 70S ribosome, which differs structurally from the eukaryotic 40S subunit, giving selective toxicity.
the eukaryotic mitochondrial cristae
Mitochondrial cristae are not the target of streptomycin.
questions.x: Streptomycin binds the bacterial 30S subunit of the 70S ribosome, which differs structurally from the eukaryotic 40S subunit, giving selective toxicity. Trap: Remembering that bacterial ribosomes are smaller but mixing up which subunits are 30S/50S vs 40S/60S.

questions.q: Penicillin kills growing bacteria by inhibiting transpeptidase enzymes. This would be expected to be ineffective against:
o: Escherichia coli, a gram-negative rod
E. coli has a thin peptidoglycan layer and is susceptible, though the outer membrane limits entry of some drugs.
Staphylococcus aureus, a gram-positive coccus
S. aureus has thick peptidoglycan and is susceptible unless it carries resistance.
Bacillus subtilis, a spore-forming rod
B. subtilis has peptidoglycan and is susceptible when growing.
Mycoplasma, which lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall
Correct: Penicillin blocks transpeptidase cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so Mycoplasma, which has no peptidoglycan wall, is intrinsically resistant.
questions.x: Penicillin blocks transpeptidase cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so Mycoplasma, which has no peptidoglycan wall, is intrinsically resistant. Trap: Assuming gram-negative outer membrane equals no peptidoglycan; gram-negatives still have a thin wall.

questions.q: A resistance (R) plasmid spreads rapidly through a bacterial population in the absence of antibiotics. The most likely mechanism is:
o: conjugation, because the plasmid carries tra genes enabling pilus formation and transfer
Correct: Conjugative R plasmids carry tra genes encoding the pilus and transfer machinery, so they spread horizontally independent of antibiotic selection.
meiotic recombination between homologous chromosomes
Bacteria do not undergo meiosis or have homologous chromosome pairs to recombine.
vertical transmission by sexual reproduction
Bacteria do not reproduce sexually, and vertical transmission alone would not spread a plasmid so rapidly.
mitosis of bacterial cells
Mitosis does not occur in bacteria, which divide by binary fission, and division does not move plasmids between cells.
questions.x: Conjugative R plasmids carry tra genes encoding the pilus and transfer machinery, so they spread horizontally independent of antibiotic selection. Trap: Applying eukaryotic reproduction terms to bacteria.

questions.q: Which statement about the typical bacterial genome is correct?
o: It is multiple linear chromosomes wrapped around histones in a nucleus
Multiple linear histone-wrapped chromosomes in a nucleus describe eukaryotes.
It is a single circular chromosome in the nucleoid, supercoiled by DNA gyrase, without histones
Correct: Most bacteria have a single circular chromosome in the nucleoid, negatively supercoiled by DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II), without histones.
It is a double-membrane-bound circular genome packaged with histones
Bacteria have no double-membrane-bound genome and no histones.
It is a single linear chromosome attached to the nuclear envelope
Bacterial chromosomes are typically circular and there is no nuclear envelope to attach to.
questions.x: Most bacteria have a single circular chromosome in the nucleoid, negatively supercoiled by DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II), without histones. Trap: Believing bacteria have histones; archaea have histone-like proteins but bacteria generally do not.

questions.q: In the stationary phase of a bacterial batch culture, the population size is stable because:
o: cell division has completely stopped in all cells
Division does not stop completely in all cells; it is balanced by death.
cells are adapting enzymes to new media
Adapting enzymes to new media describes the lag phase.
the rate of cell division approximately equals the rate of cell death as nutrients become limiting and wastes accumulate
Correct: Stationary phase is a plateau where division rate roughly equals death rate as nutrients become limiting and wastes accumulate.
all cells are dying exponentially
All cells dying exponentially describes the death phase.
questions.x: Stationary phase is a plateau where division rate roughly equals death rate as nutrients become limiting and wastes accumulate. Trap: Confusing the lag phase (adaptation) and stationary phase (balance of growth and death).

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes archaea from bacteria?
o: Archaea have a membrane-bound nucleus
Archaea lack a membrane-bound nucleus, like bacteria.
Archaea have peptidoglycan walls with D-amino acids
Peptidoglycan with D-amino acids is a bacterial feature; archaea lack true peptidoglycan.
Archaea have 80S ribosomes
Archaea have 70S ribosomes like bacteria, not 80S.
Archaeal membrane lipids contain ether linkages to branched isoprenoid chains
Correct: Archaeal membranes use ether-linked branched isoprenoid lipids, unlike the ester-linked fatty acids of bacteria and eukaryotes.
questions.x: Archaeal membranes use ether-linked branched isoprenoid lipids, unlike the ester-linked fatty acids of bacteria and eukaryotes. Trap: Assuming archaea are eukaryote-like in all respects; they share cell organization with bacteria.

questions.q: When a bacterium moves up a gradient of an attractant, how does its movement pattern change?
o: Tumbling frequency decreases, so runs in the favorable direction lengthen
Correct: Bacteria bias a random walk by lowering tumble frequency when attractant rises, lengthening runs up the gradient.
Tumbling frequency increases so cells reverse every second
Increased tumbling occurs when attractant falls or with repellents, and not as constant reversal every second.
Flagella stop rotating and cells move by diffusion
Flagella keep rotating during chemotaxis; movement is not simple diffusion.
The cell synthesizes new flagella in the direction of the gradient
Chemotaxis changes tumble frequency and does not need new flagella synthesized toward the gradient.
questions.x: Bacteria bias a random walk by lowering tumble frequency when attractant rises, lengthening runs up the gradient. Trap: Thinking bacteria steer directly toward a gradient; they modulate tumble frequency in a biased random walk.

questions.q: In the Hershey-Chase experiment, phage were labeled with 32P in one sample and 35S in another. After blending and centrifuging, which result supported DNA as genetic material?
o: 35S was found mainly in the bacterial pellet, 32P in the supernatant
This reversed pattern would indicate protein is the genetic material, which was not observed.
32P was found mainly in the bacterial pellet, 35S mainly in the supernatant
Correct: DNA contains phosphorus, and 32P entered the bacteria (pellet), while protein contains sulfur, and 35S stayed outside in the supernatant, showing DNA is genetic material.
Both labels were found in the pellet
Both labels in the pellet would mean both entered the cell, which was not observed.
Neither label was found in the pellet
No label in the pellet would contradict the fact that infection occurred and DNA entered.
questions.x: DNA contains phosphorus, and 32P entered the bacteria (pellet), while protein contains sulfur, and 35S stayed outside in the supernatant, showing DNA is genetic material. Trap: Forgetting that DNA contains phosphorus (not sulfur) and protein contains sulfur.

questions.q: A virus has a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome. Which statement is correct?
o: The genome must first be transcribed by a host DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Host DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is not needed, since the genome is already mRNA-sense and RNA is not transcribed from DNA.
The genome is complementary to mRNA and requires a virion-carried RNA polymerase before translation
Describes a negative-sense genome, which is complementary to mRNA and needs a virion-carried RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
The genome can be translated directly by host ribosomes after entering the cell
Correct: Positive-sense RNA has the same sequence as mRNA, so host ribosomes can translate it directly after entry.
The genome must be integrated into host DNA before any protein synthesis
Integration into host DNA is a retroviral strategy, not required for plain positive-strand RNA viruses.
questions.x: Positive-sense RNA has the same sequence as mRNA, so host ribosomes can translate it directly after entry. Trap: Equating positive-sense with retrovirus; plain positive-strand RNA viruses do not integrate.

questions.q: In bacteria, which location houses the electron transport chain used for aerobic respiration?
o: Mitochondrial inner membrane
The mitochondrial inner membrane is eukaryotic; bacteria have no mitochondria.
Thylakoid-free cytoplasm only
The ETC needs a membrane to build a proton gradient, so cytoplasm alone cannot host it.
The outer membrane
The outer membrane of gram-negatives is a permeability barrier and does not host the ETC.
The plasma membrane
Correct: Bacteria lack mitochondria, so the aerobic electron transport chain is embedded in the plasma membrane, which pumps protons out across it.
questions.x: Bacteria lack mitochondria, so the aerobic electron transport chain is embedded in the plasma membrane, which pumps protons out across it. Trap: Importing eukaryotic organelle locations into bacterial cells.

questions.q: In Griffith's experiment, mice injected with heat-killed smooth (virulent) strain plus live rough (nonvirulent) strain died. This occurred because:
o: live rough bacteria took up genetic material from the dead smooth bacteria and became virulent
Correct: Naked DNA released from heat-killed smooth cells was taken up and expressed by live rough cells, transforming them to virulence.
heat-killed smooth bacteria revived and replicated in the mouse
Heat-killed cells cannot revive and replicate.
the rough strain conjugated with the smooth strain through a pilus
Griffith's experiment involved no pilus contact; transformation needs none.
a bacteriophage carried virulence genes between the strains
No bacteriophage was involved in Griffith's experiment.
questions.x: Naked DNA released from heat-killed smooth cells was taken up and expressed by live rough cells, transforming them to virulence. Trap: Believing the killed bacteria came back to life rather than donating a transforming factor.

questions.q: A human somatic cell is in G2 of interphase. How many chromosomes and chromatids does it contain?
o: 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids
46 chromatids describes a G1 cell before replication.
46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids
Correct: After S phase each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids, so G2 cells have 46 chromosomes (counted by centromeres) and 92 chromatids.
92 chromosomes and 92 chromatids
92 chromosomes miscounts each replicated chromosome as two; chromosome number stays 46.
23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids
23 is the haploid number, not the count in a diploid somatic cell.
questions.x: After S phase each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids, so G2 cells have 46 chromosomes (counted by centromeres) and 92 chromatids. Trap: Counting each replicated chromosome as two chromosomes; chromosome number depends on centromeres.

questions.q: Separation of sister chromatids at the onset of anaphase requires:
o: degradation of the kinetochore by caspases
Caspases mediate apoptosis and do not degrade kinetochores for anaphase.
phosphorylation of Rb by cyclin D-CDK4
Rb phosphorylation by cyclin D-CDK4 governs the G1/S transition, not chromatid separation.
cleavage of cohesin by separase after the anaphase-promoting complex is activated
Correct: The APC/C destroys securin, freeing separase to cleave the cohesin holding sister chromatids together, allowing anaphase.
replication of centromeres by DNA polymerase
Centromere replication occurs in S phase, long before anaphase.
questions.x: The APC/C destroys securin, freeing separase to cleave the cohesin holding sister chromatids together, allowing anaphase. Trap: Thinking microtubule pulling alone separates chromatids; cohesin must first be cleaved.

questions.q: Colchicine depolymerizes microtubules. A culture of dividing cells treated with colchicine will accumulate in which stage?
o: G1, because DNA replication is blocked
Colchicine acts on microtubules and does not block DNA replication, so cells do not stall in G1.
Telophase, because the nuclear envelope reforms prematurely
Telophase occurs after anaphase, which the checkpoint prevents from happening.
Cytokinesis, because the cleavage furrow cannot constrict
Cytokinesis uses an actin-myosin ring and comes after chromosome segregation, which never occurs.
Prometaphase/metaphase, because the spindle assembly checkpoint is not satisfied
Correct: Without spindle microtubules kinetochores cannot attach, so the spindle assembly checkpoint blocks APC/C and arrests cells in prometaphase/metaphase.
questions.x: Without spindle microtubules kinetochores cannot attach, so the spindle assembly checkpoint blocks APC/C and arrests cells in prometaphase/metaphase. Trap: Placing the arrest at cytokinesis because actin, not microtubules, forms the furrow.

questions.q: Reduction in chromosome number during meiosis occurs because:
o: homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I
Correct: Anaphase I separates homologous chromosomes into different cells, halving ploidy from 2n to n.
sister chromatids separate in anaphase I
Sister chromatid separation occurs in anaphase II and does not reduce chromosome number.
DNA replicates twice before one division
DNA replicates only once in meiosis, followed by two divisions.
homologs fail to pair in prophase I
Homologs do pair (synapsis) in prophase I; failure to pair is not what reduces chromosome number.
questions.x: Anaphase I separates homologous chromosomes into different cells, halving ploidy from 2n to n. Trap: Mixing up which division separates homologs and which separates sister chromatids.

questions.q: Which statement about crossing over is correct?
o: It occurs between sister chromatids during prophase II
Prophase II has no homolog pairs, and exchange between sister chromatids yields identical DNA.
It occurs between nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I and generates recombinant chromatids
Correct: Chiasmata form where nonsister chromatids of homologs exchange segments in prophase I, producing recombinant chromatids.
It prevents independent assortment of chromosomes
Crossing over adds variation and does not prevent independent assortment.
It occurs during S phase between different chromosomes
Crossing over occurs in prophase I between homologs, not in S phase between different chromosomes.
questions.x: Chiasmata form where nonsister chromatids of homologs exchange segments in prophase I, producing recombinant chromatids. Trap: Thinking sister chromatid exchange generates variation; sisters are genetically identical.

questions.q: Nondisjunction of one homologous pair during meiosis I in a primary spermatocyte would result in:
o: two normal gametes, one n+1 and one n-1
Two normal gametes plus abnormal ones is the pattern for nondisjunction in meiosis II, not I.
four normal haploid gametes
Four normal haploid gametes requires proper segregation of every pair.
four aneuploid gametes: two with n+1 and two with n-1 for that chromosome
Correct: Nondisjunction in meiosis I sends both homologs to one daughter cell, so all four products are aneuploid: two n+1 and two n-1.
two gametes with 2n and two with no chromosomes
2n and empty gametes would require failure of all chromosomes, not one pair.
questions.x: Nondisjunction in meiosis I sends both homologs to one daughter cell, so all four products are aneuploid: two n+1 and two n-1. Trap: Remembering the meiosis II pattern for meiosis I errors.

questions.q: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity oscillates through the cell cycle mainly because:
o: CDK is synthesized and degraded each cycle while cyclin is constant
Reverses the roles: CDK is relatively constant while cyclin is cycled.
CDK is a transcription factor that turns on during G1 only
CDKs are protein kinases, not transcription factors, and act throughout the cycle.
cyclins are phosphatases that inactivate CDK
Cyclins are regulatory subunits that activate CDKs, not phosphatases.
cyclin concentrations rise and fall while CDK concentrations remain relatively constant
Correct: CDKs need cyclin partners to be active, and cyclin levels rise and fall through synthesis and degradation while CDK levels stay fairly constant.
questions.x: CDKs need cyclin partners to be active, and cyclin levels rise and fall through synthesis and degradation while CDK levels stay fairly constant. Trap: Assuming the kinase level changes rather than the cyclin partner.

questions.q: A cell with DNA damage normally undergoes G1 arrest via p53. Which sequence best describes this?
o: p53 is stabilized, induces p21, and p21 inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes
Correct: DNA damage stabilizes p53, which induces p21, a CDK inhibitor that blocks cyclin-CDK complexes and halts progression into S phase.
p53 is degraded, which activates cyclin-CDK complexes
Degraded p53 would permit division, not cause arrest.
p53 phosphorylates Rb to release E2F
Rb is phosphorylated by cyclin-CDK complexes, not p53, and that would promote S phase entry.
p53 inhibits caspases to prevent apoptosis
p53 promotes apoptosis when damage is irreparable rather than inhibiting caspases.
questions.x: DNA damage stabilizes p53, which induces p21, a CDK inhibitor that blocks cyclin-CDK complexes and halts progression into S phase. Trap: Thinking p53 promotes proliferation; it is a tumor suppressor.

questions.q: In a normal G1 cell, which event allows progression to S phase?
o: Dephosphorylation of Rb, which frees E2F
Dephosphorylated (hypophosphorylated) Rb binds and inhibits E2F, blocking S phase entry.
Phosphorylation of Rb by cyclin D-CDK4/6, releasing E2F to activate S-phase genes
Correct: Cyclin D-CDK4/6 hyperphosphorylates Rb, releasing E2F to activate S-phase genes.
Binding of p21 to cyclin D-CDK4/6
p21 binding inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes and causes arrest.
Binding of Rb to E2F with increased affinity
Tighter Rb-E2F binding would keep E2F inactive and prevent progression.
questions.x: Cyclin D-CDK4/6 hyperphosphorylates Rb, releasing E2F to activate S-phase genes. Trap: Reversing the effect of Rb phosphorylation.

questions.q: How does cytokinesis differ between animal and plant cells?
o: Animal cells form a cell plate; plant cells form a cleavage furrow
Reverses the two mechanisms.
Both use microtubule-based contractile rings
Contractile rings are actin-myosin, not microtubule-based, and plants do not use them.
Animal cells use an actin-myosin contractile ring forming a cleavage furrow; plant cells build a cell plate from Golgi-derived vesicles
Correct: Animal cells pinch with an actin-myosin contractile ring forming a cleavage furrow, while plant cells with rigid walls build a cell plate from Golgi-derived vesicles.
Plant cells do not undergo cytokinesis, only nuclear division
Plant cells do undergo cytokinesis, via the cell plate.
questions.x: Animal cells pinch with an actin-myosin contractile ring forming a cleavage furrow, while plant cells with rigid walls build a cell plate from Golgi-derived vesicles. Trap: Swapping the animal and plant cytokinesis mechanisms.

questions.q: Mature neurons in the adult brain are best described as being in:
o: S phase, continuously replicating DNA
Neurons do not replicate DNA, so they are not in S phase.
G2, awaiting mitosis
G2 cells are poised for mitosis, whereas mature neurons do not divide.
M phase, arrested at metaphase
Neurons are not arrested in metaphase; they have left the cell cycle.
G0, a nondividing state in which they are metabolically active
Correct: Terminally differentiated neurons exit the cycle into G0 yet remain metabolically active.
questions.x: Terminally differentiated neurons exit the cycle into G0 yet remain metabolically active. Trap: Assuming nondividing means metabolically inactive.

questions.q: A hematopoietic stem cell that can give rise to all blood cell types but not neurons is:
o: multipotent
Correct: Hematopoietic stem cells are multipotent, giving multiple related cell types within the blood lineage.
totipotent
Totipotent cells can form a whole organism including placenta, which blood stem cells cannot.
pluripotent
Pluripotent cells give rise to all three germ layers, including neurons, which these cells cannot.
unipotent
Unipotent cells give only one cell type, but these give many blood cell types.
questions.x: Hematopoietic stem cells are multipotent, giving multiple related cell types within the blood lineage. Trap: Choosing pluripotent for any stem cell that makes more than one cell type.

questions.q: The cloning of Dolly from a differentiated mammary cell nucleus demonstrated that:
o: differentiation involves irreversible loss of genes
Successful cloning contradicts irreversible gene loss.
differentiated cells retain the complete genome and can be reprogrammed by the oocyte cytoplasm
Correct: Dolly showed a differentiated nucleus keeps the full genome and can be reprogrammed by oocyte cytoplasm, so differentiation reflects differential expression.
mitochondrial DNA determines cell identity
Mitochondrial DNA does not determine cell identity, and the experiment transferred a nucleus.
somatic nuclei cannot support embryonic development
Somatic nuclei did support embryonic development to produce a live animal.
questions.x: Dolly showed a differentiated nucleus keeps the full genome and can be reprogrammed by oocyte cytoplasm, so differentiation reflects differential expression. Trap: Believing differentiated cells discard genes they do not use.

questions.q: Which event is a hallmark of intrinsic apoptosis?
o: Cell swelling and lysis with inflammation
Swelling, lysis and inflammation describe necrosis.
Telomerase reactivation
Telomerase reactivation promotes proliferation and immortality, not cell death.
Release of cytochrome c from mitochondria, activating caspases
Correct: Intrinsic apoptosis releases cytochrome c from mitochondria, which with Apaf-1 forms the apoptosome and activates caspase 9.
Increased cyclin D expression
Increased cyclin D drives G1 progression, not apoptosis.
questions.x: Intrinsic apoptosis releases cytochrome c from mitochondria, which with Apaf-1 forms the apoptosome and activates caspase 9. Trap: Confusing apoptosis with necrosis.

questions.q: Which pairing of mutation and genetic behavior is correct?
o: Loss of one p53 allele alone fully removes tumor suppression
One functional p53 allele usually retains substantial suppressor function, so losing one does not fully remove it.
Oncogenes require two mutated alleles to cause transformation
Oncogenes act dominantly, so one mutated allele suffices.
Tumor suppressors are activated by gain-of-function mutations
Tumor suppressors are inactivated by loss-of-function mutations, not activated by gain-of-function.
A gain-of-function Ras mutation acts dominantly, whereas loss of Rb function usually requires both alleles to be inactivated
Correct: Gain-of-function Ras mutations act dominantly, whereas tumor suppressors like Rb are typically recessive at the cell level and need both alleles inactivated (two-hit).
