questions.x: Zn2+ is 3d10, with all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic. Trap: Assuming ions of transition metals are paramagnetic.

questions.q: Atoms emit discrete lines in their emission spectra because:
o: electrons orbit continuously with varying radii
continuous orbits of varying radii would give a continuous spectrum.
nuclei emit photons of random energy
nuclei do not emit the visible and UV emission lines, and random energies would give a continuum.
electrons can only occupy quantized energy levels
Correct: Electrons occupy only quantized energy levels, and transitions between fixed levels emit photons of specific energies, giving discrete lines.
photons are not quantized
photon energy is quantized as E = hf.
questions.x: Electrons occupy only quantized energy levels, and transitions between fixed levels emit photons of specific energies, giving discrete lines. Trap: Thinking light emission is continuous.

questions.q: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle implies that:
o: electrons follow fixed circular orbits
fixed circular orbits belong to the Bohr model.
the position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known with arbitrary precision
Correct: The uncertainty product of position and momentum has a lower bound of h/4pi, so both cannot be known with arbitrary precision.
two electrons cannot have the same spin
that is a garbled Pauli exclusion principle, which concerns four quantum numbers.
electrons occupy the lowest energy orbitals first
that is the Aufbau principle.
questions.x: The uncertainty product of position and momentum has a lower bound of h/4pi, so both cannot be known with arbitrary precision. Trap: Confusing the uncertainty principle with the Bohr model, Pauli exclusion or Aufbau principles because they all concern electrons.

questions.q: A sample of ancient wood contains 25% of the carbon-14 of living wood. Given a half-life of 5730 years, the approximate age is:
o: 5730 years
5730 years is one half-life, which leaves 50%.
22,920 years
22,920 years is four half-lives, which leaves 6.25%.
11,460 years
Correct: 25% remaining means two half-lives, so the age is 2 x 5730 = 11,460 years.
17,190 years
17,190 years is three half-lives, which leaves 12.5%.
questions.x: 25% remaining means two half-lives, so the age is 2 x 5730 = 11,460 years. Trap: Mapping 25% to one or four half-lives instead of two, since (1/2)^2 = 1/4.

questions.q: In positron emission tomography, the detected photons come from:
o: annihilation of a positron with an electron, producing two 511 keV photons moving in opposite directions
Correct: A positron meets an electron and annihilates into two back-to-back 511 keV gamma photons, which the PET detectors register.
alpha particles emitted by the tracer
alpha particles are stopped within the tissue and are not detected externally.
neutrons from fission of the tracer
PET tracers do not undergo fission or emit neutrons.
beta-minus particles passing through tissue
beta-minus particles are not detected in PET, which uses beta-plus emitters.
questions.x: A positron meets an electron and annihilates into two back-to-back 511 keV gamma photons, which the PET detectors register. Trap: Thinking the positron is detected directly.

questions.q: Which ordering of penetrating power is correct, from least to greatest?
o: gamma, beta, alpha
this reverses the correct ordering and puts gamma least penetrating.
beta, alpha, gamma
it places alpha above beta in penetrating power.
alpha, gamma, beta
it places gamma below beta, though gamma penetrates more.
alpha, beta, gamma
Correct: Alpha particles are massive and charged and stopped by paper, beta by aluminum, and gamma requires dense lead, so penetration increases alpha < beta < gamma.
questions.x: Alpha particles are massive and charged and stopped by paper, beta by aluminum, and gamma requires dense lead, so penetration increases alpha < beta < gamma. Trap: Assuming heavier particles penetrate more.

questions.q: Moving from sodium to chlorine across period 3, the effective nuclear charge experienced by valence electrons:
o: decreases, because more electrons are added
added electrons go into the same shell and shield poorly, so Zeff does not decrease.
increases, because shielding by inner electrons stays about the same while Z increases
Correct: Across period 3, protons are added while same-shell electrons shield poorly and inner shielding stays about the same, so Zeff increases and the radius shrinks.
stays constant
Zeff rises as protons are added.
increases, because more shells are added
no new shell is added across a period.
questions.x: Across period 3, protons are added while same-shell electrons shield poorly and inner shielding stays about the same, so Zeff increases and the radius shrinks. Trap: Thinking added electrons increase shielding in the same shell.

questions.q: Heavy stable nuclei have more neutrons than protons because neutrons:
o: are lighter than protons
neutrons are slightly heavier than protons, and mass does not explain stability.
carry negative charge
neutrons are neutral.
repel protons
neutrons carry no charge and do not repel protons electrostatically.
add attractive strong force without adding electrostatic repulsion
Correct: The short-range strong force binds all nucleons; extra neutrons add attraction without adding electrostatic repulsion, which stabilizes large nuclei.
questions.x: The short-range strong force binds all nucleons; extra neutrons add attraction without adding electrostatic repulsion, which stabilizes large nuclei. Trap: Thinking neutrons are negatively charged.

questions.q: Reactivity of alkali metals with water increases down the group primarily because:
o: ionization energy decreases as the valence electron lies farther from the nucleus
Correct: Ionization energy decreases down the group as the valence electron lies farther from the nucleus, so heavier alkali metals lose it more easily and react more vigorously.
electronegativity increases
electronegativity decreases down the group.
atomic radius decreases
atomic radius increases down the group.
effective nuclear charge increases greatly
effective nuclear charge stays nearly constant down a group because shielding grows with added shells.
questions.x: Ionization energy decreases down the group as the valence electron lies farther from the nucleus, so heavier alkali metals lose it more easily and react more vigorously. Trap: Assuming smaller atoms are more reactive.

questions.q: An element has the following successive ionization energies in kJ/mol: 577, 1817, 2745, 11,577. The element most likely has how many valence electrons?
o: 2 would put the jump after the second value;
4 would put it after the fourth;
Correct: The large jump after the third ionization energy (2745 to 11,577) means the fourth electron comes from an inner shell, so there are three valence electrons.
1 would put it after the first. The jump position, not the size of the first value, gives the valence count.
questions.x: The large jump after the third ionization energy (2745 to 11,577) means the fourth electron comes from an inner shell, so there are three valence electrons. Trap: Reading the jump position incorrectly.

questions.q: Water (molar mass 18 g/mol) boils at a much higher temperature than hydrogen sulfide (molar mass 34 g/mol). Which factor best explains this difference?
o: Extensive hydrogen bonding among water molecules
Correct: Water molecules are hydrogen-bonded (H on highly electronegative O), and breaking these intermolecular attractions on boiling requires much more energy.
Stronger London dispersion forces in water because of its larger electron cloud
Describes London forces in water, but sulfur is larger and more polarizable so H2S has the stronger dispersion forces.
A stronger covalent O-H bond compared with the S-H bond
Cites covalent O-H bond strength, which is intramolecular and not broken on boiling.
The greater molar mass of water
Cites greater molar mass for water, but water (18) is lighter than H2S (34).
questions.x: Water molecules are hydrogen-bonded (H on highly electronegative O), and breaking these intermolecular attractions on boiling requires much more energy. Trap: Students attribute boiling point to molar mass or covalent bond strength instead of intermolecular forces.

questions.q: Which property of water most directly explains why large bodies of water moderate local temperature changes?
o: Low density of liquid water relative to ice
Ice being less dense than water is true but does not govern heat capacity.
High specific heat resulting from hydrogen bonds that absorb thermal energy
Correct: Much of the added heat breaks or loosens hydrogen bonds rather than raising molecular kinetic energy, so the temperature changes slowly (high specific heat).
High dielectric constant that dissolves salts
Dielectric constant explains salt dissolving, not temperature buffering.
Amphoteric behavior in acid-base reactions
Amphoterism concerns acid-base behavior, not heat absorption.
questions.x: Much of the added heat breaks or loosens hydrogen bonds rather than raising molecular kinetic energy, so the temperature changes slowly (high specific heat). Trap: Choosing a true property of water that is unrelated to the temperature-buffering question asked.

questions.q: Ice floats on liquid water. Which statement best explains this?
o: Hydrogen bonds are absent in ice, which makes it less dense
Claims hydrogen bonds are absent in ice, but hydrogen bonding is maximal in ice.
Ice has a lower molar mass than liquid water
Claims lower molar mass, but mass per molecule is identical in both phases.
Ice forms an open hydrogen-bonded lattice in which molecules are farther apart on average than in the liquid
Correct: Each water molecule in ice makes four tetrahedrally arranged hydrogen bonds, creating an open lattice of lower density than the liquid.
Ice molecules move faster and so occupy more volume
Claims faster-moving ice molecules, but molecules in ice move less, not more.
questions.x: Each water molecule in ice makes four tetrahedrally arranged hydrogen bonds, creating an open lattice of lower density than the liquid. Trap: Believing hydrogen bonds are weaker in the solid; they are actually more fully formed and more ordered in ice.

questions.q: When NaCl dissolves in water, which interaction stabilizes Na+ in solution?
o: Attraction between Na+ and the partial positive hydrogens of water
Describes the hydrogens (delta+) facing Na+, but they orient toward anions like Cl-.
Covalent bonding between Na+ and oxygen
Proposes covalent Na+-O bonding, but solvation is a noncovalent ion-dipole interaction.
London dispersion with nonpolar regions of water
Proposes dispersion with nonpolar regions, but water has no nonpolar region relevant here.
Attraction between Na+ and the partial negative oxygen atoms of water
Correct: Cations are surrounded by water dipoles oriented with the partially negative oxygen toward the ion (ion-dipole attraction).
questions.x: Cations are surrounded by water dipoles oriented with the partially negative oxygen toward the ion (ion-dipole attraction). Trap: Reversing the orientation of the water dipole around cations versus anions.

questions.q: Nonpolar molecules tend to aggregate in water. The main driving force is:
o: An increase in the entropy of water as ordered water cages around nonpolar surfaces are released
Correct: Aggregation reduces exposed nonpolar surface, freeing ordered water cages and raising the entropy of the solvent (hydrophobic effect).
Strong attractions between nonpolar molecules and water
Claims strong nonpolar-water attractions, but those interactions are weak.
Formation of covalent bonds between nonpolar molecules
Claims covalent bonds form between nonpolar molecules, but aggregation involves only weak noncovalent forces.
A decrease in the entropy of the water
Claims water's entropy decreases, which is the opposite of what happens.
questions.x: Aggregation reduces exposed nonpolar surface, freeing ordered water cages and raising the entropy of the solvent (hydrophobic effect). Trap: Thinking the hydrophobic effect is an attraction between nonpolar molecules rather than an entropy-driven solvent effect.

questions.q: What is the pH at 25 C of a 2.0 x 10^-4 M Ba(OH)2 solution? (log 2 = 0.30)
o: 3.4 is the pOH, not the pH.
Correct: Ba(OH)2 releases 2 OH-, so [OH-] = 4.0 x 10^-4 M; pOH = 4 - log 4 = 3.4; pH = 14 - 3.4 = 10.6.
10.3 results from forgetting the factor of 2 in hydroxide concentration.
9.7 is not obtained from a valid calculation.
questions.x: Ba(OH)2 releases 2 OH-, so [OH-] = 4.0 x 10^-4 M; pOH = 4 - log 4 = 3.4; pH = 14 - 3.4 = 10.6. Trap: Forgetting that each formula unit gives two hydroxides, or reporting pOH as pH.

questions.q: A buffer contains acetic acid (pKa 4.76) and acetate with [acetate]/[acetic acid] = 10. What is the pH?
o: 3.76 results from inverting the base/acid ratio.
4.76 applies only at a 1:1 ratio.
Correct: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = 4.76 + log 10 = 5.76.
6.76 adds 2 instead of 1, as if the ratio were 100.
questions.x: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = 4.76 + log 10 = 5.76. Trap: Inverting the base/acid ratio in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

questions.q: At 50 C, Kw is about 5.5 x 10^-14 and pure water has pH near 6.6. Which statement is correct?
o: The water is acidic because pH is below 7
Says water is acidic because pH is below 7, but pH 7 is neutral only at 25 C.
The water is basic because Kw increased
Says water is basic because Kw increased, but higher Kw raises H+ and OH- equally.
The water is neutral only if pH is exactly 7
Says neutral requires pH exactly 7, but neutral pH shifts with temperature.
The water is still neutral because [H+] equals [OH-]
Correct: Autoionization is endothermic, so Kw rises with temperature; neutrality means [H+] = [OH-], not pH = 7.
questions.x: Autoionization is endothermic, so Kw rises with temperature; neutrality means [H+] = [OH-], not pH = 7. Trap: Equating neutral with pH 7 at all temperatures.

questions.q: A sparingly soluble salt AB2 has Ksp = 4.0 x 10^-12. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
o: 2.0 x 10^-6 is sqrt(Ksp), ignoring stoichiometry.
1.6 x 10^-11 squares Ksp, which has no meaning here.
4.0 x 10^-12 equates solubility with Ksp itself.
questions.x: Ksp = s(2s)^2 = 4s^3 = 4.0 x 10^-12, so s^3 = 1.0 x 10^-12 and s = 1.0 x 10^-4 M. Trap: Using Ksp = s^2 for a salt that gives three ions.

questions.q: Solid AgCl is in equilibrium with its saturated solution. Adding solid NaCl will cause:
o: Ksp of AgCl to increase
Says Ksp increases, but Ksp depends only on temperature.
Additional AgCl to precipitate and Ag+ concentration to fall
Correct: Extra Cl- shifts the dissolution equilibrium toward solid (common-ion effect), lowering [Ag+] while Ksp stays constant.
Ag+ concentration to rise
Says Ag+ rises, but the equilibrium shifts left, so Ag+ falls.
No change because NaCl is a different salt
Says no change because NaCl is different, ignoring that Cl- is shared by both salts.
questions.x: Extra Cl- shifts the dissolution equilibrium toward solid (common-ion effect), lowering [Ag+] while Ksp stays constant. Trap: Believing a different salt cannot affect solubility even when it shares an ion.

questions.q: Which 0.10 m aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point?
o: NaCl
NaCl gives only about 2 particles per formula unit.
Glucose
Glucose does not dissociate (i = 1).
CaCl2
Correct: Freezing point depression = i Kf m; CaCl2 dissociates into about 3 particles per formula unit, giving the largest effect.
Sucrose
Sucrose does not dissociate (i = 1).
questions.x: Freezing point depression = i Kf m; CaCl2 dissociates into about 3 particles per formula unit, giving the largest effect. Trap: Comparing molality alone without counting dissolved particles.

questions.q: A red blood cell is placed in a 3% (w/v) NaCl solution, which is hypertonic relative to the cell. What happens?
o: Water enters the cell and it lyses
Describes water entry and lysis, which occur in hypotonic solutions.
Na+ and Cl- diffuse freely into the cell with no volume change
Claims ions diffuse freely with no volume change, but the membrane is not freely permeable to ions.
Nothing, because osmosis stops at the membrane
Claims nothing happens, but osmosis does occur across the membrane.
Water leaves the cell and the cell shrinks (crenation)
Correct: Water diffuses toward the higher solute concentration across the membrane, so the cell in hypertonic solution loses water and crenates.
questions.x: Water diffuses toward the higher solute concentration across the membrane, so the cell in hypertonic solution loses water and crenates. Trap: Reversing the direction of water movement relative to the solute gradient.

questions.q: In aqueous solution above its critical micelle concentration, a soap forms micelles in which:
o: Hydrophilic heads face the water and hydrocarbon tails cluster inside
Correct: The amphipathic structure lets hydrophilic heads hydrogen-bond or ion-pair with water while hydrocarbon tails sequester inside.
Hydrocarbon tails face the water and heads cluster inside
Describes the reverse arrangement, which forms in nonpolar solvents.
Molecules form a single flat layer with no curvature in the bulk
Describes a flat layer with no curvature, but micelles are curved aggregates.
All molecules remain dissolved as individual ions
Describes individual dissolved ions, but above the CMC aggregation dominates.
questions.x: The amphipathic structure lets hydrophilic heads hydrogen-bond or ion-pair with water while hydrocarbon tails sequester inside. Trap: Placing the hydrophobic tails toward the water.

questions.q: Water climbs the narrow xylem of a plant against gravity. Which pair of properties is most responsible?
o: High density and low viscosity
Density and viscosity do not explain upward movement against gravity.
Adhesion to vessel walls and cohesion among water molecules
Correct: Hydrogen bonding makes water cohesive and adhesive to polar wall surfaces, supporting capillary rise and continuous water columns.
Nonpolarity and low surface tension
Water is polar with high, not low, surface tension.
Ionization and high pH
Ionization is negligible and high pH is irrelevant to xylem transport.
questions.x: Hydrogen bonding makes water cohesive and adhesive to polar wall surfaces, supporting capillary rise and continuous water columns. Trap: Naming surface tension reduction instead of the cohesion-adhesion pair.

questions.q: Why does adding a surfactant to water lower its surface tension?
o: Surfactants raise the temperature of the water
Surfactants do not heat water.
Surfactants form covalent bonds with water
Surfactants do not covalently bond to water.
Amphipathic molecules at the surface disrupt the hydrogen-bond network between surface water molecules
Correct: Surface tension arises from net inward cohesion; amphipathic surfactants at the surface interpose and weaken the hydrogen-bonded interactions.
Surfactants increase the density of water
Density change is not the cause of lowered surface tension.
questions.x: Surface tension arises from net inward cohesion; amphipathic surfactants at the surface interpose and weaken the hydrogen-bonded interactions. Trap: Confusing surface tension with bulk density.

questions.q: Evaporation of sweat cools the skin primarily because:
o: Water is a poor conductor of heat
Poor heat conduction is not the cooling mechanism.
Sweat has a lower specific heat than skin
Sweat having lower specific heat than skin is not the reason.
Evaporation releases heat to the skin
Evaporation absorbs heat rather than releasing it.
The most energetic molecules leave, and water has a large heat of vaporization due to hydrogen bonds
Correct: Vaporization is endothermic; the most energetic molecules escape, and water's large heat of vaporization (hydrogen bonds) carries away much energy, cooling the skin.
questions.x: Vaporization is endothermic; the most energetic molecules escape, and water's large heat of vaporization (hydrogen bonds) carries away much energy, cooling the skin. Trap: Thinking evaporation is exothermic because condensation feels warm.

questions.q: A researcher needs to buffer a solution at pH 7.2. Which weak acid (pKa given) is the best choice?
o: pKa 7.1
Correct: A buffer works best within about one pH unit of its pKa, with maximal capacity where pH = pKa, so pKa 7.1 suits pH 7.2.
pKa 3.1
pKa 3.1 is over 4 pH units from 7.2, giving poor capacity.
pKa 5.0
pKa 5.0 is more than 2 pH units away, giving poor capacity.
pKa 9.3
pKa 9.3 is more than 2 pH units away, giving poor capacity.
questions.x: A buffer works best within about one pH unit of its pKa, with maximal capacity where pH = pKa, so pKa 7.1 suits pH 7.2. Trap: Choosing based on a strong acid or a pKa far from the target pH.

questions.q: A weak monoprotic acid HA is titrated with NaOH. At the half-equivalence point the pH is 4.2. What is the pKa of HA?
o: 8.4 doubles the pH with no basis.
Correct: At half-equivalence [HA] = [A-], so pH = pKa = 4.2.
2.1 halves the pH with no basis.
7.0 is not the half-equivalence pH for a weak acid titrated with strong base.
questions.x: At half-equivalence [HA] = [A-], so pH = pKa = 4.2. Trap: Confusing the half-equivalence point with the equivalence point, where pH exceeds 7.

questions.q: What is the pH of a 0.10 M weak acid with Ka = 1.0 x 10^-5? (Assume x is small.)
o: 5.0 sets pH equal to pKa, which applies only to buffers at half-neutralization.
1.0 treats the acid as fully dissociated (strong).
Correct: [H+] = sqrt(Ka C) = sqrt(1.0 x 10^-6) = 1.0 x 10^-3 M, so pH = 3.0.
2.0 comes from an incorrect square-root calculation.
questions.x: [H+] = sqrt(Ka C) = sqrt(1.0 x 10^-6) = 1.0 x 10^-3 M, so pH = 3.0. Trap: Treating a weak acid as fully dissociated or setting pH equal to pKa.

questions.q: Why do fish in warm water sometimes show distress from low oxygen?
o: Warm water contains more hydrogen bonds
Claims warm water has more hydrogen bonds, but it has fewer.
Oxygen becomes more polar when heated
Claims oxygen becomes more polar when heated, but its polarity is unchanged.
Henry's law states solubility is independent of temperature
Claims Henry's law solubility is temperature independent, but Henry's constant depends on temperature.
Dissolution of gases in water is exothermic, so solubility decreases as temperature rises
Correct: Gas dissolution in water is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier gas solubility falls as temperature rises, leaving less dissolved O2.
questions.x: Gas dissolution in water is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier gas solubility falls as temperature rises, leaving less dissolved O2. Trap: Assuming all dissolution processes become more favorable with heat, as is true for many solids.

questions.q: In the reaction NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-, water acts as:
o: A Bronsted-Lowry acid
Correct: Water donates a proton to ammonia, so it is the Bronsted acid and OH- is its conjugate base.
A Bronsted-Lowry base
Water would be a base only if it accepted a proton (as with HCl).
A spectator
Water is not a spectator; it participates directly in proton transfer.
A Lewis acid only
Lewis acid only ignores that the Bronsted proton-transfer role is what is defined here.
questions.x: Water donates a proton to ammonia, so it is the Bronsted acid and OH- is its conjugate base. Trap: Assuming water is always the base or always the acid.

questions.q: CO2 has polar C=O bonds yet has no net dipole moment. This is because:
o: The C=O bonds are nonpolar
Says the C=O bonds are nonpolar, but O is more electronegative than C so each bond is polar.
Its linear geometry causes the bond dipoles to cancel
Correct: The two equal C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions in a linear molecule, so the vector sum is zero.
Carbon and oxygen have equal electronegativities
Says C and O have equal electronegativities, which is false (O is 3.5, C is 2.5).
The molecule is bent and the dipoles cancel
Says CO2 is bent, but it is linear.
questions.x: The two equal C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions in a linear molecule, so the vector sum is zero. Trap: Assuming polar bonds always yield a polar molecule.

questions.q: Which statement about SO2 is correct?
o: It is linear and nonpolar
Linear would require no lone pair and cannot be reached with three domains.
It is trigonal planar and nonpolar
Trigonal planar describes the electron geometry; the lone pair makes the molecular shape bent and polar.
It is bent and polar
Correct: Sulfur has two bonded oxygens and one lone pair (three electron domains), giving a bent shape with a net dipole.
It is tetrahedral and polar
Tetrahedral would need four electron domains.
questions.x: Sulfur has two bonded oxygens and one lone pair (three electron domains), giving a bent shape with a net dipole. Trap: Ignoring the lone pair when predicting molecular shape.

questions.q: Why is the H-O-H bond angle in water (about 104.5 degrees) smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5 degrees?
o: The oxygen is sp2 hybridized
Says oxygen is sp2, but oxygen in water is approximately sp3.
Hydrogen atoms repel each other more strongly than lone pairs do
Says H atoms repel more than lone pairs, but lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs.
Oxygen has no lone pairs
Says oxygen has no lone pairs, but it has two.
Lone pair-bonding pair repulsion exceeds bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion
Correct: Lone pairs occupy more space, so lone pair-bonding pair repulsion exceeds bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion and compresses the angle below 109.5.
questions.x: Lone pairs occupy more space, so lone pair-bonding pair repulsion exceeds bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion and compresses the angle below 109.5. Trap: Counting only bonded atoms when deciding geometry.

questions.q: Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) boils at 78 C while dimethyl ether (CH3OCH3), its isomer, boils at about -24 C. The best explanation is:
o: Ethanol can hydrogen bond to itself, whereas dimethyl ether cannot
Correct: Ethanol has an O-H group that serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, whereas the ether has no H on oxygen.
Ethanol has a higher molar mass
Cites higher molar mass, but the two are isomers with identical molar mass.
Dimethyl ether has stronger dispersion forces
Claims dimethyl ether has stronger dispersion forces, but they are comparable and cannot explain a 100 C gap.
Dimethyl ether is nonpolar
Claims dimethyl ether is nonpolar, but its bent C-O-C geometry makes it polar.
questions.x: Ethanol has an O-H group that serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, whereas the ether has no H on oxygen. Trap: Attributing the difference to molar mass when the compounds are isomers.

questions.q: Which has the lower boiling point, n-pentane or neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane), and why?
o: n-Pentane, because it is more branched
Says n-pentane is more branched, but n-pentane is the unbranched isomer.
Neopentane, because its compact shape reduces surface area for dispersion forces
Correct: Branching lowers contact surface area, weakening London dispersion forces, so compact neopentane boils lower.
Neopentane, because it has lower molar mass
Says neopentane has lower molar mass, but both are C5H12 with identical mass.
They are equal because they are isomers
Says isomers have equal boiling points, but shape changes dispersion forces.
questions.x: Branching lowers contact surface area, weakening London dispersion forces, so compact neopentane boils lower. Trap: Assuming isomers have the same physical properties.

questions.q: What is the hybridization of each carbon in ethyne (HC≡CH)?
o: sp2
sp2 corresponds to three electron domains.
sp3
sp3 corresponds to four electron domains.
sp
Correct: Each carbon has two electron domains (one sigma bond to H, one to C), requiring sp hybrids; the two pi bonds use unhybridized p orbitals.
sp3d
sp3d is not used for carbon.
questions.x: Each carbon has two electron domains (one sigma bond to H, one to C), requiring sp hybrids; the two pi bonds use unhybridized p orbitals. Trap: Counting bonds rather than electron domains.

questions.q: How many sigma and pi bonds are in acetonitrile, CH3-C≡N?
o: 4 sigma and 3 pi
4 sigma omits one sigma bond and 3 pi counts the triple bond as all pi.
3 sigma and 3 pi
3 sigma omits the C-C and C-N sigma bonds and 3 pi overcounts pi bonds.
5 sigma and 3 pi
5 sigma with 3 pi overcounts pi bonds; a triple bond has one sigma and two pi.
5 sigma and 2 pi
Correct: Three C-H sigma bonds, one C-C sigma bond and one C-N sigma bond give 5 sigma; the triple bond contains 2 pi bonds.
questions.x: Three C-H sigma bonds, one C-C sigma bond and one C-N sigma bond give 5 sigma; the triple bond contains 2 pi bonds. Trap: Counting a triple bond as three pi bonds or forgetting the C-H bonds.

questions.q: Which ordering of carbon-carbon bonds is correct for bond length (longest to shortest)?
o: C-C > C=C > C≡C
Correct: Higher bond order pulls the atoms closer, so C-C is longest, then C=C, then C≡C shortest.
C≡C > C=C > C-C
Reverses the order, placing the triple bond longest.
C=C > C-C > C≡C
Places C=C longest and scrambles the bond-order ranking.
C-C > C≡C > C=C
Places the triple bond ahead of the double bond in length, contradicting bond order.
questions.x: Higher bond order pulls the atoms closer, so C-C is longest, then C=C, then C≡C shortest. Trap: Assuming stronger bonds are longer.

questions.q: Which bond is the most polar?
o: C-O
C-O has a smaller difference since O (3.5) is less electronegative than F.
C-F
Correct: Polarity increases with electronegativity difference; F is the most electronegative partner (4.0 vs 2.5 for C).
C-N
C-N has a smaller difference since N (3.0) is less electronegative than F.
C-Cl
C-Cl has a smaller difference since Cl (3.0) is less electronegative than F.
questions.x: Polarity increases with electronegativity difference; F is the most electronegative partner (4.0 vs 2.5 for C). Trap: Picking oxygen because it is common in biomolecules.

questions.q: What is the formal charge on oxygen in the hydronium ion, H3O+?
o: 0 would require 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs, as in neutral water.
-1 would need one bond and three lone pairs, as in hydroxide.
Correct: Oxygen has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair: 6 - 2 - 3 = +1.
+2 does not result from any valid count for this structure.
questions.x: Oxygen has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair: 6 - 2 - 3 = +1. Trap: Forgetting to count lone-pair electrons in formal charge.

questions.q: In the carbonate ion, CO3^2-, how do the three C-O bond lengths compare?
o: One is shorter than the other two
Says one bond is shorter, treating one resonance structure as real.
Two are single and one is double
Says two are single and one double, again treating a single Lewis structure as the real structure.
All are single bonds
Says all are single bonds, ignoring the partial double-bond character.
All three are equal, intermediate between single and double bonds
Correct: Resonance delocalizes charge and double-bond character evenly over three equivalent oxygens (bond order about 1.33), so all C-O bonds are equal.
questions.x: Resonance delocalizes charge and double-bond character evenly over three equivalent oxygens (bond order about 1.33), so all C-O bonds are equal. Trap: Treating one resonance structure as the real structure.

questions.q: At the same temperature, which liquid has the highest vapor pressure?
o: Diethyl ether
Correct: Diethyl ether lacks hydrogen-bond donors and has weaker intermolecular forces, so more molecules escape to the vapor.
Ethanol
Ethanol is strongly hydrogen bonded, lowering its vapor pressure.
Water
Water is strongly hydrogen bonded, lowering its vapor pressure.
Ethylene glycol
Ethylene glycol has two OH groups and strong hydrogen bonding, giving very low vapor pressure.
questions.x: Diethyl ether lacks hydrogen-bond donors and has weaker intermolecular forces, so more molecules escape to the vapor. Trap: Linking higher molar mass with higher vapor pressure.

questions.q: Which solute is most soluble in hexane?
o: NaCl
NaCl is ionic and does not interact favorably with hexane.
I2
Correct: Hexane is nonpolar; nonpolar I2 dissolves through dispersion interactions (like dissolves like).
Glucose
Glucose is highly polar with many OH groups, so it is poorly soluble in hexane.
KOH
KOH is ionic and insoluble in nonpolar hexane.
questions.x: Hexane is nonpolar; nonpolar I2 dissolves through dispersion interactions (like dissolves like). Trap: Choosing based on molecular size instead of polarity.

questions.q: Which ranking of typical interaction strengths is correct, strongest to weakest?
o: London dispersion > hydrogen bond > ion-dipole > dipole-dipole
Places dispersion first and ion-dipole and dipole-dipole in reverse order.
Dipole-dipole > ion-dipole > London dispersion > hydrogen bond
Places dipole-dipole first and hydrogen bonds last, which scrambles the order.
Ion-dipole > hydrogen bond > dipole-dipole > London dispersion (for comparable small molecules)
Correct: Charge-involving interactions are strongest, followed by hydrogen bonds, then permanent dipoles, then transient induced dipoles.
Hydrogen bond > London dispersion > ion-dipole > dipole-dipole
Places hydrogen bond above ion-dipole and dispersion above dipole-dipole, both incorrect.
questions.x: Charge-involving interactions are strongest, followed by hydrogen bonds, then permanent dipoles, then transient induced dipoles. Trap: Forgetting that ion-dipole interactions outrank hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: Which noble gas has the highest boiling point?
o: Neon
Neon has few electrons and weak induced dipoles.
Helium
Helium has the fewest electrons and the lowest boiling point of all.
Argon
Argon is more polarizable than Ne and He but less than Xe.
Xenon
Correct: Larger atoms are more polarizable, so dispersion forces and boiling points increase down the group; Xe is the largest.
questions.x: Larger atoms are more polarizable, so dispersion forces and boiling points increase down the group; Xe is the largest. Trap: Assuming heavier atoms have lower boiling points like in some other periodic trends.

questions.q: Which compound cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor to itself?
o: Acetone (CH3COCH3)
Correct: Acetone has no H attached to O, N or F, so it can accept but not donate hydrogen bonds.
Ethanol
Ethanol has an O-H donor hydrogen.
Acetic acid
Acetic acid has an O-H donor hydrogen (and forms dimers).
Methylamine
Methylamine has N-H donor hydrogens.
questions.x: Acetone has no H attached to O, N or F, so it can accept but not donate hydrogen bonds. Trap: Thinking any compound with an oxygen can donate hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: A DNA duplex rich in G-C pairs has a higher melting temperature than an A-T-rich duplex because:
o: G-C pairs form covalent bonds
Says G-C pairs form covalent bonds, but base pairs are held by non-covalent hydrogen bonds.
G-C pairs share three hydrogen bonds, A-T pairs only two
Correct: G-C pairs share three hydrogen bonds versus two for A-T, and stack more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate the strands.
A-T pairs contain more phosphate
Says A-T pairs contain more phosphate, but phosphates are in the backbone, not the pairing.
G is a pyrimidine and A is a purine
Says G is a pyrimidine and A a purine, but both are purines.
questions.x: G-C pairs share three hydrogen bonds versus two for A-T, and stack more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate the strands. Trap: Confusing hydrogen bond count between G-C and A-T.

questions.q: In an alpha helix, hydrogen bonds form between:
o: The side chains of adjacent residues only
Says side chains of adjacent residues bond, but side chains are not the main source.
Backbone atoms of residues on different strands
Describes cross-strand backbone bonds, which are the pattern in beta sheets.
The backbone C=O of residue i and the backbone N-H of residue i+4
Correct: In an alpha helix the backbone C=O of residue i hydrogen bonds to the backbone N-H of residue i+4, parallel to the helix axis.
Disulfide-bonded cysteines
Disulfides are covalent bonds, not hydrogen bonds.
questions.x: In an alpha helix the backbone C=O of residue i hydrogen bonds to the backbone N-H of residue i+4, parallel to the helix axis. Trap: Mixing up alpha-helix and beta-sheet hydrogen bonding patterns.

questions.q: Why does NaCl have a much higher melting point than methane?
o: Methane has strong hydrogen bonds
Methane cannot hydrogen bond since it has no O-H, N-H or F-H.
NaCl has stronger dispersion forces
NaCl does not owe its melting point to dispersion forces; its ionic attractions are much stronger.
Methane has covalent network bonding
Methane is a molecular solid, not a covalent network.
Strong electrostatic forces in the ionic lattice must be overcome
Correct: Strong Coulombic attractions in the ionic lattice must be overcome to melt NaCl, far stronger than dispersion forces between methane molecules.
questions.x: Strong Coulombic attractions in the ionic lattice must be overcome to melt NaCl, far stronger than dispersion forces between methane molecules. Trap: Thinking covalent bonds within methane must break on melting.

questions.q: Compressing ice at a temperature slightly below 0 C can cause it to melt. Which feature of the phase diagram explains this?
o: The solid-liquid boundary has a negative slope
Correct: Because ice is less dense than water, increased pressure favors the liquid, so the solid-liquid boundary slopes backward (negative slope).
The triple point lies at high pressure
The triple point location does not explain melting under compression.
The critical point is above 100 C
The critical point concerns liquid-gas behavior, not ice melting under pressure.
The sublimation curve is horizontal
Sublimation curves slope upward, not horizontally, and relate to solid-gas transition.
questions.x: Because ice is less dense than water, increased pressure favors the liquid, so the solid-liquid boundary slopes backward (negative slope). Trap: Assuming the solid-liquid line always slopes positively.

questions.q: A solution has a solvent mole fraction of 0.80, and the pure solvent has vapor pressure 100 torr. Assuming ideal behavior, what is the solvent vapor pressure above the solution?
o: 20 torr
20 torr uses the solute mole fraction instead of the solvent's.
80 torr
Correct: Raoult's law gives P = X(solvent) x P° = 0.80 x 100 = 80 torr.
125 torr
125 torr inverts the relation by dividing by 0.80.
100 torr
100 torr ignores the dissolved solute, which lowers vapor pressure.
questions.x: Raoult's law gives P = X(solvent) x P° = 0.80 x 100 = 80 torr. Trap: Using solute mole fraction in Raoult's law.

questions.q: Which statement about 1,2-dichloroethene is correct?
o: The trans isomer is polar and has the higher boiling point
Says trans is polar, but the trans isomer has zero net dipole.
Both isomers are nonpolar
Says both are nonpolar, but both contain polar C-Cl bonds and cis has a net dipole.
The cis isomer is polar and has the higher boiling point
Correct: In the cis isomer the C-Cl dipoles add; in the trans isomer they cancel, so dipole-dipole forces raise the cis boiling point.
Both isomers have identical dipole moments
Says dipole moments are identical, but cis has a net dipole and trans has none.
questions.x: In the cis isomer the C-Cl dipoles add; in the trans isomer they cancel, so dipole-dipole forces raise the cis boiling point. Trap: Assuming the symmetric trans isomer must be the polar one, or that both isomers behave identically because they have the same bonds.

questions.q: The nitrogen in an amide is planar rather than pyramidal because:
o: It has no lone pair
Says N has no lone pair, but it does, and that lone pair is what delocalizes.
It is sp3 hybridized
Says N is sp3, but a localized sp3 nitrogen would be pyramidal.
Hydrogen bonding forces it to flatten
Says hydrogen bonding flattens N, but the planarity arises from resonance.
Resonance delocalizes its lone pair into the carbonyl, giving partial double-bond character
Correct: Resonance delocalizes the N lone pair into the carbonyl, giving partial C-N double-bond character, planar geometry and restricted rotation.
questions.x: Resonance delocalizes the N lone pair into the carbonyl, giving partial C-N double-bond character, planar geometry and restricted rotation. Trap: Assuming nitrogen always remains sp3.

questions.q: Using bond energies (H-H 436, Cl-Cl 243, H-Cl 431 kJ/mol), what is the estimated delta H for H2 + Cl2 -> 2 HCl?
o: -183 kJ/mol
Correct: delta H = bonds broken - bonds formed = (436 + 243) - 2(431) = 679 - 862 = -183 kJ/mol.
+183 kJ/mol
+183 reverses the sign by subtracting broken from formed.
-862 kJ/mol
-862 counts only the bonds formed.
+679 kJ/mol
+679 counts only the bonds broken.
questions.x: delta H = bonds broken - bonds formed = (436 + 243) - 2(431) = 679 - 862 = -183 kJ/mol. Trap: Reversing bonds broken and formed.

questions.q: Which molecule contains a central atom with an expanded octet?
o: CF4
Carbon in CF4 has 8 electrons and obeys the octet.
SF6
Correct: Sulfur, a third-period element, can accommodate 12 electrons around it in SF6, an expanded octet.
NF3
Nitrogen in NF3 has 8 electrons and is a second-period atom.
OF2
Oxygen in OF2 has 8 electrons and is a second-period atom.
questions.x: Sulfur, a third-period element, can accommodate 12 electrons around it in SF6, an expanded octet. Trap: Applying the octet rule to third-period atoms.

questions.q: Which molecule is polar?
o: CCl4
CCl4 is symmetric tetrahedral, so its C-Cl dipoles cancel.
CH4
CH4 is symmetric tetrahedral with nearly nonpolar bonds.
CHCl3
Correct: CHCl3 has asymmetric bond dipoles (C-H and C-Cl differ) that do not cancel, giving a net dipole.
CF4
CF4 is symmetric tetrahedral, so its C-F dipoles cancel.
questions.x: CHCl3 has asymmetric bond dipoles (C-H and C-Cl differ) that do not cancel, giving a net dipole. Trap: Judging polarity only from the presence of polar bonds.

questions.q: In a soluble globular protein, nonpolar side chains are typically found:
o: On the surface exposed to water
Says they sit on the surface, but surface residues are mostly polar or charged.
Only at the N-terminus
Says they appear only at the N-terminus, but location is not terminus-dependent.
Only in disulfide bonds
Says they appear only in disulfides, but disulfides involve cysteine only.
In the interior, away from water
Correct: Burying nonpolar side chains minimizes unfavorable contact with water, driving folding (hydrophobic effect).
questions.x: Burying nonpolar side chains minimizes unfavorable contact with water, driving folding (hydrophobic effect). Trap: Reversing the pattern for membrane versus soluble proteins.

questions.q: What are the bond angles in PCl5, which has trigonal bipyramidal geometry?
o: 90 and 120 degrees
Correct: In trigonal bipyramidal geometry axial-equatorial angles are 90 degrees and equatorial-equatorial angles are 120 degrees.
109.5 degrees only
109.5 describes tetrahedral geometry.
180 degrees only
180 degrees alone describes a linear arrangement (axial-axial is only one of the angles).
90 degrees only
90 only describes octahedral-like angles, missing the 120 degree equatorial angles.
questions.x: In trigonal bipyramidal geometry axial-equatorial angles are 90 degrees and equatorial-equatorial angles are 120 degrees. Trap: Using a single ideal angle for all five-domain geometries.

questions.q: At room temperature Br2 is a liquid while Cl2 is a gas. The best explanation is:
o: Br2 forms hydrogen bonds
Says Br2 hydrogen bonds, but it has no H on N, O or F.
Br2 is larger and more polarizable, giving stronger dispersion forces
Correct: Br2 is larger and more polarizable, so its dispersion forces are stronger, making it liquid at room temperature.
Br2 has a larger permanent dipole
Says Br2 has a permanent dipole, but homonuclear diatomics are nonpolar.
Br2 has a stronger covalent bond than Cl2
Cites stronger covalent bond, but vaporization overcomes intermolecular forces, and the Br-Br bond is actually weaker.
questions.x: Br2 is larger and more polarizable, so its dispersion forces are stronger, making it liquid at room temperature. Trap: Attributing physical state to bond strength or permanent dipoles.

questions.q: Which ordering of boiling points (lowest to highest) is correct for butane, propanal and 1-propanol?
o: Propanal < butane < 1-propanol
Puts propanal below butane, ignoring propanal's dipole-dipole attractions.
1-Propanol < propanal < butane
Reverses the order, placing hydrogen-bonding 1-propanol lowest.
Butane < propanal < 1-propanol
Correct: Butane has only dispersion forces, propanal adds dipole-dipole, and 1-propanol hydrogen bonds, giving the highest boiling point.
Butane < 1-propanol < propanal
Places 1-propanol below propanal, underestimating hydrogen bonding.
questions.x: Butane has only dispersion forces, propanal adds dipole-dipole, and 1-propanol hydrogen bonds, giving the highest boiling point. Trap: Ignoring forces when molar masses are similar.

questions.q: Which diatomic molecule has the highest bond dissociation energy?
o: O2
O2 has only a double bond.
F2
F2 has only a weak single bond.
Cl2
Cl2 has only a single bond.
N2
Correct: The triple bond of N2 (about 945 kJ/mol) is very strong.
questions.x: The triple bond of N2 (about 945 kJ/mol) is very strong. Trap: Choosing based on atomic size.

questions.q: Which statement describes the formation of NH4+ from NH3 and H+?
o: Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H+, forming a coordinate covalent bond
Correct: A lone pair on N is shared with the proton, forming a coordinate covalent bond; all four N-H bonds are then equivalent.
Hydrogen donates an electron pair to nitrogen
Says hydrogen donates a pair, but H+ has no electrons to donate.
An ionic bond forms between N and H+
Says an ionic bond forms, but the bond is covalent.
Nitrogen loses an electron to hydrogen
Says nitrogen loses an electron to hydrogen, but no electron transfer occurs.
questions.x: A lone pair on N is shared with the proton, forming a coordinate covalent bond; all four N-H bonds are then equivalent. Trap: Reversing the role of Lewis acid and Lewis base.

questions.q: Which ionic compound has the larger lattice energy, MgO or NaCl?
o: NaCl, because it has a larger ion
Says NaCl is larger because of a larger ion, but larger ions lower lattice energy.
MgO, because the ions have higher charges
Correct: Lattice energy scales with the product of charges (2+/2- vs 1+/1-) and inversely with ion separation, so MgO is much larger.
NaCl, because Na+ is a smaller ion
Says NaCl is larger because Na+ is smaller, ignoring that MgO ions are even smaller and more highly charged.
They are equal
Says they are equal, but the charges differ.
questions.x: Lattice energy scales with the product of charges (2+/2- vs 1+/1-) and inversely with ion separation, so MgO is much larger. Trap: Focusing on radius alone while ignoring charge.

questions.q: Why does water boil at a lower temperature at high altitude?
o: The covalent bonds in water are weaker
Says covalent bonds weaken, but altitude does not change O-H bond strength.
Water has fewer hydrogen bonds at altitude
Says fewer hydrogen bonds at altitude, but hydrogen bonding depends on temperature, not altitude.
Boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals the lower external pressure
Correct: Boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals external pressure; at altitude the external pressure is lower, so boiling occurs at a lower temperature.
Water has a lower specific heat at altitude
Says specific heat is lower at altitude, but specific heat is unaffected.
questions.x: Boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals external pressure; at altitude the external pressure is lower, so boiling occurs at a lower temperature. Trap: Treating boiling as a function of bond strength.

questions.q: o-Nitrophenol has a lower boiling point than p-nitrophenol. This is best explained by:
o: Greater molar mass of the para isomer
Says the para isomer has greater mass, but the isomers have equal mass.
Weaker covalent bonds in the ortho isomer
Says covalent bonds are weaker in ortho, but covalent strength is not what is overcome in boiling.
Absence of an -OH group in the ortho isomer
Says ortho lacks an OH group, but both isomers have the same groups.
Intramolecular hydrogen bonding in the ortho isomer reduces intermolecular attractions
Correct: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding in the ortho isomer leaves fewer groups free to bond between molecules, lowering the boiling point.
questions.x: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding in the ortho isomer leaves fewer groups free to bond between molecules, lowering the boiling point. Trap: Assuming all hydrogen bonding raises boiling point.

questions.q: A dipole consists of charges +q and -q separated by distance d. If d doubles while q remains the same, the dipole moment:
o: Doubles
Correct: Dipole moment mu = q x d, so doubling d doubles mu.
Halves
Halving would require an inverse relationship, which does not apply.
Quadruples
Quadrupling would require a quadratic dependence on d.
Stays unchanged
Staying unchanged ignores that mu depends linearly on separation.
questions.x: Dipole moment mu = q x d, so doubling d doubles mu. Trap: Misapplying inverse-square relationships from Coulomb's law.

questions.q: Which is the largest ion among O2-, F-, Na+ and Mg2+?
o: F-
F- has 9 protons, so it is pulled in more than O2-.
Correct: These ions are isoelectronic (10 electrons); O2- has the fewest protons (8), the weakest nuclear pull, and the largest radius.
Na+
Na+ has 11 protons, pulling the same 10 electrons more tightly.
Mg2+
Mg2+ has 12 protons and is the smallest of the group.
questions.x: These ions are isoelectronic (10 electrons); O2- has the fewest protons (8), the weakest nuclear pull, and the largest radius. Trap: Assuming anions are always larger than cations of the next period without comparing protons.

questions.q: Rotation about a carbon-carbon double bond is restricted because:
o: Sigma bonds cannot rotate
Says sigma bonds cannot rotate, but sigma bonds rotate freely.
The double bond is longer than a single bond
Says double bonds are longer, but they are shorter, and length does not cause the restriction.
Rotation would break the overlap of the pi bond
Correct: Pi overlap between parallel p orbitals is lost on twisting 90 degrees, so rotation is restricted and cis/trans isomers are stable.
Hydrogen bonding locks it
Says hydrogen bonding locks it, which has nothing to do with alkene rotation.
questions.x: Pi overlap between parallel p orbitals is lost on twisting 90 degrees, so rotation is restricted and cis/trans isomers are stable. Trap: Believing sigma bonds restrict rotation.

questions.q: Which molecule is trigonal planar?
o: NF3
NF3 has a lone pair on N, giving trigonal pyramidal shape.
PCl3
PCl3 has a lone pair on P, giving trigonal pyramidal shape.
NH3
NH3 has a lone pair on N, giving trigonal pyramidal shape.
BF3
Correct: Boron in BF3 has three bonding domains and no lone pair, giving trigonal planar geometry.
questions.x: Boron in BF3 has three bonding domains and no lone pair, giving trigonal planar geometry. Trap: Ignoring lone pairs on central atoms.

questions.q: In the reaction BF3 + NH3 -> F3B-NH3, which species is the Lewis acid?
o: BF3, which accepts an electron pair
Correct: Boron in BF3 has an incomplete octet and accepts the nitrogen lone pair, so BF3 is the Lewis acid.
NH3, which accepts an electron pair
Says NH3 accepts a pair, but NH3 donates its lone pair and is the Lewis base.
BF3, which donates an electron pair
Says BF3 donates a pair, but it accepts one.
NH3, which donates a proton
Says NH3 donates a proton, but no proton transfer occurs here.
questions.x: Boron in BF3 has an incomplete octet and accepts the nitrogen lone pair, so BF3 is the Lewis acid. Trap: Confusing Lewis definitions with Bronsted definitions.

questions.q: A mixture of benzoic acid and naphthalene in diethyl ether is shaken with aqueous NaOH. Which species ends up mainly in the aqueous layer?
o: Naphthalene
Naphthalene is nonpolar and neutral, so it remains in the ether.
Benzoic acid
Benzoic acid is protonated and neutral only without base; with NaOH it is converted to its salt.
Sodium benzoate
Correct: NaOH deprotonates benzoic acid to the ionic, water-soluble sodium benzoate, which partitions into the aqueous layer while naphthalene stays in the ether.
Diethyl ether
Diethyl ether is the organic solvent, not a solute in the aqueous layer.
questions.x: NaOH deprotonates benzoic acid to the ionic, water-soluble sodium benzoate, which partitions into the aqueous layer while naphthalene stays in the ether. Trap: Forgetting that ionization makes an organic acid water soluble.

questions.q: Which aqueous wash would best remove an amine impurity from an organic layer?
o: Dilute NaOH
Dilute NaOH keeps the amine neutral, so it stays in the organic layer.
Saturated NaCl only
Brine alone does not ionize the amine, so it stays organic.
Pure water
Pure water does not protonate the amine, so little is removed.
Dilute HCl
Correct: Dilute HCl protonates the amine to a water-soluble ammonium salt that moves into the aqueous layer.
questions.x: Dilute HCl protonates the amine to a water-soluble ammonium salt that moves into the aqueous layer. Trap: Using base to extract a basic compound.

questions.q: Dichloromethane (density 1.33 g/mL) is shaken with water in a separatory funnel. Where is the organic layer?
o: On the bottom
Correct: The denser liquid sits at the bottom; dichloromethane (1.33 g/mL) is denser than water and immiscible with it, so it forms the bottom layer.
On the top
Top would apply to a less dense solvent like diethyl ether.
It forms a single layer
A single layer would require miscibility, but DCM and water are immiscible.
It sits in the stopcock
The stopcock is a valve, not a layer location.
questions.x: The denser liquid sits at the bottom; dichloromethane (1.33 g/mL) is denser than water and immiscible with it, so it forms the bottom layer. Trap: Assuming organic layers are always on top.

questions.q: Two miscible liquids have boiling points of 80 C and 90 C. Which technique is best to separate them?
o: Simple distillation
Simple distillation works only if the difference is large (about 25 C or more).
Fractional distillation
Correct: A fractionating column provides many vaporization-condensation cycles, needed when boiling points differ by only about 10 C.
Filtration
Filtration separates solids from liquids, not miscible liquids.
Recrystallization
Recrystallization purifies solids, not liquid mixtures.
questions.x: A fractionating column provides many vaporization-condensation cycles, needed when boiling points differ by only about 10 C. Trap: Choosing simple distillation for close boiling points.

questions.q: Vacuum distillation is used for compounds that:
o: Boil below room temperature
Compounds boiling below room temperature do not need vacuum.
Are solids at room temperature
Solids are purified by other methods such as recrystallization.
Have very high boiling points or decompose when heated
Correct: Lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point, so high-boiling or heat-sensitive compounds distill without decomposing.
Are immiscible with water
Water immiscibility is irrelevant to vacuum distillation.
questions.x: Lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point, so high-boiling or heat-sensitive compounds distill without decomposing. Trap: Thinking vacuum raises boiling point.

questions.q: Fractional distillation of an ethanol-water mixture cannot produce pure ethanol because:
o: Water and ethanol are immiscible
Ethanol and water are fully miscible.
Ethanol decomposes upon heating
Ethanol does not decompose at its boiling point.
Water has a lower boiling point than ethanol
than ethanol (78 C), not lower.
A minimum-boiling azeotrope forms near 95% ethanol
Correct: A minimum-boiling azeotrope forms near 95% ethanol, where vapor and liquid have the same composition, so further enrichment is impossible.
questions.x: A minimum-boiling azeotrope forms near 95% ethanol, where vapor and liquid have the same composition, so further enrichment is impossible. Trap: Assuming distillation can separate any mixture of liquids.

questions.q: The ideal recrystallization solvent dissolves the compound:
o: Well when hot and poorly when cold
Correct: The compound dissolves when hot and crystallizes when cold, leaving soluble impurities in the mother liquor.
Well at all temperatures
Dissolving well at all temperatures gives no crystals on cooling.
Poorly at all temperatures
Dissolving poorly at all temperatures never dissolves the compound.
Poorly when hot and well when cold
This reverses the temperature dependence and would precipitate on heating.
questions.x: The compound dissolves when hot and crystallizes when cold, leaving soluble impurities in the mother liquor. Trap: Reversing the temperature dependence.

questions.q: Slow cooling during recrystallization generally yields:
o: Smaller crystals with more impurities trapped
Smaller crystals with trapped impurities result from rapid cooling.
Larger, purer crystals
Correct: Slow growth lets the crystal lattice exclude foreign molecules, giving larger, purer crystals.
Amorphous liquid
Slow cooling gives crystals, not an amorphous liquid.
Lower purity because crystals grow too slowly
Slow cooling improves purity, not lowers it.
questions.x: Slow growth lets the crystal lattice exclude foreign molecules, giving larger, purer crystals. Trap: Believing fast cooling is better.

questions.q: In TLC, a compound spot travels 2.4 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. What is the Rf?
o: 3.3 inverts the ratio (8.0/2.4).
0.70 is 1 - 0.30, the fraction of the front not travelled.
Correct: Rf = distance by compound / distance by solvent front = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30.
0.19 has no basis in the data.
questions.x: Rf = distance by compound / distance by solvent front = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30. Trap: Inverting the ratio and reporting solvent-front over spot distance instead of spot over front.

questions.q: On a silica gel TLC plate, which compound will generally have the lowest Rf?
o: The least polar compound
The least polar compound travels farthest, giving the highest Rf.
The smallest compound
Size alone is not the determinant of Rf on silica.
The most volatile compound
Volatility is not the determinant of Rf on silica.
The most polar compound
Correct: Polar compounds adsorb more strongly to polar silica and move less, giving the lowest Rf.
questions.x: Polar compounds adsorb more strongly to polar silica and move less, giving the lowest Rf. Trap: Assuming polar compounds travel farther.

questions.q: Increasing the polarity of the eluent in normal-phase chromatography will generally:
o: Increase the Rf values of the compounds
Correct: A more polar eluent competes with analytes for silica binding sites, moving them farther and raising Rf.
Decrease the Rf values
Decreasing Rf would require a less polar eluent.
Have no effect
Eluent polarity does change Rf values.
Reverse the stationary phase
The stationary phase remains polar silica; it is not reversed.
questions.x: A more polar eluent competes with analytes for silica binding sites, moving them farther and raising Rf. Trap: Thinking a more polar solvent holds compounds back.

questions.q: In normal-phase column chromatography on silica, which compound elutes first?
o: The most polar
The most polar binds silica strongly and elutes last.
The least polar
Correct: Weakly adsorbed nonpolar compounds are retained least on silica, so the least polar elutes first.
The largest
Size is not the main basis in adsorption chromatography.
The one with the highest charge
Charge is not the main basis; polar groups bind silica and slow elution.
questions.x: Weakly adsorbed nonpolar compounds are retained least on silica, so the least polar elutes first. Trap: Mixing up normal and reverse phase elution order.

questions.q: In reverse-phase HPLC with a C18 column, which compound elutes first?
o: The most nonpolar
The most nonpolar compound interacts strongly with C18 and is retained longest.
The largest hydrocarbon
The largest hydrocarbon is highly nonpolar and is retained strongly.
The most polar
Correct: The C18 stationary phase is nonpolar; polar compounds interact least with it and elute first.
The compound with the longest alkyl chain
The longest alkyl chain is the most nonpolar and is retained strongly.
questions.x: The C18 stationary phase is nonpolar; polar compounds interact least with it and elute first. Trap: Applying normal-phase rules to reverse-phase systems.

questions.q: In size-exclusion chromatography, which molecules elute first?
o: The smallest molecules
Small molecules enter the pores and elute later.
The most negatively charged
Charge is not the basis of separation in size exclusion.
The most hydrophobic
Hydrophobicity is not the basis of separation in size exclusion.
The largest molecules
Correct: Large molecules cannot enter the bead pores and take the shorter path, eluting first.
questions.x: Large molecules cannot enter the bead pores and take the shorter path, eluting first. Trap: Assuming small molecules travel fastest.

questions.q: A protein with pI 9.0 is applied at pH 7 to a column containing negatively charged resin (a cation exchanger). The protein will:
o: Bind to the column because it is positively charged
Correct: At pH 7, below the pI of 9.0, the protein has a net positive charge and binds the negatively charged resin.
Pass through because it is positive
Passing through because it is positive is wrong; positive charge causes binding.
Bind because it is negatively charged
It is positive, not negative, at pH below its pI, and negative would be repelled.
Pass through because it has no charge
It is not neutral at pH 7; it is neutral only at its pI of 9.0.
questions.x: At pH 7, below the pI of 9.0, the protein has a net positive charge and binds the negatively charged resin. Trap: Reversing the charge relative to pI.

questions.q: A protein bound to a cation-exchange column can be eluted by:
o: Decreasing the salt concentration
Decreasing salt reduces competition and increases binding.
Increasing the salt concentration
Correct: Increasing salt provides competing cations that displace the protein from the negatively charged resin.
Lowering the pH below the pI
Lowering the pH below the pI increases positive charge and binding.
Cooling the column
Cooling has little effect on electrostatic binding.
questions.x: Increasing salt provides competing cations that displace the protein from the negatively charged resin. Trap: Believing lower pH helps release a cation-bound protein.

questions.q: A His-tagged protein is purified on a nickel column. How is it commonly eluted?
o: With high pH water only
High pH water alone would not disrupt metal coordination effectively.
By increasing size cutoff
Size cutoff is not the basis of affinity chromatography.
With imidazole, which competes for nickel
Correct: Imidazole mimics the histidine ring and competes for nickel, displacing the His tag.
With nonpolar solvents
Nonpolar solvents would denature the protein and do not target nickel binding.
questions.x: Imidazole mimics the histidine ring and competes for nickel, displacing the His tag. Trap: Ignoring specific competitive elution.

questions.q: In SDS-PAGE, proteins separate primarily by:
o: Intrinsic charge
Native charge is masked by SDS.
Isoelectric point
pI-based separation requires isoelectric focusing, not SDS-PAGE.
Hydrophobicity
Hydrophobicity is masked by SDS coating and is not the separation basis.
Molecular mass
Correct: SDS denatures proteins and imparts uniform negative charge per mass, so migration depends on molecular mass.
questions.x: SDS denatures proteins and imparts uniform negative charge per mass, so migration depends on molecular mass. Trap: Assuming charge drives SDS-PAGE separation.

questions.q: In native PAGE, migration depends on:
o: Charge, size and shape
Correct: Proteins remain folded and keep native charge, so migration depends on charge, size and shape.
Mass only
Mass only describes SDS-PAGE, where charge-to-mass is uniform.
Number of disulfide bonds only
Disulfide count alone does not determine native migration.
Amino acid sequence alone
Sequence alone ignores folding, charge and shape effects.
questions.x: Proteins remain folded and keep native charge, so migration depends on charge, size and shape. Trap: Confusing native and denaturing gels.

questions.q: In isoelectric focusing, a protein stops migrating when:
o: The gel runs out of buffer
Running out of buffer is not the stopping mechanism.
The pH equals its pI so its net charge is zero
Correct: Along the pH gradient the protein moves until pH equals its pI, where net charge is zero.
It reaches the largest pore
Pore size is not the basis in isoelectric focusing.
It becomes positively charged
A positively charged protein would still migrate toward the cathode.
questions.x: Along the pH gradient the protein moves until pH equals its pI, where net charge is zero. Trap: Mixing up pI with molecular weight.

questions.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments migrate toward the:
o: Cathode, with larger fragments moving faster
Cathode with larger fragments faster is wrong on both direction and size dependence.
Anode, with larger fragments moving faster
Anode with larger fragments faster is right on direction but reverses size dependence.
Anode (positive electrode), with smaller fragments moving faster
Correct: The phosphate backbone is negatively charged so DNA moves toward the anode, and smaller fragments pass through pores more easily.
Cathode, with smaller fragments moving faster
Cathode with smaller fragments faster is wrong on direction because negative DNA does not go to the negative electrode.
questions.x: The phosphate backbone is negatively charged so DNA moves toward the anode, and smaller fragments pass through pores more easily. Trap: Forgetting that DNA is negatively charged, so it moves to the positive electrode, or reversing which fragments move faster through the gel.

questions.q: Which gel is best to resolve very small DNA fragments differing by a few base pairs?
o: Low-percentage agarose
Low-percentage agarose has large pores that resolve only larger fragments.
Paper
Paper is not an electrophoresis sieving matrix for DNA fragments.
Starch-free medium
A starch-free medium names no sieving matrix and offers no resolving power.
Polyacrylamide
Correct: Polyacrylamide has smaller, more uniform pores that resolve fragments differing by a few base pairs.
questions.x: Polyacrylamide has smaller, more uniform pores that resolve fragments differing by a few base pairs. Trap: Using agarose for every DNA size range even when pores are too large for tiny fragments.

questions.q: In differential centrifugation of a cell homogenate at low speed, which pellets first?
o: Nuclei and unbroken cells
Correct: Larger, denser components such as nuclei and unbroken cells sediment at the lowest g-force.
Ribosomes
Ribosomes are very small and need ultracentrifugation speeds.
Soluble enzymes
Soluble enzymes remain in the supernatant at low speed.
Small vesicles
Small vesicles need higher speeds than nuclei to pellet.
questions.x: Larger, denser components such as nuclei and unbroken cells sediment at the lowest g-force. Trap: Assuming small components pellet first.

questions.q: In equilibrium density gradient centrifugation, particles stop at the position where:
o: Their mass is greatest
Mass does not determine the final position in an equilibrium gradient.
Their density equals the gradient density
Correct: At equilibrium, a particle's buoyant density equals the medium density, so net force is zero and it stops.
They reach the bottom
Particles stop at their matching density, not necessarily at the bottom.
Their charge is neutral
Charge neutrality is not the stopping criterion in centrifugation.
questions.x: At equilibrium, a particle's buoyant density equals the medium density, so net force is zero and it stops. Trap: Treating this as a velocity-based sedimentation.

questions.q: In gas chromatography with a nonpolar column, which compound generally elutes first?
o: The one with the highest boiling point
The highest-boiling compound is retained longest on the column.
The one with the largest mass
Mass alone does not set elution order; boiling point does.
The one with the lowest boiling point
Correct: More volatile, lower-boiling compounds spend more time in the mobile gas phase, so they elute first.
The most polar
The most polar compound is retained more on a nonpolar column and elutes later.
questions.x: More volatile, lower-boiling compounds spend more time in the mobile gas phase, so they elute first. Trap: Reversing volatility so that the highest-boiling compound is assumed to elute first.

questions.q: Dialysis tubing is used to:
o: Separate large molecules from each other
Dialysis cannot separate macromolecules of similar size from each other.
Concentrate small molecules
Dialysis removes small molecules rather than concentrating them.
Separate by charge
Dialysis separates by size cutoff, not by charge.
Remove small solutes from a solution of large molecules
Correct: Small solutes diffuse across the semipermeable membrane while macromolecules remain inside the tubing.
questions.x: Small solutes diffuse across the semipermeable membrane while macromolecules remain inside the tubing. Trap: Mistaking dialysis for chromatography.

questions.q: Hot filtration during recrystallization is used to:
o: Remove insoluble impurities
Correct: Insoluble material stays on the filter while the hot product solution passes through.
Remove soluble impurities
Soluble impurities stay in solution and are removed in the cold mother liquor, not by hot filtration.
Induce crystallization
Hot filtration is done while hot to prevent crystallization; crystallization is induced by cooling afterward.
Dry the product
Drying is a separate later step.
questions.x: Insoluble material stays on the filter while the hot product solution passes through. Trap: Confusing the purpose of hot filtration with cooling.

questions.q: Which compound mixture could be purified by sublimation?
o: Two liquids with similar boiling points
Two liquids of similar boiling points would need fractional distillation.
A solid that has a significant vapor pressure below its melting point mixed with nonvolatile impurities
Correct: A solid with significant vapor pressure below its melting point vaporizes and re-deposits on a cold surface, leaving nonvolatile impurities behind.
A salt dissolved in water
A salt dissolved in water is separated by evaporation or crystallization, not sublimation.
Two proteins of differing mass
Two proteins of differing mass are separated by chromatography or electrophoresis.
questions.x: A solid with significant vapor pressure below its melting point vaporizes and re-deposits on a cold surface, leaving nonvolatile impurities behind. Trap: Assuming sublimation only applies to dry ice.

questions.q: To extract the most solute from water into an organic solvent using a fixed total volume of solvent, it is best to:
o: Use one large portion
A single large portion is less efficient than several small portions.
Use pure water repeatedly
Pure water is the original solvent and would not extract into the organic phase.
Use several smaller portions
Correct: Multiple small extractions remove more solute than a single extraction using the same total solvent volume.
Heat the mixture
Heating does not improve the distribution and may evaporate the solvent.
questions.x: Multiple small extractions remove more solute than a single extraction using the same total solvent volume. Trap: Assuming one extraction is enough.

questions.q: A solute has K = [ether]/[water] = 4. A 100 mL aqueous solution contains 1.0 g of solute. One extraction with 100 mL ether removes how much solute?
o: 0.50 g would result from K = 1.
0.20 g is the fraction remaining in the water, not the amount extracted.
4.0 g exceeds the 1.0 g total present.
Correct: Fraction extracted = K V_o/(K V_o + V_w) = 400/(400 + 100) = 0.80, so 0.80 g is removed.
questions.x: Fraction extracted = K V_o/(K V_o + V_w) = 400/(400 + 100) = 0.80, so 0.80 g is removed. Trap: Ignoring volumes in an extraction calculation.

questions.q: In paper chromatography of amino acids, ninhydrin is used to:
o: Visualize the spots
Correct: Ninhydrin reacts with amino groups to produce a colored product, visualizing the spots.
Move amino acids
It does not drive migration; the solvent does.
Remove cellulose
It does not remove cellulose.
Neutralize charge
It is a stain, not a charge neutralizer.
questions.x: Ninhydrin reacts with amino groups to produce a colored product, visualizing the spots. Trap: Thinking ninhydrin is the mobile phase.

questions.q: Adding high concentrations of ammonium sulfate to a protein solution typically:
o: Denatures protein irreversibly
Says irreversible denaturation, but proteins often remain active.
Precipitates proteins by reducing their solubility
Correct: High salt competes for water, reducing protein solubility and promoting aggregation (salting out), usually without denaturing.
Increases solubility
Says solubility increases, but it decreases at high salt.
Cuts peptide bonds
Says peptide bonds are cut, but no hydrolysis occurs.
questions.x: High salt competes for water, reducing protein solubility and promoting aggregation (salting out), usually without denaturing. Trap: Assuming precipitation equals denaturation.

questions.q: In fractional distillation, the vapor at the top of the column is enriched in the:
o: Less volatile component
Says the less volatile component, but it condenses lower in the column.
Nonvolatile solute
A nonvolatile solute does not enter the vapor.
More volatile component
Correct: Repeated condensation and vaporization concentrate the lower-boiling, more volatile component at the top.
Component with higher boiling point
Says the higher-boiling component, but it condenses and falls back down the column.
questions.x: Repeated condensation and vaporization concentrate the lower-boiling, more volatile component at the top. Trap: Reversing enrichment so the higher-boiling component is assumed to collect at the column top.

questions.q: Why are boiling chips added to a liquid before distillation?
o: To raise the boiling point
They do not meaningfully change the boiling temperature.
To remove water
They are not drying agents and remove no water.
To catalyze evaporation
They do not catalyze evaporation; they only supply nucleation sites.
To promote smooth boiling and prevent bumping
Correct: Boiling chips provide nucleation sites for bubbles, promoting smooth boiling and preventing bumping.
questions.x: Boiling chips provide nucleation sites for bubbles, promoting smooth boiling and preventing bumping. Trap: Thinking chips act as drying agents.

questions.q: In a simple distillation, where should the thermometer bulb be placed?
o: Just below the side arm leading to the condenser
Correct: The bulb just below the side arm measures the temperature of the vapor entering the condenser.
In the boiling liquid
Placing it in the boiling liquid reads the liquid temperature, which exceeds the vapor temperature.
Above the condenser
Above the condenser is not in the vapor path at all.
In the receiving flask
In the receiving flask it would read distillate temperature, not boiling vapor.
questions.x: The bulb just below the side arm measures the temperature of the vapor entering the condenser. Trap: Measuring liquid instead of vapor.

questions.q: Anhydrous magnesium sulfate is added to an organic layer to:
o: Neutralize acid
It is not an acid-base reagent and does not neutralize acid.
Remove dissolved water
Correct: Anhydrous MgSO4 binds water as hydrates and is then filtered off, drying the organic layer.
Extract amines
Extracting amines requires an acid wash, not a drying agent.
Increase polarity
It removes water; it does not change solvent polarity.
questions.x: Anhydrous MgSO4 binds water as hydrates and is then filtered off, drying the organic layer. Trap: Confusing drying with extraction.

questions.q: After extracting benzoate into aqueous NaOH, which step recovers benzoic acid?
o: Add more NaOH
More NaOH keeps it as benzoate in water.
Evaporate ether
Evaporating ether does nothing since benzoate is in the aqueous layer.
Acidify with HCl to precipitate benzoic acid
Correct: Acidifying with HCl protonates benzoate, regenerating neutral, poorly water-soluble benzoic acid that precipitates.
Add brine
Brine would not protonate benzoate or precipitate the acid.
questions.x: Acidifying with HCl protonates benzoate, regenerating neutral, poorly water-soluble benzoic acid that precipitates. Trap: Forgetting the neutralization.

questions.q: Why does HPLC require high pressure?
o: The sample is a gas
HPLC uses a liquid mobile phase, so the sample is not a gas.
The analytes are volatile
Analytes in HPLC need not be volatile; that describes GC.
Pressure creates separation by charge
Pressure only pushes solvent; separation arises from interactions with the stationary phase.
Small particles in the column create high resistance to flow
Correct: Small stationary-phase particles improve resolution but resist solvent flow, requiring high pressure.
questions.x: Small stationary-phase particles improve resolution but resist solvent flow, requiring high pressure. Trap: Believing pressure itself separates compounds.

questions.q: In gel filtration, a small molecule elutes later than a large protein because:
o: It enters the pores and has a longer path
Correct: Small molecules enter the bead pores and take a longer path, so they elute later.
It binds the beads covalently
No covalent binding is involved in gel filtration.
It is more positively charged
Charge is not the basis of separation in gel filtration.
It is more hydrophobic
Hydrophobicity is not the basis of separation in gel filtration.
questions.x: Small molecules enter the bead pores and take a longer path, so they elute later. Trap: Assuming binding explains retention.

questions.q: Adding beta-mercaptoethanol to a sample before SDS-PAGE allows resolution of:
o: Intact noncovalent complexes
SDS and reducing agent disrupt noncovalent complexes rather than preserving them.
Individual subunits linked by disulfide bonds
Correct: Beta-mercaptoethanol reduces disulfide bonds, so subunits linked by disulfides separate into individual chains on the gel.
Native charge
Native charge is masked by SDS.
Oligomeric state in solution
Oligomeric state in solution is lost by denaturation.
questions.x: Beta-mercaptoethanol reduces disulfide bonds, so subunits linked by disulfides separate into individual chains on the gel. Trap: Forgetting that SDS alone does not break disulfides.

questions.q: What is the predominant net charge of glycine (pKa1 2.3, pKa2 9.6) at pH 1?
o: 0 is the zwitterion that predominates between pH 2.3 and 9.6.
-1 occurs above pKa2 (9.6), when the amino group is deprotonated.
+2 is impossible for glycine, which has only one cationic group.
Correct: Below pKa1 both groups are protonated (COOH and NH3+), giving a net charge of +1.
questions.x: Below pKa1 both groups are protonated (COOH and NH3+), giving a net charge of +1. Trap: Assuming the zwitterion predominates at all pH values.

questions.q: Aspartic acid has pKa values of 1.9 (alpha-COOH), 3.9 (side chain) and 9.8 (alpha-NH3+). What is its pI?
o: Correct: pI is the average of the two pKa values flanking the neutral species: (1.9 + 3.9)/2 = 2.9.
5.9 averages the lowest and highest pKa values, which do not flank the neutral form.
6.9 averages 3.9 and 9.8, which would apply to a basic amino acid.
3.9 is a single pKa, not an average.
