questions.x: pI is the average of the two pKa values flanking the neutral species: (1.9 + 3.9)/2 = 2.9. Trap: Averaging the wrong pair of pKa values.

questions.q: At physiological pH, lysine's side chain is:
o: Deprotonated and negative
Deprotonated and negative describes acidic residues such as Asp and Glu.
Protonated and positively charged
Correct: The epsilon-amino group (pKa about 10.5) is protonated at pH 7.4, giving a positive charge.
Neutral and nonpolar
Lysine's side chain is a charged amine, not neutral and nonpolar.
Polar and uncharged
Lysine's side chain is charged at physiological pH, not polar uncharged.
questions.x: The epsilon-amino group (pKa about 10.5) is protonated at pH 7.4, giving a positive charge. Trap: Confusing lysine with an acidic residue.

questions.q: Which statement describes the peptide bond?
o: It rotates freely
Free rotation would require a pure single bond.
It is an ionic bond
The peptide bond is covalent, not ionic.
It is planar with partial double-bond character due to resonance
Correct: Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl gives partial double-bond character, restricting rotation and holding six atoms in a plane.
It is a bond between side chains
It links backbone atoms (carbonyl C and amide N), not side chains.
questions.x: Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl gives partial double-bond character, restricting rotation and holding six atoms in a plane. Trap: Believing peptide bonds are free to rotate.

questions.q: Which standard amino acid is achiral?
o: Alanine
Alanine has four different groups on its alpha carbon.
Proline
Proline has four different groups on its alpha carbon.
Serine
Serine has four different groups on its alpha carbon.
Glycine
Correct: Glycine's alpha carbon bears two hydrogens, so it has no stereocenter and is achiral.
questions.x: Glycine's alpha carbon bears two hydrogens, so it has no stereocenter and is achiral. Trap: Selecting the smallest chiral residue.

questions.q: Most L-amino acids are S, but L-cysteine is R. Why?
o: The CH2SH group outranks COOH in CIP priority
Correct: The sulfur in CH2SH gives the side chain higher CIP priority than COOH, reversing the descriptor to R with the same spatial arrangement as other L-amino acids.
Cysteine is a D-amino acid
Cysteine is an L-amino acid, not D.
Sulfur is lighter than carbon
Sulfur is heavier than carbon, not lighter, which is why priority changes.
L-cysteine has no stereocenter
The alpha carbon of L-cysteine is a stereocenter.
questions.x: The sulfur in CH2SH gives the side chain higher CIP priority than COOH, reversing the descriptor to R with the same spatial arrangement as other L-amino acids. Trap: Equating L with S in all amino acids.

questions.q: Disulfide bonds in proteins form between:
o: Two serine side chains
Serine has a hydroxyl, not a thiol, so it cannot form disulfides.
Two cysteine side chains upon oxidation
Correct: Thiol groups on two cysteines are oxidized to an S-S covalent link that stabilizes tertiary or quaternary structure.
Backbone carbonyls
Backbone carbonyls form hydrogen bonds, not disulfides.
Lysine and aspartate
Lysine and aspartate form salt bridges (ionic), not disulfides.
questions.x: Thiol groups on two cysteines are oxidized to an S-S covalent link that stabilizes tertiary or quaternary structure. Trap: Confusing disulfides with salt bridges.

questions.q: Proline is frequently found in turns and disrupts alpha helices because:
o: It is highly charged
Proline is neutral, not highly charged.
It forms disulfides
Proline has no thiol and cannot form disulfides.
Its cyclic side chain restricts rotation and its amide nitrogen lacks an H for hydrogen bonding
Correct: Proline's ring locks the phi angle and its amide nitrogen has no H, so it cannot donate a helix hydrogen bond.
It is too large
Proline is relatively small.
questions.x: Proline's ring locks the phi angle and its amide nitrogen has no H, so it cannot donate a helix hydrogen bond. Trap: Assuming proline disrupts helices due to charge.

questions.q: In beta sheets, hydrogen bonds form between:
o: Side chains of the same residue
Side chains project above and below the sheet and do not form its hydrogen bonds.
Cysteines
Cysteines form disulfides, which are covalent rather than hydrogen bonds.
Carboxyl groups only
Hydrogen bonds involve backbone N-H and C=O, not carboxyl groups only.
Backbone groups of adjacent strands
Correct: Backbone N-H and C=O groups on neighboring strands hydrogen bond to stabilize the sheet.
questions.x: Backbone N-H and C=O groups on neighboring strands hydrogen bond to stabilize the sheet. Trap: Mixing helix and sheet bonding.

questions.q: Treating a protein with urea would disrupt:
o: Noncovalent interactions, leaving primary structure intact
Correct: Urea breaks hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic packing, unfolding the protein while leaving covalent primary structure intact.
Peptide bonds
Peptide bonds need hydrolysis, not urea, to break.
The amino acid sequence
The amino acid sequence is covalent and unchanged by denaturation.
Carbon-carbon bonds
Carbon-carbon bonds are strong covalent bonds unaffected by urea.
questions.x: Urea breaks hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic packing, unfolding the protein while leaving covalent primary structure intact. Trap: Thinking denaturation changes sequence.

questions.q: Glucose in its cyclic form is a:
o: Ketal
A ketal would form from a ketone with two alcohols.
Hemiacetal
Correct: The C5 hydroxyl adds to the aldehyde C1, forming a cyclic hemiacetal.
Ester
An ester would form from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
Ether only
Cyclic glucose has a hemiacetal carbon bearing both OR and OH, not only an ether.
questions.x: The C5 hydroxyl adds to the aldehyde C1, forming a cyclic hemiacetal. Trap: Confusing hemiacetal with acetal.

questions.q: Alpha- and beta-D-glucose differ only in configuration at:
o: C2
A difference at C2 would produce an epimer (mannose), not an anomer.
C4
A difference at C4 would produce galactose.
C1, the anomeric carbon
Correct: Ring closure creates a new stereocenter at C1, the anomeric carbon, where alpha and beta differ.
C6
C6 is not a stereocenter in glucose.
questions.x: Ring closure creates a new stereocenter at C1, the anomeric carbon, where alpha and beta differ. Trap: Calling all stereoisomeric sugars anomers.

questions.q: D-Glucose and D-galactose differ only at C4. They are:
o: Anomers
Anomers differ at the anomeric carbon (C1), not C4.
Enantiomers
Enantiomers differ at all stereocenters.
Constitutional isomers
Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity, but glucose and galactose have the same connectivity.
Epimers
Correct: Diastereomers that differ at a single stereocenter are epimers.
questions.x: Diastereomers that differ at a single stereocenter are epimers. Trap: Confusing epimers with enantiomers.

questions.q: When pure alpha-D-glucose is dissolved in water, its optical rotation changes over time because:
o: The ring opens and reforms, interconverting alpha and beta forms
Correct: Through the open-chain aldehyde form, alpha and beta anomers interconvert until equilibrium (mutarotation), changing the rotation.
The sugar is oxidized
Oxidation is not required for mutarotation.
The sugar becomes a ketose
Conversion to a ketose is not involved; it is isomerization at C1 only.
Glycosidic bonds hydrolyze
Glucose is a monosaccharide with no glycosidic bonds to hydrolyze.
questions.x: Through the open-chain aldehyde form, alpha and beta anomers interconvert until equilibrium (mutarotation), changing the rotation. Trap: Assuming optical rotation changes require reaction.

questions.q: Humans can digest starch but not cellulose because:
o: Cellulose contains peptide bonds
Cellulose has glycosidic bonds between glucose units, not peptide bonds.
Cellulose has beta(1-4) linkages that human enzymes cannot cleave
Correct: Cellulose has beta(1-4) linkages that human enzymes cannot cleave, whereas amylase cleaves alpha linkages in starch.
Starch is a lipid
Starch is a carbohydrate (glucose polymer), not a lipid.
Cellulose has alpha(1-6) branches
Cellulose is unbranched beta(1-4); alpha(1-6) branches are found in starch and glycogen.
questions.x: Cellulose has beta(1-4) linkages that human enzymes cannot cleave, whereas amylase cleaves alpha linkages in starch. Trap: Assuming the monomer differs, when the anomeric linkage geometry determines enzymatic digestibility.

questions.q: Sucrose does not give a positive Benedict's test because:
o: It has no hydroxyl groups
Sucrose has many hydroxyl groups.
It is a ketose only
Sucrose is a glucose-fructose disaccharide whose anomeric carbons are locked, not simply a ketose.
Its anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond
Correct: Both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so no free hemiacetal can open to an aldehyde.
It is a lipid
Sucrose is a carbohydrate, not a lipid.
questions.x: Both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so no free hemiacetal can open to an aldehyde. Trap: Assuming every sugar reduces, even when the anomeric carbons are locked in a glycosidic bond.

questions.q: A positive Tollens test (silver mirror) indicates:
o: A ketone
Ketones resist mild oxidation and give no mirror.
An alkane
Alkanes lack oxidizable groups.
An ether
Ethers lack oxidizable groups.
An aldehyde
Correct: Aldehydes are oxidized to carboxylates while Ag+ is reduced to metallic silver.
questions.x: Aldehydes are oxidized to carboxylates while Ag+ is reduced to metallic silver. Trap: Assuming ketones also give a silver mirror, although ketones resist mild oxidation.

questions.q: Compared with a saturated fatty acid of the same length, a cis-unsaturated fatty acid has a:
o: Lower melting point because of kinks that prevent tight packing
Correct: Cis double bonds introduce bends that reduce packing and dispersion contacts, lowering the melting point.
Higher melting point
Higher melting point is wrong because saturated chains pack more tightly.
Same melting point
Same melting point ignores the kink effect on packing.
Higher melting point because of more dispersion
More dispersion would apply to straight saturated chains, not kinked cis chains.
questions.x: Cis double bonds introduce bends that reduce packing and dispersion contacts, lowering the melting point. Trap: Thinking more double bonds raise melting point.

questions.q: Base hydrolysis of a triacylglycerol yields:
o: Glucose and amino acids
Triglycerides contain no sugar or amino acids.
Glycerol and fatty acid salts
Correct: Saponification produces glycerol and carboxylate salts (soaps).
Cholesterol and phosphate
Cholesterol and phosphate are not triglyceride components.
Only glycerol
Only glycerol ignores the fatty acid salts also formed.
questions.x: Saponification produces glycerol and carboxylate salts (soaps). Trap: Forgetting the products are salts.

questions.q: At physiological temperatures, cholesterol in membranes:
o: Only increases fluidity
Says it only increases fluidity, but it also decreases fluidity at high temperature.
Forms covalent bonds with phospholipids
It does not covalently bind phospholipids; it inserts through noncovalent interactions.
Reduces fluidity at high temperature and prevents tight packing at low temperature
Correct: Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it restrains phospholipid motion at high temperature and prevents tight packing at low temperature.
Is found only in plants
Cholesterol is found in animal cell membranes, not only in plants.
questions.x: Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it restrains phospholipid motion at high temperature and prevents tight packing at low temperature. Trap: Thinking cholesterol has one effect only.

questions.q: Steroids are characterized by:
o: A glycerol backbone
Says a glycerol backbone, but glycerol is found in triglycerides and phospholipids.
A peptide backbone
Says a peptide backbone, but steroids are lipids, not peptides.
Two fused rings
Says two fused rings, but the steroid nucleus has four.
Four fused rings
Correct: The steroid nucleus has four fused rings (three six-membered and one five-membered).
questions.x: The steroid nucleus has four fused rings (three six-membered and one five-membered). Trap: Confusing steroids with glycerolipids.

questions.q: RNA is less stable than DNA in base because:
o: The 2'-OH can attack the phosphodiester backbone
Correct: The 2'-hydroxyl acts as an internal nucleophile attacking the phosphodiester backbone under basic conditions, cleaving RNA.
RNA has deoxyribose
RNA contains ribose, while deoxyribose is DNA's sugar.
RNA lacks phosphate
RNA has phosphate in its backbone just like DNA.
RNA has thymine
Thymine is found in DNA; RNA has uracil.
questions.x: The 2'-hydroxyl acts as an internal nucleophile attacking the phosphodiester backbone under basic conditions, cleaving RNA. Trap: Thinking deoxyribose is in RNA.

questions.q: Which pair contains only purines?
o: Cytosine and thymine
Cytosine and thymine are both single-ring pyrimidines.
Adenine and guanine
Correct: Adenine and guanine are the purines, with two fused rings.
Adenine and uracil
Adenine is a purine but uracil is a pyrimidine.
Guanine and cytosine
Guanine is a purine but cytosine is a pyrimidine.
questions.x: Adenine and guanine are the purines, with two fused rings. Trap: Mixing purine and pyrimidine lists.

questions.q: In double-stranded DNA, adenine makes up 22% of bases. What percentage is guanine?
o: 22% would equal the A percentage, not G.
44% is A + T combined.
Correct: Chargaff's rules give A = T = 22% (44% total), leaving 56% split equally: G = C = 28%.
56% is G + C combined, not G alone.
questions.x: Chargaff's rules give A = T = 22% (44% total), leaving 56% split equally: G = C = 28%. Trap: Forgetting that G and C split the remainder.

questions.q: In a DNA strand, the phosphodiester bond connects:
o: Two bases
Bases are linked by hydrogen bonds across strands, not by phosphodiester bonds.
Two 5' carbons
Connecting two 5' carbons does not match the 3'-5' linkage.
Base and sugar of one nucleotide
Base-to-sugar attachment within a nucleotide is a glycosidic bond, not phosphodiester.
The 3' carbon of one sugar and 5' carbon of the next
Correct: A phosphate bridges the 3'-OH of one sugar and the 5'-OH of the next, forming the backbone.
questions.x: A phosphate bridges the 3'-OH of one sugar and the 5'-OH of the next, forming the backbone. Trap: Confusing glycosidic and phosphodiester bonds.

questions.q: Which carboxylic acid derivative is most reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
o: Acid chloride
Correct: Chloride is an excellent leaving group and offers little resonance donation, so acid chlorides are most reactive.
Amide
Amides have strong resonance donation from N and are least reactive among neutral derivatives.
Ester
Esters are less reactive than acid chlorides because alkoxide is a poorer leaving group.
Carboxylate
Carboxylates are negatively charged and resist nucleophilic attack.
questions.x: Chloride is an excellent leaving group and offers little resonance donation, so acid chlorides are most reactive. Trap: Ranking by size rather than leaving group.

questions.q: Heating acetic acid and ethanol with an acid catalyst gives:
o: Acetamide
No amine is present for amide formation.
Ethyl acetate and water
Correct: Acid-catalyzed condensation (Fischer esterification) of the acid and alcohol forms ethyl acetate and water.
Acetaldehyde
Acetaldehyde would require oxidation or reduction, not condensation.
Diethyl ether only
Ether formation from ethanol alone is not the favored acid-with-alcohol outcome here.
questions.x: Acid-catalyzed condensation (Fischer esterification) of the acid and alcohol forms ethyl acetate and water. Trap: Thinking alcohols make amides.

questions.q: Peptide bonds are stable in water at neutral pH because:
o: They are ionic
Peptide bonds are covalent, not ionic.
They are electrophilic like acid chlorides
Peptide bonds are less electrophilic than acid chlorides.
Amide resonance makes hydrolysis slow without a catalyst
Correct: Amide resonance stabilization raises the barrier, so hydrolysis is slow without a catalyst.
Water is unreactive with all bonds
Water does react with bonds under catalysis; peptide bonds are just kinetically stable.
questions.x: Amide resonance stabilization raises the barrier, so hydrolysis is slow without a catalyst. Trap: Thinking low reactivity means thermodynamic stability.

questions.q: Cyclization of fructose to a five-membered ring forms a:
o: Hemiacetal
Hemiacetals arise from aldehydes, not ketones.
Acetal
An acetal requires two alkoxy groups, not a single intramolecular addition.
Anhydride
An anhydride requires two carboxyl-derived acyl groups.
Hemiketal
Correct: The ketone at C2 reacts with the C5 hydroxyl to form a cyclic hemiketal (five-membered ring).
questions.x: The ketone at C2 reacts with the C5 hydroxyl to form a cyclic hemiketal (five-membered ring). Trap: Confusing ketose and aldose cyclization.

questions.q: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols mainly because:
o: The carboxylate is resonance stabilized
Correct: The carboxylate conjugate base is resonance stabilized, with charge delocalized over two oxygens.
Their O-H bond is longer
A longer O-H bond is not the main reason for acidity.
They have more carbons
Number of carbons does not explain the difference.
They form hydrogen bonds
Alcohols also hydrogen bond, so this cannot account for the difference.
questions.x: The carboxylate conjugate base is resonance stabilized, with charge delocalized over two oxygens. Trap: Attributing acidity to hydrogen bonding or O-H bond features instead of resonance stabilization of the conjugate base.

questions.q: Niacin is a precursor for:
o: FAD
FAD comes from riboflavin.
NAD+
Correct: Niacin (B3) is incorporated into NAD+ and NADP+.
CoA
CoA comes from pantothenate.
Heme
Heme is synthesized from glycine and succinyl-CoA, not niacin.
questions.x: Niacin (B3) is incorporated into NAD+ and NADP+. Trap: Confusing which B vitamin feeds which cofactor, such as attributing FAD or CoA to niacin.

questions.q: The alpha-amino group of alanine (pKa 9.69) provides its best buffering against added acid or base near which pH?
o: pH 6.0 is near the pI, where alanine is almost entirely zwitterionic and has minimal buffering.
pH 4.0 is far from either pKa.
Correct: A group buffers best within about one unit of its pKa, where protonated and deprotonated forms are present in similar amounts.
pH 7.4 is far from either pKa (2.3 and 9.7).
questions.x: A group buffers best within about one unit of its pKa, where protonated and deprotonated forms are present in similar amounts. Trap: Thinking the pI is where an amino acid buffers best.

questions.q: The Strecker synthesis from an aldehyde, NH3 and HCN, followed by hydrolysis, gives:
o: A single L-amino acid
A single L-amino acid would require an enantioselective catalyst or enzyme.
A beta-amino acid
Beta-amino acids would have the amine on the beta carbon, but Strecker puts it on the alpha carbon.
A fatty acid
A fatty acid is not formed from an aldehyde, ammonia and cyanide.
A racemic alpha-amino acid
Correct: Strecker synthesis has no chiral control, so the product is a racemic alpha-amino acid.
questions.x: Strecker synthesis has no chiral control, so the product is a racemic alpha-amino acid. Trap: Assuming synthesis produces one enantiomer.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol?
o: LiAlH4
Correct: Lithium aluminum hydride is strong enough to reduce carboxylic acids to primary alcohols.
NaBH4
NaBH4 is too weak to reduce carboxylic acids.
PCC
PCC is an oxidant, not a reducing agent.
H2O
Water is not a reducing agent.
questions.x: Lithium aluminum hydride is strong enough to reduce carboxylic acids to primary alcohols. Trap: Treating NaBH4 and LiAlH4 as equivalent.

questions.q: PCC oxidizes a primary alcohol to:
o: A carboxylic acid
Carboxylic acids result from strong oxidants such as chromic acid.
An aldehyde
Correct: PCC is a mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage.
A ketone
A ketone arises from oxidizing a secondary alcohol, not a primary one.
An ester
An ester would require a different coupling, not simple oxidation.
questions.x: PCC is a mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage. Trap: Overoxidizing in the answer: assuming PCC takes a primary alcohol all the way to the carboxylic acid like strong oxidants do.

questions.q: Which set contains only fat-soluble vitamins?
o: B, C, D, K
Choosing B, C, D, K includes water-soluble B vitamins and C.
A, B, C, E
Choosing A, B, C, E includes water-soluble B vitamins and C.
A, D, E, K
Correct: Vitamins A, D, E and K are lipophilic and stored in fat.
B, C, E, K
Choosing B, C, E, K includes water-soluble B vitamins and C.
questions.x: Vitamins A, D, E and K are lipophilic and stored in fat. Trap: Assuming the B vitamins and vitamin C are fat-soluble, or forgetting which letters are lipophilic.

questions.q: Collagen's triple helix requires which amino acid at every third position?
o: Cysteine
Cysteine is larger and is not required at every third position.
Tryptophan
Tryptophan is too bulky for the helix interior.
Leucine
Leucine is too bulky for the helix interior.
Glycine
Correct: Glycine's small side chain fits into the crowded core of the triple helix, appearing at every third position.
questions.x: Glycine's small side chain fits into the crowded core of the triple helix, appearing at every third position. Trap: Picking cysteine because of cross-links.

questions.q: Protein solubility is typically lowest at:
o: The pI
Correct: At the pI the net charge is zero, so repulsion is minimal and proteins aggregate and precipitate.
Very low pH
Very low pH gives net positive charge, which helps solubility.
Very high pH
Very high pH gives net negative charge, which helps solubility.
Any pH equally
Solubility depends on pH through net charge, so it is not equal.
questions.x: At the pI the net charge is zero, so repulsion is minimal and proteins aggregate and precipitate. Trap: Thinking solubility peaks at pI.

questions.q: ATP hydrolysis is highly exergonic partly because:
o: The adenine is cleaved
Adenine remains intact during hydrolysis.
Charge repulsion among phosphates is relieved
Correct: Charge repulsion among the phosphate groups is relieved on hydrolysis, along with resonance stabilization of the products.
Peptide bonds form
Peptide bonds are formed in translation, not by ATP hydrolysis itself.
Water is consumed as fuel
Water is a reactant in hydrolysis, not a fuel.
questions.x: Charge repulsion among the phosphate groups is relieved on hydrolysis, along with resonance stabilization of the products. Trap: Calling the phosphate bond energy-rich in itself.

questions.q: Reaction of an aldehyde with excess alcohol under acid catalysis gives, after the hemiacetal, a(n):
o: Ester
Esters require a carboxylic acid derivative, not an aldehyde and alcohol.
Carboxylic acid
No oxidation occurs, so no carboxylic acid forms.
Acetal
Correct: The hemiacetal hydroxyl is protonated and replaced by a second alkoxy group, forming the acetal (as in glycosidic bonds).
Amide
Amides require an amine and an acid derivative.
questions.x: The hemiacetal hydroxyl is protonated and replaced by a second alkoxy group, forming the acetal (as in glycosidic bonds). Trap: Assuming alcohols oxidize aldehydes to acids.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +40 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100 J/mol·K. Above approximately what temperature is the reaction spontaneous?
o: Correct: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = 0 when T = 40,000 J/mol ÷ 100 J/mol·K = 400 K; above this, TΔS exceeds ΔH so ΔG is negative.
40 K comes from failing to convert kJ to J (40/100 = 0.4 scaled wrongly).
4000 K is off by a factor of 10 in the division.
200 K would result from halving the ratio, with no basis in ΔG = 0.
questions.x: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = 0 when T = 40,000 J/mol ÷ 100 J/mol·K = 400 K; above this, TΔS exceeds ΔH so ΔG is negative. Trap: Forgetting that ΔH is in kJ while ΔS is in J, which shifts the answer by a factor of 1000.

questions.q: A reaction has a large negative ΔG°. Which statement about its equilibrium constant is correct?
o: K is much less than 1, so reactants are favored
K < 1 corresponds to a positive ΔG°, favoring reactants.
K is much greater than 1, so products are favored at equilibrium
Correct: ΔG° = -RT ln K, so a large negative ΔG° gives ln K > 0 and K much greater than 1, favoring products.
K equals 1 because ΔG° = 0 at equilibrium
It is ΔG, not ΔG°, that is zero at equilibrium; K = 1 only when ΔG° = 0, which is not the case here.
K cannot be determined without the reaction rate
K is a thermodynamic quantity set by ΔG° and is independent of reaction rate.
questions.x: ΔG° = -RT ln K, so a large negative ΔG° gives ln K > 0 and K much greater than 1, favoring products. Trap: Confusing ΔG = 0 at equilibrium with ΔG° = 0; ΔG° is 0 only when K = 1.

questions.q: For a reaction at constant temperature, Q is less than K. Which is true?
o: ΔG is positive and the reaction proceeds in the forward direction
A positive ΔG would mean Q > K, so no forward drive.
ΔG is negative and the reaction proceeds in reverse
A negative ΔG means spontaneous forward direction, not reverse.
ΔG is negative and the reaction proceeds in the forward direction
Correct: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K); when Q < K the log is negative, so ΔG < 0 and the reaction proceeds forward, making products until Q = K.
ΔG is zero and the system is at equilibrium
ΔG = 0 only when Q = K, which is not the case here.
questions.x: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K); when Q < K the log is negative, so ΔG < 0 and the reaction proceeds forward, making products until Q = K. Trap: Reversing the Q/K comparison: Q < K means too many reactants, so forward shift.

questions.q: Adding a catalyst to a reversible reaction will most likely:
o: lower the activation energy only of the forward reaction
The catalyst lowers Ea for forward and reverse equally, not just forward.
increase K by making ΔG more negative
K depends only on ΔG°, which a catalyst does not alter.
increase the enthalpy change of the reaction
The enthalpy change is a state-function difference between reactants and products and is unaffected.
lower the activation energy of both forward and reverse reactions without changing ΔG
Correct: A catalyst provides a lower-energy pathway for both directions, so equilibrium is reached faster while K and ΔG are unchanged.
questions.x: A catalyst provides a lower-energy pathway for both directions, so equilibrium is reached faster while K and ΔG are unchanged. Trap: Thinking a catalyst makes a reaction more spontaneous; it only changes kinetics.

questions.q: Doubling the concentration of A quadruples the initial rate of a reaction, while changing [B] has no effect. The rate law is:
o: rate = k[A]^2
Correct: Rate scales as 2^n = 4, so n = 2 in A, and no dependence on B means zero order in B, giving rate = k[A]^2.
rate = k[A]
First order in A would only double the rate.
rate = k[A][B]
Including [B] contradicts the observation that B has no effect.
rate = k[A]^4
The exponent 4 confuses the rate factor with the order; 2^4 would give a 16-fold change.
questions.x: Rate scales as 2^n = 4, so n = 2 in A, and no dependence on B means zero order in B, giving rate = k[A]^2. Trap: Reporting the rate factor (4) as the order instead of the exponent that gives it.

questions.q: A first-order decay has k = 0.0231 min^-1 (t1/2 = 30 min). What fraction of the reactant remains after 90 minutes?
o: 25% is the amount left after only two half-lives (60 min).
Correct: 90 min is three half-lives (90/30), so the fraction left is (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 12.5%.
33% has no basis in first-order decay and would imply a linear loss.
6.25% is the amount left after four half-lives (120 min).
questions.x: 90 min is three half-lives (90/30), so the fraction left is (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 12.5%. Trap: Miscounting half-lives or treating decay as linear.

questions.q: Why does raising the temperature typically increase a reaction rate constant?
o: The activation energy decreases as temperature rises
Ea is a property of the pathway and does not fall with temperature (that is what a catalyst does).
The reaction becomes more exothermic
Temperature does not change the sign or size of ΔH, so the reaction does not become more exothermic.
A larger fraction of collisions have energy equal to or exceeding the activation energy
Correct: Per the Arrhenius equation k = Ae^(-Ea/RT), higher T raises the fraction of collisions with energy at or above Ea, so k increases.
The reactant concentration increases
Concentration is not changed by heating a fixed sample and does not enter k.
questions.x: Per the Arrhenius equation k = Ae^(-Ea/RT), higher T raises the fraction of collisions with energy at or above Ea, so k increases. Trap: Assuming temperature lowers Ea the way a catalyst does.

questions.q: A→B has ΔH = -100 kJ and B→C has ΔH = +30 kJ. What is ΔH for A→C?
o: -130 kJ subtracts the second step from the first.
+70 kJ
+70 kJ flips the net sign.
+130 kJ flips the sign and subtracts the steps.
-70 kJ
Correct: Enthalpies of sequential steps add: -100 + 30 = -70 kJ.
questions.x: Enthalpies of sequential steps add: -100 + 30 = -70 kJ. Trap: Sign errors when summing step enthalpies.

questions.q: Which statement about bond energies is correct?
o: Breaking bonds requires energy input, and forming bonds releases energy
Correct: Bond breaking is endothermic and bond formation is exothermic, so ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed).
Breaking bonds releases energy
Breaking bonds requires energy input; it never releases energy.
Forming bonds requires energy input
Forming bonds releases energy rather than requiring it.
Breaking and forming bonds are both exothermic
Breaking is endothermic, so the two processes cannot both be exothermic.
questions.x: Bond breaking is endothermic and bond formation is exothermic, so ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed). Trap: Thinking energy is released when a bond 'breaks', as in ATP hydrolysis folklore.

questions.q: Which process has the largest positive ΔS?
o: H2O(g) → H2O(l)
Condensing gas to liquid sharply decreases entropy (negative ΔS).
CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g)
Correct: Decomposing a solid into a solid plus a gas creates gas moles from none, greatly increasing disorder and giving the largest positive ΔS.
Four moles of gas become two, so ΔS is negative.
Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) → AgCl(s)
Two free aqueous ions combine into a solid precipitate, lowering entropy.
questions.x: Decomposing a solid into a solid plus a gas creates gas moles from none, greatly increasing disorder and giving the largest positive ΔS. Trap: Focusing on enthalpy rather than counting moles of gas.

questions.q: How much heat is absorbed by 50 g of water heated from 20 °C to 30 °C? (c = 4.18 J/g·°C)
o: 209 J is off by a factor of 10 (using ΔT = 1 °C).
4180 J would correspond to 100 g of water, not 50 g.
Correct: q = mcΔT = 50 g × 4.18 J/g·°C × 10 °C = 2090 J.
1250 J has no basis in mcΔT and does not follow from any plausible arithmetic of these values.
questions.x: q = mcΔT = 50 g × 4.18 J/g·°C × 10 °C = 2090 J. Trap: Multiplying mcΔT with the wrong temperature change or mass, such as using 1 °C instead of 10 °C for ΔT.

questions.q: A mechanism has a slow first step A + B → C and a fast second step C + B → D. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[A][B]^2
Squaring [B] uses the overall stoichiometry (two B consumed) rather than the slow step.
rate = k[C][B]
C is an intermediate and its step is fast, so it cannot be in the rate law.
rate = k[D]
D is the final product and does not influence the rate.
rate = k[A][B]
Correct: The rate law follows the slow (rate-determining) step, whose reactants are A and B, each first order, so rate = k[A][B].
questions.x: The rate law follows the slow (rate-determining) step, whose reactants are A and B, each first order, so rate = k[A][B]. Trap: Using overall stoichiometry for the rate law rather than the slowest step.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔG° = +10 kJ/mol but proceeds spontaneously in a cell. Which best explains this?
o: The reaction quotient Q is small enough that ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q is negative
Correct: Actual conditions set spontaneity through ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q; a small Q (for example products continually removed) can make ΔG negative despite a positive ΔG°.
ΔG° determines spontaneity under all conditions
ΔG° applies only to standard-state conditions, not all conditions.
A catalyst lowered ΔG°
Catalysts change kinetics, not ΔG°.
Entropy of the surroundings always decreases
The surroundings' entropy does not always decrease, and this claim does not explain the cell's behavior.
questions.x: Actual conditions set spontaneity through ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q; a small Q (for example products continually removed) can make ΔG negative despite a positive ΔG°. Trap: Equating positive ΔG° with nonspontaneity under any conditions.

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction, which statement is correct?
o: Half-life is independent of initial concentration
A concentration-independent half-life is a first-order property; zero-order half-life is [A]0/2k.
A plot of [A] versus time is a straight line with slope -k
Correct: For zero order, rate = k, so [A] = [A]0 - kt, a straight line with slope -k.
A plot of ln[A] versus time is linear
A linear ln[A] versus t plot indicates first order.
The rate doubles when [A] doubles
Zero order means the rate is independent of [A].
questions.x: For zero order, rate = k, so [A] = [A]0 - kt, a straight line with slope -k. Trap: Mixing up the linear plots of zero- versus first-order reactions.

questions.q: An exothermic reaction is carried out in an insulated calorimeter. What is observed?
o: The temperature of the surroundings decreases and ΔH is negative
Surroundings cooling would indicate an endothermic reaction, though ΔH negative is mismatched with it.
The temperature increases and ΔH is positive
A temperature rise is correct, but exothermic reactions have negative, not positive, ΔH.
The temperature of the surroundings increases and ΔH is negative
Correct: An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings, raising their temperature, and ΔH < 0.
The temperature is unchanged because energy is conserved
Energy is conserved but is transferred as heat, so temperature changes.
questions.x: An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings, raising their temperature, and ΔH < 0. Trap: Taking the system's perspective and assuming an exothermic reaction cools, when the surroundings absorb the released heat.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of ATP has ΔG = -30.5 kJ/mol. When coupled to a reaction with ΔG = +20 kJ/mol, the net ΔG is:
o: +50.5 kJ/mol
+50.5 subtracts the ATP term with the wrong sign.
-50.5 kJ/mol
-50.5 treats the +20 as -20.
+10.5 kJ/mol
+10.5 gets the net sign wrong, since the larger magnitude is the negative term.
-10.5 kJ/mol
Correct: Free energies are additive: -30.5 + 20 = -10.5 kJ/mol, so the coupled process is spontaneous.
questions.x: Free energies are additive: -30.5 + 20 = -10.5 kJ/mol, so the coupled process is spontaneous. Trap: Subtracting free energies instead of summing them.

questions.q: On a reaction coordinate diagram, the transition state is:
o: the highest-energy point along the pathway, which cannot be isolated
Correct: The transition state is the energy maximum along the reaction coordinate, and it is too short-lived to isolate.
a local energy minimum between steps
A local energy minimum between steps is an intermediate, which can sometimes be isolated.
the energy of the products
The energy of the products is the final level on the diagram, not a peak.
the difference between reactants and products
The difference between reactants and products is ΔG (or ΔH), not a species on the pathway.
questions.x: The transition state is the energy maximum along the reaction coordinate, and it is too short-lived to isolate. Trap: Confusing transition states with reaction intermediates.

questions.q: For an exothermic reaction at equilibrium, increasing temperature will:
o: increase K, shifting toward products
Increased K and a product shift would apply to an endothermic reaction.
decrease K, shifting toward reactants
Correct: For an exothermic reaction, heat acts like a product, so raising T shifts equilibrium toward reactants and lowers K (van't Hoff).
not change K
Temperature is the one perturbation that does change K.
increase K and decrease the rate
Higher temperature raises, not lowers, rates, and K would not increase here.
questions.x: For an exothermic reaction, heat acts like a product, so raising T shifts equilibrium toward reactants and lowers K (van't Hoff). Trap: Assuming higher temperature always favors products.

questions.q: A reaction is second order overall. What are the units of its rate constant?
o: s^-1 is the unit for a first-order constant.
M s^-1
M s^-1 is the unit for zero order.
Correct: Rate (M/s) = k[M]^2 requires k to have units of M^-1 s^-1.
M^-2 s^-1 is the unit for third order.
questions.x: Rate (M/s) = k[M]^2 requires k to have units of M^-1 s^-1. Trap: Memorizing units without deriving from rate = k[conc]^n.

questions.q: A reaction with negative ΔH and negative ΔS is:
o: spontaneous at all temperatures
Spontaneity at all temperatures needs negative ΔH and positive ΔS.
spontaneous at high temperature only
High-temperature-only spontaneity needs positive ΔH and positive ΔS.
nonspontaneous at all temperatures
Nonspontaneity at all temperatures needs positive ΔH and negative ΔS.
spontaneous at low temperature only
Correct: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS; with both negative, the negative ΔH dominates at low T (ΔG < 0) but -TΔS turns positive at high T.
questions.x: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS; with both negative, the negative ΔH dominates at low T (ΔG < 0) but -TΔS turns positive at high T. Trap: Mixing up which sign combinations give temperature-dependent spontaneity.

questions.q: At its melting point, a solid has ΔHfus = 6.0 kJ/mol at 273 K. What is ΔS of fusion?
o: about 22 J/mol·K
Correct: At the melting point ΔG = 0, so ΔS = ΔH/T = 6000 J/mol ÷ 273 K ≈ 22 J/mol·K.
about 22 kJ/mol·K
22 kJ/mol·K is a unit error by a factor of 1000.
about 0.022 J/mol·K
0.022 J/mol·K comes from dividing 6.0 (kJ) by 273 without converting to J.
about 1640 J/mol·K
1640 J/mol·K comes from multiplying 6.0 kJ by T instead of dividing.
questions.x: At the melting point ΔG = 0, so ΔS = ΔH/T = 6000 J/mol ÷ 273 K ≈ 22 J/mol·K. Trap: Unit mistakes (kJ vs J) or multiplying by T.

questions.q: Which feature best characterizes rod photoreceptors?
o: High sensitivity in dim light but poor color discrimination and low acuity
Correct: Rods contain rhodopsin, are abundant in the periphery, and function in dim light with low acuity and no color discrimination.
Concentrated in the fovea and responsible for color vision
Foveal concentration and color vision describe cones.
Require bright light and provide high spatial acuity
Needing bright light and giving high acuity also describes cones.
Three types sensitive to different wavelengths
Three wavelength-sensitive types describes cones; rods are a single type.
questions.x: Rods contain rhodopsin, are abundant in the periphery, and function in dim light with low acuity and no color discrimination. Trap: Assigning color vision and acuity to rods because they are more numerous.

questions.q: A person with damage limited to the fovea would most likely have difficulty with:
o: seeing in dim light at the periphery
Dim-light peripheral vision relies on rods, which are outside the fovea.
reading fine print and distinguishing colors in bright light
Correct: The fovea is packed with cones, which support fine acuity and color vision in bright light, so damage impairs reading and color discrimination.
detecting motion at the edge of the visual field
Motion detection at the visual field edge depends on peripheral rod-rich retina.
adapting to darkness
Dark adaptation is a rod function (rhodopsin regeneration).
questions.x: The fovea is packed with cones, which support fine acuity and color vision in bright light, so damage impairs reading and color discrimination. Trap: Thinking central vision relies on rods.

questions.q: The absolute threshold is best defined as the:
o: minimum difference between two stimuli detected 50% of the time
This describes the difference threshold (just noticeable difference), which concerns two stimuli.
intensity at which a stimulus is detected 100% of the time
There is no intensity at which detection is a certain 100%, because of noise.
minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time
Correct: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time, since detection is probabilistic.
intensity at which a stimulus becomes painful
The point where a stimulus becomes painful is a pain threshold, not the absolute threshold.
questions.x: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time, since detection is probabilistic. Trap: Confusing absolute threshold with the difference threshold.

questions.q: A person can just notice a 2 g difference when holding a 100 g weight. According to Weber's law, what difference is needed to just notice a change from a 500 g weight?
o: 2 g
2 g treats the JND as a constant, ignoring proportionality.
5 g
5 g divides 500 by 100 rather than applying the 0.02 fraction.
50 g applies a 10% fraction, ten times too large.
Correct: Weber's law says JND is proportional to baseline: fraction = 2/100 = 0.02, and 0.02 × 500 g = 10 g.
questions.x: Weber's law says JND is proportional to baseline: fraction = 2/100 = 0.02, and 0.02 × 500 g = 10 g. Trap: Assuming the JND is constant rather than proportional to baseline.

questions.q: In a signal detection task, a participant is told that missing a signal carries a heavy penalty while false alarms carry none. What is most likely to happen?
o: The participant adopts a liberal criterion, increasing both hits and false alarms
Correct: Payoffs shift response bias, so with a heavy penalty for misses the participant adopts a liberal criterion, raising both hits and false alarms.
The participant adopts a conservative criterion, reducing false alarms
A conservative criterion would follow heavy penalties for false alarms, the opposite situation.
Sensitivity (d') decreases substantially
Sensitivity (d') reflects signal discriminability, not payoffs, and does not change.
The absolute threshold drops to zero
The absolute threshold is not driven to zero by incentives.
questions.x: Payoffs shift response bias, so with a heavy penalty for misses the participant adopts a liberal criterion, raising both hits and false alarms. Trap: Interpreting a shift in response bias as a change in sensory sensitivity.

questions.q: After a few minutes in a room, you no longer notice a perfume odor. This is an example of:
o: habituation to a cognitive expectation
Habituation is a central decline in response to repeated stimuli and is not tied to a cognitive expectation here.
sensory adaptation
Correct: A decrease in receptor responsiveness to a constant stimulus is sensory adaptation.
absolute threshold elevation due to damage
No damage occurred; the odor is noticed again when the stimulus changes.
selective attention to the odor
Selective attention would be a shift of focus, not a fading of perception under constant stimulation.
questions.x: A decrease in receptor responsiveness to a constant stimulus is sensory adaptation. Trap: Confusing sensory adaptation (receptor-level) with habituation (central).

questions.q: Staring at a green image and then seeing a red afterimage on a white wall is best explained by:
o: trichromatic theory of cone types alone
Trichromatic theory explains receptor-level color matching, not afterimages.
the volley principle
The volley principle concerns auditory frequency coding.
opponent-process theory in retinal ganglion and thalamic cells
Correct: Opponent-process theory explains afterimages: fatigue of green-signaling members of the red-green pair produces a rebound red signal.
lateral inhibition in the cochlea
The cochlea is in the ear, not the visual system.
questions.x: Opponent-process theory explains afterimages: fatigue of green-signaling members of the red-green pair produces a rebound red signal. Trap: Using trichromatic theory to explain afterimages.

questions.q: According to place theory, high-frequency sounds are encoded by hair cells located:
o: near the apex of the basilar membrane
The apex is wide and flexible, tuned to low frequencies.
in the semicircular canals
The semicircular canals handle balance, not pitch.
at the tympanic membrane
The tympanic membrane transmits vibrations but has no frequency-tuned hair cells.
near the base of the basilar membrane
Correct: The base of the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff and vibrates maximally to high frequencies.
questions.x: The base of the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff and vibrates maximally to high frequencies. Trap: Reversing base and apex tuning.

questions.q: In hearing, mechanical energy is converted to neural signals by:
o: hair cells in the organ of Corti bending against the tectorial membrane
Correct: Hair cells in the organ of Corti are bent against the tectorial membrane, opening ion channels and depolarizing them (transduction).
the ossicles vibrating the round window
The ossicles amplify mechanical vibration and push on the oval window, not the round window, without transducing.
photoreceptors in the cochlea
The cochlea contains hair cells, not photoreceptors.
the tympanic membrane generating action potentials
The eardrum vibrates mechanically and does not generate action potentials.
questions.x: Hair cells in the organ of Corti are bent against the tectorial membrane, opening ion channels and depolarizing them (transduction). Trap: Thinking the eardrum or ossicles perform transduction.

questions.q: Which structures detect rotational head movement?
o: Otolith organs (utricle and saccule)
The utricle and saccule sense linear acceleration and gravity.
Semicircular canals
Correct: Fluid in the three semicircular canals lags behind head rotation, bending hair cells.
Cochlea
The cochlea is for hearing.
Tympanic membrane
The tympanic membrane transmits sound vibration.
questions.x: Fluid in the three semicircular canals lags behind head rotation, bending hair cells. Trap: Confusing canals (rotation) with otoliths (linear).

questions.q: Olfaction differs from other senses because olfactory information:
o: is processed only in the brainstem
Olfactory processing is not limited to the brainstem.
travels through the optic nerve
Olfaction travels via cranial nerve I, not the optic nerve (II).
reaches the olfactory cortex and limbic structures without first relaying through the thalamus
Correct: Olfactory bulb axons project directly to the piriform cortex, amygdala, and limbic structures without a thalamic relay first.
requires mechanoreceptors
Olfaction uses chemoreceptors, not mechanoreceptors.
questions.x: Olfactory bulb axons project directly to the piriform cortex, amygdala, and limbic structures without a thalamic relay first. Trap: Assuming all senses relay through the thalamus first.

questions.q: Which taste quality is primarily triggered by glutamate?
o: Sweet
Sweet receptors detect sugars.
Bitter
Bitter receptors detect potential toxins such as alkaloids.
Sour
Sour receptors detect acids (H+).
Umami
Correct: Umami (savory) receptors respond to glutamate.
questions.x: Umami (savory) receptors respond to glutamate. Trap: Matching the savory taste of MSG to saltiness rather than to its own glutamate-sensing receptor.

questions.q: Rubbing a bumped elbow reduces pain according to the gate control theory because:
o: large-diameter touch fibers activate inhibitory interneurons that close the spinal gate
Correct: Large-diameter A-beta touch fibers activate inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, closing the gate on small nociceptive fibers.
pain fibers are destroyed
Pain fibers are not destroyed by rubbing.
the thalamus blocks all signals
The thalamus does not block all signals.
endorphins are always released at the cortex
Endorphin release is not always cortical and is not the proposed gate mechanism.
questions.x: Large-diameter A-beta touch fibers activate inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, closing the gate on small nociceptive fibers. Trap: Assuming the gate is closed by pain fibers themselves.

questions.q: Which type of fiber carries fast, sharp pain?
o: Unmyelinated C fibers
Unmyelinated C fibers carry slow, dull, burning pain.
Myelinated A-delta fibers
Correct: Myelinated A-delta fibers conduct quickly and carry fast, sharp pain.
A-beta fibers
A-beta fibers carry touch.
Motor neuron axons
Motor neuron axons are efferent and carry commands, not pain.
questions.x: Myelinated A-delta fibers conduct quickly and carry fast, sharp pain. Trap: Swapping the roles of A-delta and C fibers.

questions.q: The face and hands occupy disproportionately large areas of the somatosensory cortex because:
o: they contain more muscle mass
Muscle mass does not determine sensory maps.
they are closer to the brain
Proximity to the brain is irrelevant.
they have high receptor density and fine sensory discrimination
Correct: Cortical representation reflects receptor density and fine discrimination, so sensitive regions like the face and hands get more cortex.
they send larger motor signals
Motor output relates to the motor cortex, not somatosensory area.
questions.x: Cortical representation reflects receptor density and fine discrimination, so sensitive regions like the face and hands get more cortex. Trap: Thinking cortical area reflects body part size.

questions.q: Proprioception relies primarily on receptors located in:
o: the cochlea
The cochlea serves hearing.
the retina
The retina serves vision.
the olfactory epithelium
The olfactory epithelium serves smell.
muscles, tendons, and joints
Correct: Muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors signal body position.
questions.x: Muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors signal body position. Trap: Equating proprioception with the vestibular system alone.

questions.q: Lateral inhibition in the retina enhances:
o: contrast at edges
Correct: Stimulated cells inhibit their neighbors, sharpening contrast at edges.
color constancy
Color constancy involves cortical processing and not lateral inhibition.
absolute threshold
Absolute threshold is a detection limit not set by lateral inhibition.
pupil size
Pupil size is controlled by the iris muscles via autonomic input.
questions.x: Stimulated cells inhibit their neighbors, sharpening contrast at edges. Trap: Thinking lateral inhibition blurs or reduces contrast, when neighboring suppression actually sharpens edges.

questions.q: A tumor pressing on the optic chiasm typically produces:
o: blindness in one eye
One-eye blindness results from optic nerve damage before the chiasm.
bitemporal hemianopia
Correct: Crossing nasal retinal fibers carry the temporal visual fields, so a chiasm lesion produces bitemporal hemianopia.
homonymous hemianopia
Homonymous hemianopia follows post-chiasm (tract or cortex) lesions.
loss of central vision in both eyes only
Loss of central vision in both eyes is not the typical chiasm pattern.
questions.x: Crossing nasal retinal fibers carry the temporal visual fields, so a chiasm lesion produces bitemporal hemianopia. Trap: Forgetting that nasal fibers cross.

questions.q: Hubel and Wiesel discovered that neurons in the primary visual cortex:
o: respond only to color
V1 neurons are not color-only responders.
are identical in firing across stimuli
Neurons fire selectively, not identically across stimuli.
respond selectively to specific features such as edge orientation
Correct: V1 simple and complex cells respond selectively to features such as edge orientation.
are found only in the retina
Cortical neurons are found in the brain, not only the retina.
questions.x: V1 simple and complex cells respond selectively to features such as edge orientation. Trap: Assuming V1 neurons respond to whole objects.

questions.q: Why does it take about 20-30 minutes to see well after moving from bright light into a dark room?
o: Cones need time to produce color pigment
Cones do not need to synthesize color pigment and adapt faster.
The pupil takes that long to constrict
The pupil dilates, not constricts, in dim light and does so within seconds.
The optic nerve stops firing
The optic nerve keeps firing; retinal sensitivity is what changes.
Rhodopsin in rods must regenerate
Correct: Bleached rhodopsin in rods slowly regenerates over 20-30 minutes, raising rod sensitivity.
questions.x: Bleached rhodopsin in rods slowly regenerates over 20-30 minutes, raising rod sensitivity. Trap: Attributing dark adaptation primarily to pupil changes, when pupil dilation is fast and rhodopsin regeneration is slow.

questions.q: Sensory transduction refers to:
o: conversion of physical stimulus energy into neural signals
Correct: Transduction is the conversion of physical stimulus energy into neural signals (graded or action potentials) by receptors.
conscious interpretation of a stimulus
Conscious interpretation of a stimulus is perception.
adaptation to constant stimuli
Reduced response to constant stimuli is adaptation.
the storage of sensory input
Storage of sensory input is memory, not transduction.
questions.x: Transduction is the conversion of physical stimulus energy into neural signals (graded or action potentials) by receptors. Trap: Mixing up transduction (energy conversion at receptors) with perception (interpretation in the brain).

questions.q: Which structure serves as the main relay for most sensory information en route to the cortex?
o: Hypothalamus
The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and hormones.
Thalamus
Correct: The thalamus relays visual, auditory, and somatosensory input to the cortex (olfaction being the exception).
Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.
Hippocampus
The hippocampus forms new declarative memories.
questions.x: The thalamus relays visual, auditory, and somatosensory input to the cortex (olfaction being the exception). Trap: Confusing the thalamus, the sensory relay, with the similarly named hypothalamus, which regulates homeostasis.

questions.q: In darkness, vertebrate photoreceptors:
o: are hyperpolarized and release no glutamate
Hyperpolarization with no glutamate release occurs in light.
fire action potentials
Photoreceptors use graded potentials, not action potentials.
are depolarized and continuously release glutamate
Correct: In darkness the dark current keeps photoreceptors depolarized so they continuously release glutamate; light closes Na+ channels and hyperpolarizes them.
are inactive
They are highly active in darkness, not inactive.
questions.x: In darkness the dark current keeps photoreceptors depolarized so they continuously release glutamate; light closes Na+ channels and hyperpolarizes them. Trap: Expecting light to depolarize photoreceptors.

questions.q: In dim light, the pupil dilates due to action of the:
o: circular muscle under parasympathetic control
Parasympathetic contraction of the circular muscle constricts the pupil.
lens ciliary muscle
The ciliary muscle adjusts lens shape for accommodation.
cornea
The cornea is a fixed refractive surface and does not control pupil size.
radial muscle of the iris under sympathetic control
Correct: In dim light, sympathetic stimulation contracts the iris radial muscle, widening the pupil.
questions.x: In dim light, sympathetic stimulation contracts the iris radial muscle, widening the pupil. Trap: Swapping sympathetic and parasympathetic effects.

questions.q: Which physical property of a sound wave determines its perceived loudness?
o: Amplitude
Correct: Larger amplitude means higher intensity and a louder perceived sound.
Frequency
Frequency determines pitch.
Wavelength
Wavelength is inversely tied to frequency and thus also relates to pitch.
Complexity of waveform
Waveform complexity determines timbre.
questions.x: Larger amplitude means higher intensity and a louder perceived sound. Trap: Equating loudness with pitch, when amplitude sets loudness and frequency sets pitch.

questions.q: Two instruments play the same note at the same loudness, yet sound different. This difference is attributed to:
o: amplitude
Amplitude (loudness) is stated to be equal.
timbre, from differing harmonic overtones
Correct: Timbre arises from the differing harmonic overtone patterns of complex waves, so the same note sounds different.
frequency
The fundamental frequency (pitch) is the same note.
wavelength of the fundamental
The wavelength of the fundamental is identical for the same pitch.
questions.x: Timbre arises from the differing harmonic overtone patterns of complex waves, so the same note sounds different. Trap: Treating timbre as a loudness effect.

questions.q: Low-frequency sounds up to about 1000 Hz are thought to be encoded in part by:
o: place along the cochlea only
Place coding alone does not explain low-pitch perception.
retinal ganglion cells
Retinal ganglion cells are part of vision.
the firing rate of auditory neurons matching the sound frequency (volley principle)
Correct: Auditory nerve firing synchronizes with low frequencies, with groups of neurons firing in volleys (volley principle).
the vestibular nerve
The vestibular nerve carries balance, not hearing, information.
questions.x: Auditory nerve firing synchronizes with low frequencies, with groups of neurons firing in volleys (volley principle). Trap: Assuming only place coding explains pitch.

questions.q: Red-green color blindness is more common in males because the genes are:
o: Y-linked
Y-linked inheritance would affect only males and be passed father to son, which is not the pattern.
autosomal dominant
Autosomal dominance would affect the sexes equally.
mitochondrial
Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal and affects both sexes equally.
X-linked recessive
Correct: The genes are X-linked recessive; males have one X, so a single recessive allele is expressed.
questions.x: The genes are X-linked recessive; males have one X, so a single recessive allele is expressed. Trap: Assuming it is autosomal dominant.

questions.q: The correct sequence of sound transmission through the middle ear is:
o: tympanic membrane, malleus, incus, stapes, oval window
Correct: Sound vibrates the tympanic membrane, then the malleus, incus, and stapes, which pushes on the oval window.
tympanic membrane, stapes, incus, malleus, oval window
This reverses the order of the ossicles.
oval window, malleus, incus, stapes, tympanic membrane
This runs the chain backward from the inner ear.
malleus, tympanic membrane, incus, stapes, round window
The malleus attaches to the tympanic membrane first, and the stapes leads to the oval window, not the round window.
questions.x: Sound vibrates the tympanic membrane, then the malleus, incus, and stapes, which pushes on the oval window. Trap: Reversing the ossicle chain order or ending at the round window instead of the oval window.

questions.q: The blind spot is caused by:
o: a lesion in the occipital lobe
An occipital lesion causes a field defect that is not the normal physiologic blind spot.
the absence of photoreceptors where the optic nerve exits the retina
Correct: The optic disc, where the optic nerve exits, has no rods or cones, producing the blind spot.
damage to the fovea
Fovea damage impairs central acuity, not the blind spot.
the lens being cloudy
A cloudy lens (cataract) blurs vision generally.
questions.x: The optic disc, where the optic nerve exits, has no rods or cones, producing the blind spot. Trap: Confusing the optic disc with the fovea.

questions.q: Damage to the ossicles or tympanic membrane would cause:
o: sensorineural hearing loss
Sensorineural loss involves hair cells or the auditory nerve.
tinnitus only
Tinnitus is a ringing sensation, not the deficit from mechanical damage.
conduction hearing loss
Correct: Damage to the ossicles or tympanic membrane impairs mechanical sound transmission, causing conduction hearing loss.
vestibular loss exclusively
The vestibular system serves balance, not sound conduction.
questions.x: Damage to the ossicles or tympanic membrane impairs mechanical sound transmission, causing conduction hearing loss. Trap: Mixing up conduction and sensorineural causes.

questions.q: After spinning and stopping abruptly, a person feels dizzy because:
o: the cochlea overstimulates
The cochlea encodes sound, not rotation.
proprioceptors fatigue
Proprioceptor fatigue does not produce this illusion.
the retina is overstimulated
The retina is not the source of the vestibular dizziness.
fluid in the semicircular canals continues to move
Correct: Inertia keeps endolymph in the semicircular canals moving after you stop, bending hair cells and signaling continued rotation.
questions.x: Inertia keeps endolymph in the semicircular canals moving after you stop, bending hair cells and signaling continued rotation. Trap: Attributing dizziness to the cochlea.

questions.q: Supertasters typically have:
o: a higher density of fungiform papillae and taste buds
Correct: Supertasters have a higher density of fungiform papillae and taste buds, intensifying taste.
no taste buds
They have more, not zero, taste buds.
less bitterness sensitivity
They are more, not less, sensitive to bitterness.
decreased smell
Smell is not reduced in supertasters.
questions.x: Supertasters have a higher density of fungiform papillae and taste buds, intensifying taste. Trap: Assuming supertasters are less sensitive.

questions.q: If an image is held perfectly stable on the retina, it fades from perception. This illustrates:
o: lack of rods
A lack of rods would not cause fading of a stabilized image.
the need for change in stimulation to maintain neural responses
Correct: Sensory systems respond to change, so a perfectly stabilized retinal image fades; eye micromovements normally prevent this.
blind spot formation
The blind spot is a fixed anatomical gap, not an effect of stability.
color constancy
Color constancy is stable color perception under changing light.
questions.x: Sensory systems respond to change, so a perfectly stabilized retinal image fades; eye micromovements normally prevent this. Trap: Overlooking constant stimulation reducing neural response.

questions.q: Pheromones are detected primarily by:
o: photoreceptors
Photoreceptors detect light.
hair cells
Hair cells detect mechanical stimuli in hearing and balance.
olfactory chemoreceptors, with the vomeronasal organ in many mammals
Correct: Pheromones are chemical signals detected by olfactory chemoreceptors, with the vomeronasal organ in many mammals.
Pacinian corpuscles
Pacinian corpuscles detect deep pressure and vibration.
questions.x: Pheromones are chemical signals detected by olfactory chemoreceptors, with the vomeronasal organ in many mammals. Trap: Picking a non-chemical receptor type, forgetting that pheromones are detected by chemoreception.

questions.q: Which receptor responds best to deep pressure and vibration?
o: Meissner corpuscle
Meissner corpuscles sense light touch.
Merkel disk
Merkel disks sense sustained touch and texture.
Free nerve ending
Free nerve endings sense pain and temperature.
Pacinian corpuscle
Correct: Pacinian corpuscles are large, deep, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors tuned to deep pressure and vibration.
questions.x: Pacinian corpuscles are large, deep, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors tuned to deep pressure and vibration. Trap: Confusing Meissner corpuscles (light touch) with Pacinian corpuscles (deep pressure and vibration).

questions.q: The just noticeable difference (JND) is:
o: the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected
Correct: The JND is the smallest detectable change in a stimulus, the difference threshold.
the weakest stimulus detectable
The weakest detectable stimulus is the absolute threshold.
the largest stimulus tolerated
The largest tolerated stimulus is a tolerance or pain limit.
the time to adapt
The time to adapt is unrelated to JND.
questions.x: The JND is the smallest detectable change in a stimulus, the difference threshold. Trap: Confusing the JND (difference threshold) with the absolute threshold for detecting any stimulus.

questions.q: Which scenario best exemplifies sensation rather than perception?
o: Recognizing a friend's face in a crowd
Recognizing a face requires cognitive interpretation.
Retinal photoreceptors absorbing photons of light
Correct: Sensation is detection and transduction, such as photoreceptors absorbing photons, whereas perception is interpretation.
Interpreting a melody
Interpreting a melody is organized perception.
Judging an object's size from distance
Judging size from distance is depth and size perception.
questions.x: Sensation is detection and transduction, such as photoreceptors absorbing photons, whereas perception is interpretation. Trap: Blurring detection and interpretation.

questions.q: Prolonged exposure to loud noise causes permanent hearing loss primarily by destroying:
o: the ossicles
The ossicles are not the primary target of noise damage.
the vestibular nerve
The vestibular nerve serves balance.
hair cells in the organ of Corti
Correct: Loud noise destroys hair cells in the organ of Corti, which do not regenerate in mammals.
the Eustachian tube
The Eustachian tube equalizes pressure and is not harmed by noise.
questions.x: Loud noise destroys hair cells in the organ of Corti, which do not regenerate in mammals. Trap: Assuming hair cells regenerate in humans.

questions.q: Fibers from retinal ganglion cells form the:
o: optic tract only
Axons form the optic tract only after the chiasm, so 'only' is wrong; they first form the nerve.
oculomotor nerve
The oculomotor nerve (III) moves the eye.
vestibulocochlear nerve
The vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) carries hearing and balance.
optic nerve
Correct: Ganglion cell axons exit the eye as the optic nerve (CN II).
questions.x: Ganglion cell axons exit the eye as the optic nerve (CN II). Trap: Mixing up cranial nerve identities or choosing the post-chiasm tract instead of the optic nerve.

questions.q: Identifying an unfamiliar object by building up from its edges, colors, and textures is an example of:
o: bottom-up (data-driven) processing
Correct: Bottom-up (data-driven) processing starts with sensory features such as edges, colors, and textures and builds up to a percept.
top-down (conceptually driven) processing
Top-down processing is driven by expectations and prior knowledge, which an unfamiliar object does not offer.
perceptual set
Perceptual set is an expectation-based readiness to perceive.
gestalt closure
Gestalt closure is filling in gaps, not building from features.
questions.x: Bottom-up (data-driven) processing starts with sensory features such as edges, colors, and textures and builds up to a percept. Trap: Equating all perception with top-down processing.

questions.q: Reading a sentence with a misspelled word and not noticing the error reflects:
o: bottom-up feature analysis
Bottom-up feature analysis would detect the misspelling.
top-down processing guided by context and expectations
Correct: Top-down processing uses context and expectations to fill in the expected letters, so the error goes unnoticed.
sensory adaptation
Sensory adaptation is reduced receptor response to constant stimuli.
absolute threshold
Absolute threshold is the minimum detectable intensity and is not at issue.
questions.x: Top-down processing uses context and expectations to fill in the expected letters, so the error goes unnoticed. Trap: Assuming perception faithfully reports the stimulus.

questions.q: Seeing a set of dots arranged in pairs as groups of two because they are close together illustrates:
o: the law of similarity
Similarity groups by shared features such as color or shape, not distance.
the law of closure
Closure fills gaps to form complete figures.
the law of proximity
Correct: The law of proximity groups elements that are near each other, so close dots are seen as pairs.
the law of continuity
Continuity groups elements along smooth paths.
questions.x: The law of proximity groups elements that are near each other, so close dots are seen as pairs. Trap: Confusing proximity with similarity.

questions.q: In the classic vase/faces image, switching between seeing a vase and two faces demonstrates:
o: binocular disparity
Binocular disparity is a depth cue from the two eyes.
size constancy
Size constancy keeps perceived size stable across distance.
motion parallax
Motion parallax is a depth cue from observer movement.
figure-ground organization
Correct: Switching between vase and faces shows figure-ground organization, where which region is figure versus background reverses.
questions.x: Switching between vase and faces shows figure-ground organization, where which region is figure versus background reverses. Trap: Treating the image as a depth cue.

questions.q: Retinal disparity is a depth cue that depends on:
o: the slightly different images seen by each eye
Correct: Retinal disparity depends on the slightly different images the two eyes see, which supports stereopsis.
motion of the observer
Observer motion underlies motion parallax, a monocular cue.
relative size of objects
Relative size is a monocular pictorial cue.
overlap of objects
Overlap (interposition) is also a monocular pictorial cue.
questions.x: Retinal disparity depends on the slightly different images the two eyes see, which supports stereopsis. Trap: Classing disparity as monocular.

questions.q: Distant objects appearing smaller and parallel lines appearing to converge is a depth cue called:
o: convergence
Convergence is a binocular cue based on eye muscle tension.
linear perspective
Correct: Linear perspective, in which parallel lines converge and distant objects look smaller, is a pictorial monocular depth cue.
retinal disparity
Retinal disparity is a binocular cue from the two eyes' images.
accommodation reflex
The accommodation reflex is a monocular cue based on lens shape, not on converging lines.
questions.x: Linear perspective, in which parallel lines converge and distant objects look smaller, is a pictorial monocular depth cue. Trap: Believing all depth cues need two eyes.

questions.q: When riding in a car, nearby trees appear to move past faster than distant mountains. This depth cue is:
o: interposition
Interposition is a static cue based on overlap.
texture gradient
Texture gradient is a static cue based on texture density changes.
motion parallax
Correct: Motion parallax: nearby objects shift across the retina faster than distant ones as the observer moves.
stereopsis
Stereopsis is binocular depth from retinal disparity, not from motion.
questions.x: Motion parallax: nearby objects shift across the retina faster than distant ones as the observer moves. Trap: Confusing motion parallax with the phi phenomenon.

questions.q: A door appears rectangular even as it swings open and projects a trapezoid onto the retina. This reflects:
o: color constancy
Color constancy concerns stable color under changing light.
figure-ground
Figure-ground concerns separating object from background.
the phi phenomenon
The phi phenomenon is apparent motion from sequential flashes.
shape constancy
Correct: Shape constancy preserves the perceived rectangular shape of the door despite the changing trapezoidal retinal image.
questions.x: Shape constancy preserves the perceived rectangular shape of the door despite the changing trapezoidal retinal image. Trap: Believing perception mirrors the retinal image.

questions.q: Stationary lights flashing in sequence appear as a moving light. This is the:
o: phi phenomenon (apparent motion)
Correct: The phi phenomenon is apparent motion produced by stationary lights flashing in sequence.
autokinetic effect
The autokinetic effect is a single stationary light in darkness appearing to drift.
motion aftereffect
The motion aftereffect is an illusory opposite motion following prolonged viewing of real motion.
induced motion
Induced motion is a stationary object appearing to move because its surroundings move.
questions.x: The phi phenomenon is apparent motion produced by stationary lights flashing in sequence. Trap: Mixing phi with the autokinetic effect.

questions.q: Participants counting basketball passes often fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit. This shows:
o: change blindness
Change blindness is failing to detect a change between scenes or views.
inattentional blindness
Correct: Inattentional blindness: attention directed to counting passes prevents awareness of an unexpected stimulus such as the gorilla.
blind spot
The blind spot is the anatomical gap at the optic disc.
sensory adaptation
Sensory adaptation is reduced receptor response to constant input.
questions.x: Inattentional blindness: attention directed to counting passes prevents awareness of an unexpected stimulus such as the gorilla. Trap: Confusing inattentional with change blindness.

questions.q: Hearing your name across a noisy room while ignoring other conversations demonstrates:
o: divided attention
Divided attention means attending to multiple tasks at once, not filtering one conversation.
sensory adaptation
Sensory adaptation is receptor-level decline under constant stimulation.
selective attention with some processing of unattended input
Correct: Selective attention with partial processing of unattended input: your own name is salient enough to break through the attenuated channel (the cocktail party effect).
habituation
Habituation is a decreased response to repeated stimuli, not a salient breakthrough.
questions.x: Selective attention with partial processing of unattended input: your own name is salient enough to break through the attenuated channel (the cocktail party effect). Trap: Assuming unattended input is completely blocked.

questions.q: Treisman's attenuation model differs from Broadbent's filter model in that unattended information is:
o: fully blocked
Fully blocked describes Broadbent's filter model.
processed equally with attended
Equal processing of attended and unattended input would mean no selection at all.
processed only by motor cortex
Motor cortex has no special role in attentional filtering.
weakened rather than fully blocked
Correct: Treisman's attenuation model holds that unattended information is weakened, not fully blocked, so meaningful stimuli can still pass.
questions.x: Treisman's attenuation model holds that unattended information is weakened, not fully blocked, so meaningful stimuli can still pass. Trap: Treating attenuation as a complete block of unattended input, which is Broadbent's all-or-none filter rather than Treisman's weakened signal.

questions.q: In a visual search for a red X among blue Xs, search time is nearly independent of the number of distractors. This is:
o: pop-out via preattentive feature detection
Correct: A single distinguishing feature (red among blue) pops out through preattentive parallel detection, so set size has little effect on search time.
conjunction search
Conjunction search (e.g., red X among red Os and blue Xs) requires combining features and slows with distractors.
serial self-terminating attention
Serial self-terminating search would show time rising with distractor number.
inattentional blindness
Inattentional blindness is failing to notice an unexpected stimulus.
questions.x: A single distinguishing feature (red among blue) pops out through preattentive parallel detection, so set size has little effect on search time. Trap: Mistaking feature searches for conjunction searches.

questions.q: Expecting a pet to appear in a dark room and then mistaking a coat for the animal reflects:
o: bottom-up processing
Bottom-up processing is driven by the stimulus rather than expectation.
perceptual set
Correct: Perceptual set is an expectation that biases interpretation of an ambiguous stimulus, such as mistaking a coat for the pet.
feature detection
Feature detection is neural analysis of lines and edges.
retinal disparity
Retinal disparity is a binocular depth cue.
questions.x: Perceptual set is an expectation that biases interpretation of an ambiguous stimulus, such as mistaking a coat for the pet. Trap: Assuming perception is purely sensory-driven.

questions.q: A patient cannot recognize familiar faces but can recognize other objects. Damage is most likely to the:
o: primary visual cortex
V1 damage causes blindness in the corresponding field, impairing all objects.
Broca's area
Broca's area damage affects speech production.
fusiform face area in the temporal lobe
Correct: Prosopagnosia, impaired face recognition with intact object recognition, arises from damage to the fusiform face area in the temporal lobe.
cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates movement and is not involved in face recognition.
questions.x: Prosopagnosia, impaired face recognition with intact object recognition, arises from damage to the fusiform face area in the temporal lobe. Trap: Attributing face recognition problems to V1.

questions.q: A stroke patient eats food only from the right half of the plate and ignores the left. The lesion is most likely in the:
o: left parietal lobe
Left parietal damage rarely produces neglect and would affect the right side if it did.
left occipital lobe
Left occipital damage causes right visual field loss rather than neglect.
right frontal pole only
A right frontal pole lesion is not the classic site of hemispatial neglect.
right parietal lobe
Correct: Right parietal damage causes contralateral (left) neglect, so the patient attends only to the right side of space.
questions.x: Right parietal damage causes contralateral (left) neglect, so the patient attends only to the right side of space. Trap: Placing the lesion in the same hemisphere as the ignored side rather than the opposite one.

questions.q: Participants wearing prism glasses that shift the visual field gradually adapt and reach accurately. This demonstrates:
o: perceptual adaptation (plasticity)
Correct: Perceptual adaptation (plasticity): perception recalibrates to altered input, so reaching becomes accurate with prism glasses.
perceptual constancy
Perceptual constancy keeps object properties stable and does not explain recalibration.
figure-ground reversal
Figure-ground reversal is switching between interpretations of an ambiguous image.
signal detection
Signal detection concerns sensitivity and response bias.
questions.x: Perceptual adaptation (plasticity): perception recalibrates to altered input, so reaching becomes accurate with prism glasses. Trap: Believing perception is fixed in adults.

questions.q: Damage to the ventral (what) stream would most likely impair:
o: locating objects in space
Locating objects in space depends on the dorsal (where) stream.
recognizing objects
Correct: The ventral (what) stream through the temporal lobe handles object identification, so damage impairs recognizing objects.
hearing
Hearing is mediated by auditory pathways.
maintaining balance
Balance is handled by the vestibular system and cerebellum.
questions.x: The ventral (what) stream through the temporal lobe handles object identification, so damage impairs recognizing objects. Trap: Mixing up the two visual streams and assigning object identity to the dorsal (where/how) pathway instead of the ventral (what) pathway.

questions.q: Perceiving a circle made of dashes as a complete circle illustrates:
o: the law of proximity
Proximity groups by nearness rather than completing a shape.
motion parallax
Motion parallax is a depth cue from movement.
the law of closure
Correct: The law of closure: the mind fills in gaps so dashed outlines are seen as a complete circle.
depth constancy
