Depth constancy is not a gestalt grouping principle and does not apply to a static figure.
questions.x: The law of closure: the mind fills in gaps so dashed outlines are seen as a complete circle. Trap: Confusing closure with continuity.

questions.q: Cross-cultural studies suggest people from cultures with fewer right-angled structures are less susceptible to the Müller-Lyer illusion. This supports the role of:
o: innate reflexes alone
Innate reflexes alone would produce the same susceptibility across cultures.
retinal anatomy
Retinal anatomy is essentially the same across cultures.
absolute thresholds
Absolute thresholds are sensory detection limits and do not explain the illusion.
experience and learning in shaping perception
Correct: Reduced susceptibility in cultures with fewer right-angled structures shows that experience and learning shape perception.
questions.x: Reduced susceptibility in cultures with fewer right-angled structures shows that experience and learning shape perception. Trap: Assuming perception is entirely innate.

questions.q: A person consistently sees the letter 'A' as red. This is an example of:
o: synesthesia
Correct: Synesthesia is the consistent triggering of one sensory or cognitive experience by another, such as letters evoking colors.
hallucination
A hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus and is not consistently tied to a specific input.
perceptual constancy
Perceptual constancy is stable perception despite changing input.
sensory adaptation
Sensory adaptation is reduced response to constant stimulation.
questions.x: Synesthesia is the consistent triggering of one sensory or cognitive experience by another, such as letters evoking colors. Trap: Calling synesthesia a hallucination.

questions.q: According to the James-Lange theory, the experience of fear follows:
o: perception of one's own physiological arousal in response to a stimulus
Correct: James-Lange holds that the bodily response comes first and the emotion is the perception or interpretation of that arousal.
conscious appraisal before any arousal
Appraisal before arousal is Lazarus's cognitive theory.
simultaneous arousal and emotion
Simultaneous arousal and emotion is Cannon-Bard.
facial expression only
Facial expression alone is the facial feedback hypothesis, not James-Lange's general account.
questions.x: James-Lange holds that the bodily response comes first and the emotion is the perception or interpretation of that arousal. Trap: Assuming emotion causes the bodily response.

questions.q: Cannon-Bard theory proposes that when a threat is perceived:
o: arousal precedes and causes emotion
Arousal preceding and causing emotion is James-Lange.
the thalamus triggers physiological arousal and emotional experience simultaneously
Correct: Cannon-Bard proposes the thalamus triggers physiological arousal and emotional experience simultaneously and independently.
cognitive labeling creates the emotion
Cognitive labeling creating emotion is Schachter-Singer.
emotion is caused by facial feedback
Emotion caused by facial feedback is the facial feedback hypothesis.
questions.x: Cannon-Bard proposes the thalamus triggers physiological arousal and emotional experience simultaneously and independently. Trap: Mixing up Cannon-Bard with James-Lange.

questions.q: Participants injected with epinephrine who were placed with a euphoric confederate reported feeling happier. This supports the idea that emotion depends on:
o: arousal alone
Arousal alone is insufficient; the label differed with context.
cognitive appraisal without arousal
Appraisal without arousal ignores the epinephrine-induced arousal.
physiological arousal plus a cognitive label from the context
Correct: Two-factor theory (Schachter-Singer) holds that emotion needs physiological arousal plus a cognitive label from the situation, such as the euphoric confederate.
amygdala activation alone
Amygdala activation alone is not what the study manipulated.
questions.x: Two-factor theory (Schachter-Singer) holds that emotion needs physiological arousal plus a cognitive label from the situation, such as the euphoric confederate. Trap: Overlooking the cognitive-label component.

questions.q: In Lazarus's theory, emotion is determined by:
o: bodily arousal alone
Bodily arousal alone omits appraisal (James-Lange).
unconscious reflexes without appraisal
Unconscious reflexes without appraisal contradict the theory.
facial feedback
Facial feedback is a separate hypothesis.
cognitive appraisal of a stimulus before the emotional response
Correct: Lazarus's theory holds that cognitive appraisal of a stimulus precedes and determines the emotional response.
questions.x: Lazarus's theory holds that cognitive appraisal of a stimulus precedes and determines the emotional response. Trap: Believing emotion needs no cognition.

questions.q: Damage to the amygdala is most likely to impair:
o: recognition of fear and fear conditioning
Correct: The amygdala processes threat and emotional salience, so damage impairs fear recognition and fear conditioning.
formation of declarative memories
Declarative memory formation depends on the hippocampus.
motor coordination
Motor coordination depends on the cerebellum.
speech production
Speech production depends on Broca's area.
questions.x: The amygdala processes threat and emotional salience, so damage impairs fear recognition and fear conditioning. Trap: Confusing the amygdala with the hippocampus.

questions.q: Holding a pencil between the teeth (forcing a smile) leads people to rate cartoons as funnier. This supports:
o: the Yerkes-Dodson law
Yerkes-Dodson links arousal to performance.
the facial feedback hypothesis
Correct: The facial feedback hypothesis says facial muscle activity, like a forced smile, influences emotional experience.
the opponent-process theory
Opponent-process theory describes emotional rebound after a stimulus ends.
Maslow's hierarchy
Maslow's hierarchy concerns the ordering of needs.
questions.x: The facial feedback hypothesis says facial muscle activity, like a forced smile, influences emotional experience. Trap: Assuming the effect is large and universal.

questions.q: Ekman's cross-cultural research found that which set of emotions is recognized across cultures?
o: Pride, shame, guilt, embarrassment only
Pride, shame, guilt, and embarrassment are social emotions that vary more by culture.
Jealousy and envy only
Jealousy and envy are not among the universal expressions.
Happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust
Correct: Ekman found happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust show universal facial expressions across cultures.
Boredom and nostalgia only
Boredom and nostalgia are not universally recognized facial expressions.
questions.x: Ekman found happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust show universal facial expressions across cultures. Trap: Assuming display rules are universal too.

questions.q: A person smiles politely at a funeral. This reflects:
o: universal facial expression
A universal facial expression would be a spontaneous basic emotion, not a polite smile masking feelings.
James-Lange arousal
James-Lange arousal concerns the cause of emotion, not social expression.
the amygdala hijack
The amygdala hijack is an abrupt emotional overreaction, not a controlled smile.
display rules governing emotional expression
Correct: Display rules are culturally learned norms governing when and how emotions are shown, such as polite smiling at a funeral.
questions.x: Display rules are culturally learned norms governing when and how emotions are shown, such as polite smiling at a funeral. Trap: Confusing felt emotion with expressed emotion.

questions.q: In Selye's general adaptation syndrome, the stage in which the body mobilizes resources and then maintains elevated cortisol is the:
o: resistance stage
Correct: The resistance stage involves sustained coping with elevated stress hormones such as cortisol.
alarm stage
The alarm stage is the initial sympathetic burst.
exhaustion stage
Exhaustion is the depletion of resources after prolonged stress.
recovery stage
Recovery is not one of Selye's three stages.
questions.x: The resistance stage involves sustained coping with elevated stress hormones such as cortisol. Trap: Confusing alarm with resistance.

questions.q: The correct order of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is:
o: adrenal medulla, pituitary, hypothalamus
This lists the structures in reverse order and uses the adrenal medulla, which is part of the sympathetic system.
hypothalamus (CRH), anterior pituitary (ACTH), adrenal cortex (cortisol)
Correct: The HPA axis runs hypothalamus (CRH), anterior pituitary (ACTH), then adrenal cortex (cortisol).
hypothalamus (ACTH), pituitary (CRH), adrenal medulla
It misassigns ACTH to the hypothalamus and CRH to the pituitary, and ends in the medulla.
pituitary, hypothalamus, adrenal cortex
It starts at the pituitary before the hypothalamus, reversing the first two steps.
questions.x: The HPA axis runs hypothalamus (CRH), anterior pituitary (ACTH), then adrenal cortex (cortisol). Trap: Swapping the hormones so that ACTH is released by the hypothalamus and CRH by the pituitary, which reverses the cascade.

questions.q: Which physiological change accompanies acute stress?
o: Decreased heart rate
Decreased heart rate is parasympathetic.
Increased digestion
Increased digestion is parasympathetic.
Increased heart rate and dilated bronchioles
Correct: The sympathetic fight-or-flight response raises heart rate, dilates bronchioles, and inhibits digestion.
Pupillary constriction
Pupillary constriction is parasympathetic, whereas stress dilates the pupils.
questions.x: The sympathetic fight-or-flight response raises heart rate, dilates bronchioles, and inhibits digestion. Trap: Confusing sympathetic and parasympathetic.

questions.q: When a person first judges whether a situation is threatening, then judges whether they have resources to cope, these are respectively:
o: secondary and primary appraisal
This reverses the order of primary and secondary appraisal.
emotion- and problem-focused coping
Emotion- and problem-focused coping are coping strategies, not appraisal stages.
alarm and resistance
Alarm and resistance are stages of Selye's general adaptation syndrome.
primary and secondary appraisal
Correct: Primary appraisal evaluates whether the situation is a threat, and secondary appraisal evaluates coping resources.
questions.x: Primary appraisal evaluates whether the situation is a threat, and secondary appraisal evaluates coping resources. Trap: Reversing primary and secondary appraisal.

questions.q: A student facing an exam creates a study schedule. This is:
o: problem-focused coping
Correct: Problem-focused coping acts directly on the stressor, as when making a study schedule.
emotion-focused coping
Emotion-focused coping manages feelings rather than the stressor.
avoidance coping
Avoidance coping would mean evading the exam.
defensive denial
Defensive denial would mean refusing to acknowledge the exam.
questions.x: Problem-focused coping acts directly on the stressor, as when making a study schedule. Trap: Calling every active coping emotion-focused.

questions.q: Meditating to calm oneself after an unavoidable loss is:
o: problem-focused coping
Problem-focused coping would try to change the situation, which is impossible here.
emotion-focused coping
Correct: Meditation after an unavoidable loss manages emotional distress rather than changing the situation, which is emotion-focused coping.
the alarm stage
The alarm stage is a physiological stage of stress response, not a coping act.
learned helplessness
Learned helplessness is passivity after uncontrollable stress, not calming oneself.
questions.x: Meditation after an unavoidable loss manages emotional distress rather than changing the situation, which is emotion-focused coping. Trap: Believing emotion-focused coping is always maladaptive.

questions.q: According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, performance on a complex task is best at:
o: maximal arousal
Maximal arousal impairs performance on complex tasks.
minimal arousal
Minimal arousal gives too little engagement.
moderate arousal
Correct: Yerkes-Dodson describes an inverted-U relation between arousal and performance, with complex tasks peaking at moderate (lower) arousal.
no arousal
No arousal means no alertness and poor performance.
questions.x: Yerkes-Dodson describes an inverted-U relation between arousal and performance, with complex tasks peaking at moderate (lower) arousal. Trap: Assuming more arousal always improves performance.

questions.q: Dogs exposed to inescapable shocks later failed to escape avoidable shocks. This demonstrates:
o: classical conditioning extinction
Extinction is the loss of a conditioned response when the CS is unreinforced.
drive reduction
Drive reduction is a motivation theory.
fixed-ratio reinforcement
Fixed-ratio reinforcement is an operant schedule not involved here.
learned helplessness
Correct: Learned helplessness: Seligman found that uncontrollable shocks led dogs to passivity even when escape was possible.
questions.x: Learned helplessness: Seligman found that uncontrollable shocks led dogs to passivity even when escape was possible. Trap: Attributing the dogs' passivity to fear of the apparatus rather than learned lack of control.

questions.q: A student who believes grades depend mostly on luck has:
o: an external locus of control
Correct: An external locus of control attributes outcomes to outside factors such as luck.
an internal locus of control
An internal locus attributes outcomes to one's own actions.
high self-efficacy
High self-efficacy is belief in one's own ability, opposite to attributing grades to luck.
an intrinsic motivation
Intrinsic motivation is doing a task for its own sake, which is not a belief about control.
questions.x: An external locus of control attributes outcomes to outside factors such as luck. Trap: Equating external locus with low intelligence.

questions.q: Bandura defined self-efficacy as:
o: general self-esteem
General self-esteem is global self-worth, not task-specific.
belief in one's ability to accomplish a specific task
Correct: Bandura defined self-efficacy as belief in one's ability to accomplish a specific task.
belief that outcomes are due to fate
Belief that outcomes are due to fate is an external locus of control.
an innate drive
An innate drive is a biological motivation concept.
questions.x: Bandura defined self-efficacy as belief in one's ability to accomplish a specific task. Trap: Confusing self-efficacy with self-esteem.

questions.q: Drive reduction theory proposes that behavior is motivated by:
o: seeking optimal arousal
Seeking optimal arousal is arousal theory.
conscious goals alone
Conscious goals alone fits goal-setting theory.
the need to reduce internal tension from unmet physiological needs
Correct: Drive reduction theory holds that unmet physiological needs create internal tension (drives), and satisfying them restores homeostasis.
rewards from others
Rewards from others is incentive or extrinsic motivation, not internal drives.
questions.x: Drive reduction theory holds that unmet physiological needs create internal tension (drives), and satisfying them restores homeostasis. Trap: Mistaking drive reduction for incentive theory.

questions.q: A person buys a cake they see in a window even though they are not hungry. This is best explained by:
o: drive reduction theory
Drive reduction requires a physiological need, but the person is not hungry.
instinct theory
Instinct theory attributes behavior to innate patterns.
the Yerkes-Dodson law
Yerkes-Dodson relates arousal to performance, not motivation.
incentive theory
Correct: Incentive theory says external rewards, like a cake seen in a window, pull behavior even without an internal need.
questions.x: Incentive theory says external rewards, like a cake seen in a window, pull behavior even without an internal need. Trap: Attributing external pull to internal drive.

questions.q: In Maslow's hierarchy, which need must be satisfied first?
o: Physiological needs
Correct: Maslow's hierarchy places basic physiological needs (food, water, sleep) at the base, to be satisfied first.
Esteem
Esteem is a higher-level need.
Self-actualization
Self-actualization sits at the top of the hierarchy.
Belongingness
Belongingness comes after physiological and safety needs.
questions.x: Maslow's hierarchy places basic physiological needs (food, water, sleep) at the base, to be satisfied first. Trap: Assuming safety or belonging must be met before basic food and water needs.

questions.q: Children who were rewarded for drawing later drew less when rewards stopped. This is the:
o: Yerkes-Dodson law
Yerkes-Dodson relates arousal to performance.
overjustification effect
Correct: The overjustification effect: external rewards for an already enjoyable activity undermine intrinsic motivation, so drawing drops when rewards stop.
Garcia effect
The Garcia effect is conditioned taste aversion.
halo effect
The halo effect is generalizing one positive trait to others.
questions.x: The overjustification effect: external rewards for an already enjoyable activity undermine intrinsic motivation, so drawing drops when rewards stop. Trap: Assuming rewards always increase motivation.

questions.q: Self-determination theory identifies three basic psychological needs:
o: safety, love, esteem
Safety, love, and esteem are levels in Maslow's hierarchy.
drive, incentive, arousal
Drive, incentive, and arousal are separate motivation theories.
autonomy, competence, and relatedness
Correct: Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the basic needs that foster intrinsic motivation.
extrinsic, intrinsic, amotivation
Extrinsic, intrinsic, and amotivation are types of motivation, not needs.
questions.x: Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the basic needs that foster intrinsic motivation. Trap: Confusing self-determination theory's three needs with the levels of Maslow's hierarchy.

questions.q: Solomon's opponent-process theory of emotion explains the relief a skydiver feels after the jump through:
o: cortisol depletion
Cortisol depletion is not the proposed mechanism.
amygdala lesions
Amygdala lesions are not involved in this healthy response.
cognitive dissonance
Cognitive dissonance concerns conflicting beliefs, not emotional rebound.
a delayed opposing emotional process that counteracts the initial reaction
Correct: Solomon's opponent-process theory explains relief after the jump as a delayed opposing emotional process that counteracts the initial reaction.
questions.x: Solomon's opponent-process theory explains relief after the jump as a delayed opposing emotional process that counteracts the initial reaction. Trap: Mistaking it for the visual opponent-process theory.

questions.q: Which trait is most strongly linked with coronary heart disease risk among Type A characteristics?
o: Hostility
Correct: Hostility is the Type A characteristic most strongly predictive of cardiovascular risk.
Competitiveness
Competitiveness is less strongly linked to coronary heart disease.
Time urgency
Time urgency is a Type A trait but a weaker predictor.
Ambition
Ambition is also a weaker predictor.
questions.x: Hostility is the Type A characteristic most strongly predictive of cardiovascular risk. Trap: Assuming time urgency or competitiveness is the main Type A risk when hostility is the strongest predictor.

questions.q: Which factor is associated with reduced physiological stress responses?
o: Social isolation
Social isolation heightens stress responses.
Strong social support
Correct: Strong social support buffers stress reactivity and reduces physiological stress responses.
Daily hassles
Daily hassles accumulate and increase stress.
Unpredictability
Unpredictability raises stress.
questions.x: Strong social support buffers stress reactivity and reduces physiological stress responses. Trap: Believing social support has no effect on how strongly the body reacts to stress.

questions.q: A moderate stressor that motivates and enhances function is called:
o: distress
Distress is harmful stress.
allostatic load
Allostatic load is the cumulative wear from chronic stress.
eustress
Correct: Eustress is moderate, beneficial stress that motivates and enhances function.
burnout
Burnout is exhaustion from prolonged stress.
questions.x: Eustress is moderate, beneficial stress that motivates and enhances function. Trap: Thinking all stress is harmful, when moderate stress can motivate and improve performance.

questions.q: Chronic stress causing cumulative wear on body systems is described as:
o: homeostasis
Homeostasis is stability of internal conditions.
eustress
Eustress is beneficial stress, not wear.
incentive
Incentive is an external motivator unrelated to stress wear.
allostatic load
Correct: Allostatic load is the cumulative long-term cost of adapting to chronic stress.
questions.x: Allostatic load is the cumulative long-term cost of adapting to chronic stress. Trap: Confusing allostatic load (cumulative wear) with homeostasis (maintaining stable internal conditions).

questions.q: Chronically elevated cortisol is associated with:
o: suppressed immune function and hippocampal atrophy
Correct: Chronically elevated cortisol suppresses the immune system and damages the hippocampus, causing atrophy.
enhanced immunity
Cortisol suppresses rather than enhances immunity.
increased hippocampal volume
Hippocampal volume decreases, not increases.
lowered blood glucose
Cortisol raises, not lowers, blood glucose.
questions.x: Chronically elevated cortisol suppresses the immune system and damages the hippocampus, causing atrophy. Trap: Believing cortisol only has acute effects.

questions.q: Which structure is primarily responsible for regulating hunger, thirst, and body temperature during motivation?
o: Hippocampus
The hippocampus forms memories.
Hypothalamus
Correct: The hypothalamus governs homeostatic drives such as hunger, thirst, and temperature.
Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
Occipital cortex
The occipital cortex processes vision.
questions.x: The hypothalamus governs homeostatic drives such as hunger, thirst, and temperature. Trap: Mixing up the hypothalamus (homeostatic drives) with the similarly named hippocampus (memory).

questions.q: Phineas Gage's injury to the frontal lobe produced:
o: loss of vision
Vision loss would require occipital or visual pathway damage.
loss of memory formation
Memory formation depends on the hippocampus.
disinhibited, impulsive behavior and personality change
Correct: Ventromedial prefrontal damage, as in Phineas Gage, impairs regulation of emotion and produces disinhibited, impulsive behavior and personality change.
paralysis
Paralysis would involve motor cortex or spinal damage, which Gage did not have.
questions.x: Ventromedial prefrontal damage, as in Phineas Gage, impairs regulation of emotion and produces disinhibited, impulsive behavior and personality change. Trap: Believing frontal damage causes memory loss.

questions.q: Which hormone, secreted by fat cells, signals satiety?
o: Ghrelin
Ghrelin, from the stomach, increases hunger.
Cortisol
Cortisol is a stress hormone, not a satiety signal from fat.
Insulin from beta cells only
Insulin comes from pancreatic beta cells, not fat cells.
Leptin
Correct: Leptin, secreted by fat cells, suppresses appetite and signals satiety.
questions.x: Leptin, secreted by fat cells, suppresses appetite and signals satiety. Trap: Confusing leptin (satiety from fat cells) with ghrelin (hunger from the stomach).

questions.q: The insula is most associated with:
o: the feeling of disgust and interoception
Correct: The insula processes bodily states (interoception) and disgust.
motor planning
Motor planning involves premotor and supplementary motor areas.
language production
Language production involves Broca's area.
visual processing
Visual processing occurs in the occipital cortex.
questions.x: The insula processes bodily states (interoception) and disgust. Trap: Assuming disgust is amygdala only.

questions.q: A smoker who says 'the health risks are exaggerated' to resolve tension is reducing:
o: drive
Drive reduction concerns physiological needs.
cognitive dissonance
Correct: Dismissing the risks to resolve the tension between belief and behavior reduces cognitive dissonance.
arousal
Arousal is a general activation state, not conflicting cognitions.
allostatic load
Allostatic load is the wear from chronic stress.
questions.x: Dismissing the risks to resolve the tension between belief and behavior reduces cognitive dissonance. Trap: Thinking dissonance requires changing the behavior.

questions.q: Who first described the fight-or-flight response?
o: Hans Selye
Hans Selye described the general adaptation syndrome.
William James
William James co-authored the James-Lange theory of emotion.
Walter Cannon
Correct: Walter Cannon coined the term fight-or-flight.
Stanley Schachter
Stanley Schachter developed the two-factor theory of emotion.
questions.x: Walter Cannon coined the term fight-or-flight. Trap: Attributing fight-or-flight to Selye, who described the general adaptation syndrome instead.

questions.q: Shelley Taylor proposed that under stress, females are more likely to:
o: fight
Fight is the classic response, not Taylor's proposal.
flee
Flee is likewise part of Cannon's classic model.
freeze
Freezing is a separate threat response not part of her proposal.
tend and befriend
Correct: Taylor proposed that females more often tend and befriend under stress, a response of social affiliation mediated by oxytocin.
questions.x: Taylor proposed that females more often tend and befriend under stress, a response of social affiliation mediated by oxytocin. Trap: Assuming fight-or-flight applies equally to everyone, overlooking Taylor's tend-and-befriend proposal for females.

questions.q: Reframing a stressful event as a challenge rather than a threat is called:
o: cognitive reappraisal
Correct: Cognitive reappraisal, reframing an event as a challenge, changes its emotional impact.
suppression
Suppression inhibits the expression of emotion and is less effective.
displacement
Displacement redirects feelings onto a substitute target.
repression
Repression pushes unwanted thoughts out of awareness.
questions.x: Cognitive reappraisal, reframing an event as a challenge, changes its emotional impact. Trap: Assuming suppression of emotion works as well as reframing, when reappraisal is more effective.

questions.q: Arousal theory predicts that a bored person will:
o: reduce all stimulation
Reducing stimulation would lower arousal further.
seek stimulation to raise arousal to an optimal level
Correct: Arousal theory predicts a bored person seeks stimulation to raise arousal toward an optimal level.
become hungry
Hunger is not predicted by boredom.
decrease drive
Decreasing drive is not the arousal theory prediction.
questions.x: Arousal theory predicts a bored person seeks stimulation to raise arousal toward an optimal level. Trap: Mixing arousal theory (seeking optimal stimulation) with drive reduction (reducing internal tension).

questions.q: According to expectancy-value theory, motivation is highest when:
o: success is unlikely and valued
Unlikely success lowers expectancy even if the goal is valued.
success is likely and not valued
An unvalued outcome gives little motivation even if success is likely.
the person expects success and values the outcome
Correct: Expectancy-value theory holds that motivation is the product of expecting success and valuing the outcome.
the task is arbitrary
An arbitrary task has no value, so motivation is low.
questions.x: Expectancy-value theory holds that motivation is the product of expecting success and valuing the outcome. Trap: Thinking value alone drives motivation, ignoring the expectation of success.

questions.q: Bilateral removal of the temporal lobes including the amygdala in monkeys produced:
o: heightened aggression and fear
Fear and aggression are reduced, not heightened.
loss of vision
Vision is not lost, though objects are not recognized for what they are.
inability to form new declarative memories only
The defining features are emotional and behavioral, not a memory-only deficit.
tameness, loss of fear, and hyperorality
Correct: Bilateral temporal lobe removal including the amygdala produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality, and hypersexuality.
questions.x: Bilateral temporal lobe removal including the amygdala produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality, and hypersexuality. Trap: Assuming amygdala damage increases fear and aggression.

questions.q: Researchers compare a trait's concordance in monozygotic twins reared apart with that in dizygotic twins reared together. Higher concordance in the monozygotic pairs would most directly suggest that:
o: genetic factors contribute to variation in the trait
Correct: MZ twins share nearly all their genes, so greater concordance than DZ twins, even when reared apart, implicates genetic influence on the trait.
shared family environment is the sole determinant of the trait
Shared family environment cannot explain similarity in twins raised apart, and it is equal-ish for DZ twins reared together.
the trait is fully determined by genes with no environmental input
MZ concordance below 100% would still show environmental input, so full genetic determination is not implied.
the trait arises from random developmental error
Random developmental error would not produce systematically higher concordance in genetically identical pairs.
questions.x: MZ twins share nearly all their genes, so greater concordance than DZ twins, even when reared apart, implicates genetic influence on the trait. Trap: Equating high heritability with complete genetic determination.

questions.q: After an accident, a previously calm man becomes impulsive and irreverent, though his memory and language remain intact. Which region was most likely damaged?
o: Hippocampus
The hippocampus is needed for forming new declarative memories, which are intact here.
Prefrontal cortex
Correct: The prefrontal cortex governs impulse control, planning, and social behavior, as in the case of Phineas Gage, so damage changes personality while memory and language persist.
Broca's area
Broca's area controls speech production, and language is preserved.
Occipital lobe
The occipital lobe processes vision and would not alter personality.
questions.x: The prefrontal cortex governs impulse control, planning, and social behavior, as in the case of Phineas Gage, so damage changes personality while memory and language persist. Trap: Assuming personality change implies limbic damage only.

questions.q: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposes that positive symptoms such as hallucinations result from:
o: deficient acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions
Deficient acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions describes myasthenia-type weakness, not psychosis.
loss of GABA-mediated inhibition in the spinal cord
Loss of spinal GABA inhibition relates to spasticity or tetanus-like effects, not hallucinations.
excess dopamine activity in mesolimbic pathways
Correct: The dopamine hypothesis ties positive symptoms like hallucinations to overactivity of dopamine in mesolimbic pathways, and antipsychotics work by blocking D2 receptors.
depleted serotonin in the raphe nuclei only
Depleted serotonin in the raphe nuclei is linked to depression and is not the dopamine hypothesis.
questions.x: The dopamine hypothesis ties positive symptoms like hallucinations to overactivity of dopamine in mesolimbic pathways, and antipsychotics work by blocking D2 receptors. Trap: Confusing the dopamine deficit in Parkinson disease with the excess in schizophrenia.

questions.q: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor treats depression primarily by:
o: increasing serotonin degradation by monoamine oxidase
Increasing MAO degradation would lower serotonin; MAO inhibitors do the opposite.
blocking postsynaptic serotonin receptors
Blocking postsynaptic receptors would reduce serotonin signaling rather than enhance it.
stimulating presynaptic release of dopamine only
SSRIs act selectively on serotonin transporters and do not primarily stimulate dopamine release.
increasing serotonin availability in the synaptic cleft
Correct: SSRIs block presynaptic reuptake of serotonin, leaving more serotonin in the synaptic cleft to act on postsynaptic receptors.
questions.x: SSRIs block presynaptic reuptake of serotonin, leaving more serotonin in the synaptic cleft to act on postsynaptic receptors. Trap: Thinking SSRIs raise serotonin synthesis rather than prolong synaptic presence.

questions.q: A person described as organized, dependable, and self-disciplined would score high on which Big Five trait?
o: Conscientiousness
Correct: Conscientiousness reflects organization, dependability, and self-discipline.
Openness to experience
Openness reflects curiosity, imagination, and willingness to try new things.
Agreeableness
Agreeableness reflects cooperation, trust, and warmth toward others.
Neuroticism
Neuroticism reflects emotional instability and anxiety, the opposite of a steady, self-disciplined profile.
questions.x: Conscientiousness reflects organization, dependability, and self-discipline. Trap: Mixing up agreeableness with dependability.

questions.q: A man with strong unconscious hostility toward a coworker is excessively friendly and generous toward him. This is best described as:
o: projection
Projection attributes one's own impulse to someone else, not acting oppositely.
reaction formation
Correct: Reaction formation replaces an unacceptable impulse with its opposite behavior, here hostility expressed as excessive friendliness.
displacement
Displacement redirects the impulse to a safer target, whereas the hostility here is aimed at the coworker himself.
sublimation
Sublimation channels an impulse into a socially acceptable pursuit such as art or sport.
questions.x: Reaction formation replaces an unacceptable impulse with its opposite behavior, here hostility expressed as excessive friendliness. Trap: Choosing projection because hostility is involved.

questions.q: A student who cheats on exams insists that his classmates are the ones who cheat. This is an example of:
o: denial
Denial refuses to acknowledge reality or one's own behavior, rather than blaming others for it.
regression
Regression reverts to an earlier developmental stage of behavior.
projection
Correct: Projection attributes one's own unacceptable impulses or behaviors to others, as the cheater accuses his classmates.
intellectualization
Intellectualization manages anxiety by detached, abstract analysis of an issue.
questions.x: Projection attributes one's own unacceptable impulses or behaviors to others, as the cheater accuses his classmates. Trap: Calling it denial because he refuses to admit his own behavior.

questions.q: According to Maslow's hierarchy, once physiological and safety needs are met, an individual is next motivated by:
o: self-actualization needs
Self-actualization is the top tier and is reached last.
esteem needs, skipping belonging
Esteem follows belonging, so it cannot come directly after safety.
cognitive and aesthetic needs only
Cognitive and aesthetic needs are later additions to the model and are not the next step after safety.
love and belonging needs
Correct: In Maslow's ordering the tiers are physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, then self-actualization, so belonging comes next.
questions.x: In Maslow's ordering the tiers are physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, then self-actualization, so belonging comes next. Trap: Skipping belonging and jumping to esteem.

questions.q: According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, which situation would most likely yield peak performance?
o: Moderate arousal on a moderately difficult task
Correct: Performance follows an inverted U with arousal, and optimal arousal is moderate for a moderately difficult task.
Very high arousal on a very complex task
Very high arousal impairs performance on complex tasks, which need lower arousal.
Very low arousal on a simple task
Very low arousal on a simple task leaves the person under-aroused, below the simple-task optimum.
Maximum arousal on any task
Maximum arousal lies past the peak of the inverted U for essentially every task.
questions.x: Performance follows an inverted U with arousal, and optimal arousal is moderate for a moderately difficult task. Trap: Assuming more arousal always improves performance.

questions.q: According to drive reduction theory, a person eats a meal primarily to:
o: obtain an external reward unrelated to need
Seeking external rewards unrelated to need is incentive theory.
reduce the tension of a physiological need and restore homeostasis
Correct: Drive reduction holds that physiological needs create tension (drives), and behavior such as eating reduces the drive and restores homeostasis.
fulfill an unconscious wish
Fulfilling an unconscious wish is a psychoanalytic explanation, not drive reduction.
increase arousal to an optimal level
Raising arousal to an optimal level is arousal theory.
questions.x: Drive reduction holds that physiological needs create tension (drives), and behavior such as eating reduces the drive and restores homeostasis. Trap: Confusing drive reduction with incentive theory.

questions.q: Children who enjoyed drawing were rewarded with prizes for drawing, and later drew less when rewards stopped. This illustrates:
o: negative reinforcement strengthening drawing
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus, whereas prizes were added.
drive reduction
Drive reduction concerns satisfying biological needs, not rewards for an enjoyed hobby.
the overjustification effect reducing intrinsic motivation
Correct: Extrinsic rewards for an already enjoyed activity can undermine intrinsic motivation, the overjustification effect, so drawing drops once rewards stop.
learned helplessness
Learned helplessness follows uncontrollable aversive events and would not arise from receiving prizes.
questions.x: Extrinsic rewards for an already enjoyed activity can undermine intrinsic motivation, the overjustification effect, so drawing drops once rewards stop. Trap: Believing rewards always increase later behavior.

questions.q: According to the James-Lange theory, a person who sees a bear and then feels fear experiences emotion because:
o: the emotion and arousal occur simultaneously and independently
Simultaneous, independent arousal and emotion is the Cannon-Bard theory.
cognitive labeling of ambiguous arousal determines the emotion
Cognitive labeling of ambiguous arousal is Schachter-Singer two-factor theory.
the thalamus sends signals only to the cortex
A thalamus that signals only to the cortex does not describe any theory in which bodily feedback produces emotion, and is not James-Lange.
the perception of bodily arousal produces the emotion
Correct: James-Lange holds that the physiological response comes first and perception of that bodily arousal constitutes the emotion.
questions.x: James-Lange holds that the physiological response comes first and perception of that bodily arousal constitutes the emotion. Trap: Reversing the order of arousal and emotion.

questions.q: A theory proposing that a stimulus triggers physiological arousal and the subjective emotion at the same time, via thalamic activity, is the:
o: Cannon-Bard theory
Correct: Cannon-Bard states that a stimulus triggers arousal and emotional experience simultaneously and independently via the thalamus.
James-Lange theory
James-Lange has bodily arousal first, with emotion following from perceiving it.
Schachter-Singer theory
Schachter-Singer adds a cognitive label to arousal, so emotion is not simultaneous.
opponent-process theory
Opponent-process theory explains emotional contrast and adaptation, not the origin of arousal and emotion.
questions.x: Cannon-Bard states that a stimulus triggers arousal and emotional experience simultaneously and independently via the thalamus. Trap: Mixing up Cannon-Bard with James-Lange.

questions.q: Participants injected with epinephrine reported anger or euphoria depending on a confederate's behavior. This supports which theory?
o: James-Lange theory, in which arousal alone defines the emotion
James-Lange has no labeling step and would predict the same emotion regardless of the confederate.
Two-factor theory, in which arousal is cognitively labeled
Correct: Two-factor theory holds that emotion arises from physiological arousal plus a cognitive label drawn from context, as the confederate's behavior supplied here.
Cannon-Bard theory, in which emotion precedes arousal
Cannon-Bard claims simultaneity, not emotion preceding arousal, and ignores situational labeling.
the facial feedback hypothesis only
Facial feedback concerns facial expression influencing emotion, not injected arousal and social cues.
questions.x: Two-factor theory holds that emotion arises from physiological arousal plus a cognitive label drawn from context, as the confederate's behavior supplied here. Trap: Ignoring the role of the situational cue.

questions.q: A patient with bilateral amygdala damage would be expected to show:
o: inability to form new declarative memories
New declarative memories depend on the hippocampus.
loss of speech comprehension
Speech comprehension involves Wernicke's area.
impaired fear conditioning and recognition of fearful faces
Correct: The amygdala processes fear and threat and is key to fear learning and recognizing fearful expressions, so bilateral damage impairs both.
complete loss of vision
Vision depends on the occipital cortex and visual pathways.
questions.x: The amygdala processes fear and threat and is key to fear learning and recognizing fearful expressions, so bilateral damage impairs both. Trap: Attributing memory formation to the amygdala.

questions.q: In Lazarus's model, secondary appraisal refers to the person's:
o: initial judgment of whether an event is irrelevant, benign, or stressful
Judging an event as irrelevant, benign, or stressful is primary appraisal.
physiological alarm reaction
The physiological alarm reaction belongs to Selye's general adaptation syndrome.
unconscious displacement of anxiety
Unconscious displacement of anxiety is a Freudian defense mechanism, not an appraisal.
evaluation of whether they have resources to cope with the stressor
Correct: Primary appraisal judges the event itself, while secondary appraisal evaluates whether one has the resources to cope with it.
questions.x: Primary appraisal judges the event itself, while secondary appraisal evaluates whether one has the resources to cope with it. Trap: Swapping primary and secondary appraisal.

questions.q: In Selye's general adaptation syndrome, prolonged exposure to a stressor after sympathetic activation eventually leads to:
o: exhaustion with increased vulnerability to illness
Correct: Selye's stages are alarm, resistance, and exhaustion, and prolonged stress depletes resources, raising vulnerability to illness.
a return to baseline without physiological cost
Chronic stress carries physiological costs and does not return to baseline for free.
permanent alarm reaction only
The alarm reaction is only the first stage and does not persist alone.
parasympathetic shutdown in the alarm stage
The alarm stage involves sympathetic activation, not parasympathetic shutdown.
questions.x: Selye's stages are alarm, resistance, and exhaustion, and prolonged stress depletes resources, raising vulnerability to illness. Trap: Thinking resistance stage resolves stress.

questions.q: A person with a genetic predisposition to depression develops the disorder only after losing a job. This best fits:
o: the humanistic model
Humanistic theory concerns self-actualization and personal growth, not gene-environment triggers.
the diathesis-stress model
Correct: The diathesis-stress model says a predisposition combined with an environmental stressor triggers the disorder.
the classical conditioning model of phobia
Classical conditioning models learned associations such as phobias, not genetic vulnerability.
the drive reduction model
Drive reduction concerns motivation from physiological needs.
questions.x: The diathesis-stress model says a predisposition combined with an environmental stressor triggers the disorder. Trap: Treating genes alone as sufficient.

questions.q: Bandura's reciprocal determinism holds that behavior is determined by:
o: unconscious conflict among id, ego, and superego
Conflict among id, ego, and superego is psychoanalytic.
only stable, inherited traits
Trait-only views ignore environment and behavior, contradicting the reciprocal model.
mutual interaction of the person, behavior, and environment
Correct: Reciprocal determinism holds that personal factors (cognition), behavior, and environment influence each other bidirectionally.
only environmental reinforcement
Environment-only determinism is the behaviorist view, which Bandura rejected.
questions.x: Reciprocal determinism holds that personal factors (cognition), behavior, and environment influence each other bidirectionally. Trap: Choosing the behaviorist environment-only view.

questions.q: A student believes his exam grades result mainly from luck and the teacher's whims. He has:
o: an internal locus of control
Internal locus attributes outcomes to one's own effort or ability.
high self-efficacy
Self-efficacy is belief in one's capability to succeed, not attribution to luck.
a self-serving bias
Self-serving bias credits oneself for success and blames external factors for failure, rather than consistently attributing outcomes to luck.
an external locus of control
Correct: Attributing outcomes to outside forces such as luck and teacher whims reflects an external locus of control.
questions.x: Attributing outcomes to outside forces such as luck and teacher whims reflects an external locus of control. Trap: Confusing locus of control with self-efficacy.

questions.q: In Rogers's humanistic theory, incongruence between self and experience is most likely to result from:
o: conditional positive regard
Correct: Rogers held that conditional positive regard imposes conditions of worth, which distort the self-concept and produce incongruence between self and experience.
unconditional positive regard
Unconditional positive regard promotes congruence rather than incongruence.
fixation at a psychosexual stage
Fixation at a psychosexual stage is a Freudian concept, not part of Rogers's theory.
reciprocal determinism
Reciprocal determinism is Bandura's social-cognitive model of person, behavior, and environment.
questions.x: Rogers held that conditional positive regard imposes conditions of worth, which distort the self-concept and produce incongruence between self and experience. Trap: Reversing conditional and unconditional regard.

questions.q: Eysenck's biological theory proposed that introverts, compared with extraverts, have:
o: lower baseline cortical arousal and thus seek stimulation
This describes extraverts, who have lower baseline arousal and so seek stimulation.
higher baseline cortical arousal and thus avoid excess stimulation
Correct: Eysenck proposed that introverts have higher baseline cortical arousal, so they avoid excess stimulation, while extraverts seek it.
no biological differences
Eysenck explicitly proposed biological bases for temperament, so 'no differences' contradicts him.
greater parasympathetic dominance only
Parasympathetic dominance was not his mechanism, which centered on cortical arousal.
questions.x: Eysenck proposed that introverts have higher baseline cortical arousal, so they avoid excess stimulation, while extraverts seek it. Trap: Reversing the arousal-stimulation relation.

questions.q: Which finding is required for a diagnosis of bipolar I disorder?
o: At least one panic attack
Panic attacks define panic disorder.
Delusions lasting six months
Delusions lasting six months point toward a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder.
At least one manic episode
Correct: Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode; depressive episodes are common but not required.
Compulsive rituals
Compulsive rituals suggest obsessive-compulsive disorder.
questions.x: Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode; depressive episodes are common but not required. Trap: Assuming depression alone qualifies.

questions.q: A person washes hands dozens of times a day to relieve distressing thoughts of contamination. The repetitive washing is best termed a:
o: delusion of reference
A delusion of reference is a fixed false belief that neutral events are directed at oneself.
dissociative fugue
Dissociative fugue involves sudden travel with loss of identity or memory.
somatic symptom
A somatic symptom is distressing bodily complaint, not a ritualized behavior to relieve intrusive thoughts.
compulsion that reduces anxiety from obsessions
Correct: Compulsions are repetitive behaviors, like handwashing, performed to reduce anxiety from intrusive obsessions such as contamination fears.
questions.x: Compulsions are repetitive behaviors, like handwashing, performed to reduce anxiety from intrusive obsessions such as contamination fears. Trap: Labeling the thoughts, not the washing, as compulsions.

questions.q: A person who has two or more distinct personality states and gaps in memory for everyday events is most likely diagnosed with:
o: dissociative identity disorder
Correct: Dissociative identity disorder involves two or more distinct identities or personality states and amnesia beyond ordinary forgetting.
borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder features unstable relationships, self-image, and mood, not distinct identities.
schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder involving hallucinations and delusions, not split identities.
schizoid personality disorder
Schizoid personality disorder involves detachment and limited emotional expression, not identity fragmentation.
questions.x: Dissociative identity disorder involves two or more distinct identities or personality states and amnesia beyond ordinary forgetting. Trap: Equating schizophrenia with split personality.

questions.q: Which is a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
o: Hallucinations
Hallucinations are positive symptoms, added experiences.
Flat affect
Correct: Negative symptoms are absences of normal functions, such as flat affect or avolition.
Delusions of grandeur
Delusions of grandeur are positive symptoms, added false beliefs.
Disorganized speech
Disorganized speech is a positive (or disorganized) symptom, an added abnormal behavior.
questions.x: Negative symptoms are absences of normal functions, such as flat affect or avolition. Trap: Assuming 'negative' symptoms are the more severe ones rather than the absence of normal functions.

questions.q: Damage to the lateral hypothalamus in an animal would most likely cause:
o: overeating and obesity
Overeating and obesity follow ventromedial hypothalamus lesions, the satiety center.
loss of thirst only
Thirst is not the main function of the lateral hypothalamus, and loss of thirst alone ignores its feeding role.
reduced eating and weight loss
Correct: The lateral hypothalamus is the hunger center, so lesions reduce eating and cause weight loss.
increased body temperature set point only
Temperature set point is mainly regulated by the anterior hypothalamus, not the lateral area.
questions.x: The lateral hypothalamus is the hunger center, so lesions reduce eating and cause weight loss. Trap: Mixing up lateral and ventromedial functions.

questions.q: Which statement about appetite hormones is accurate?
o: Leptin from the stomach stimulates hunger and ghrelin from fat suppresses it
This reverses both the sources and the effects of the two hormones.
Both increase hunger
Leptin decreases hunger, so both cannot increase it.
Both are secreted by the pancreas
Neither is a pancreatic hormone; the pancreas secretes insulin and glucagon.
Ghrelin from the stomach stimulates hunger, whereas leptin from adipose tissue suppresses it
Correct: Ghrelin, secreted by the stomach, stimulates hunger, and leptin, secreted by adipose tissue, signals satiety and suppresses appetite.
questions.x: Ghrelin, secreted by the stomach, stimulates hunger, and leptin, secreted by adipose tissue, signals satiety and suppresses appetite. Trap: Swapping which hormone comes from stomach versus fat and which raises versus lowers hunger.

questions.q: A person who is not hungry still buys a dessert because it looks delicious. Which theory best explains this?
o: Incentive theory
Correct: Incentive theory holds that external rewards, like an appealing dessert, pull behavior even without an internal need.
Drive reduction theory
Drive reduction relies on an internal physiological need, but the person is not hungry.
Instinct theory
Instinct theory describes innate, fixed behavior patterns, not responses to attractive stimuli.
Arousal theory
Arousal theory addresses seeking an optimal level of arousal, not reward value.
questions.x: Incentive theory holds that external rewards, like an appealing dessert, pull behavior even without an internal need. Trap: Using drive reduction for all motivated eating.

questions.q: Self-determination theory holds that well-being is fostered when which needs are satisfied?
o: Safety, esteem, and status
Safety, esteem, and status draw on Maslow's hierarchy.
Autonomy, competence, and relatedness
Correct: Self-determination theory identifies autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the basic needs that foster well-being.
Id, ego, and superego
Id, ego, and superego are Freud's structural components.
Openness, extraversion, and neuroticism
Openness, extraversion, and neuroticism are Big Five traits, not needs.
questions.x: Self-determination theory identifies autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the basic needs that foster well-being. Trap: Mixing self-determination needs with Maslow's hierarchy of safety, esteem, and status.

questions.q: During prolonged stress, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis results in the release of:
o: epinephrine from the adrenal cortex
Epinephrine comes from the adrenal medulla, part of the sympathetic response, not the cortex.
insulin from the pancreas
Insulin is released by the pancreas and is not a stress-axis product.
cortisol from the adrenal cortex
Correct: In the HPA axis the hypothalamus releases CRH, the pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol.
oxytocin from the thyroid
Oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary, not the thyroid.
questions.x: In the HPA axis the hypothalamus releases CRH, the pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol. Trap: Confusing adrenal cortex with medulla.

questions.q: Mischel argued that behavior is often inconsistent across settings. Which view does this support?
o: Traits fully determine behavior
If traits fully determined behavior, it would be consistent across settings.
Behavior is unaffected by context
Context-free behavior is the opposite of what situationism claims.
Personality is entirely genetic
Personality as entirely genetic ignores the situational variation Mischel documented.
Situational factors strongly shape behavior
Correct: Mischel's finding of cross-situational inconsistency supports situationism, which emphasizes context over stable traits.
questions.x: Mischel's finding of cross-situational inconsistency supports situationism, which emphasizes context over stable traits. Trap: Assuming personality traits predict behavior in all contexts.

questions.q: DNA methylation altering gene expression in response to early-life stress without changing the DNA sequence is an example of:
o: epigenetic regulation
Correct: Epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation change gene expression without altering the DNA sequence.
a point mutation
A point mutation changes the nucleotide sequence itself.
chromosomal nondisjunction
Nondisjunction changes chromosome number through faulty segregation.
genetic drift
Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequency across a population.
questions.x: Epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation change gene expression without altering the DNA sequence. Trap: Assuming environmental effects require altered DNA sequence.

questions.q: A child with a genetic tendency toward sociability elicits more social attention from adults. This is an example of:
o: passive gene-environment correlation
Passive correlation arises when parents provide both genes and a matching environment.
evocative gene-environment correlation
Correct: Evocative gene-environment correlation arises when a child's genetically influenced traits, like sociability, elicit particular responses from others.
epistasis
Epistasis is interaction between genes at different loci, not gene-environment correlation.
genetic imprinting
Genetic imprinting is parent-of-origin gene silencing.
questions.x: Evocative gene-environment correlation arises when a child's genetically influenced traits, like sociability, elicit particular responses from others. Trap: Confusing evocative with passive correlation.

questions.q: A student who believes she can master calculus persists after failing a test. Her persistence is best explained by:
o: external locus of control
External locus of control attributes outcomes to outside forces and would not predict mastery-oriented persistence.
learned helplessness
Learned helplessness predicts giving up after failure.
high self-efficacy
Correct: Self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to succeed, and high self-efficacy promotes persistence after setbacks.
reaction formation
Reaction formation is a defense mechanism expressing the opposite of an impulse.
questions.x: Self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to succeed, and high self-efficacy promotes persistence after setbacks. Trap: Treating self-esteem and self-efficacy as identical.

questions.q: In Freud's structural model, the component that mediates between instinctual demands and external reality is the:
o: id
The id seeks immediate gratification without regard to reality.
superego
The superego enforces moral standards rather than mediating with reality.
preconscious
The preconscious is a level of awareness, not a structural component.
ego
Correct: The ego operates on the reality principle, mediating between the id's instinctual demands and external reality.
questions.x: The ego operates on the reality principle, mediating between the id's instinctual demands and external reality. Trap: Assigning mediation to the superego.

questions.q: A person who repeatedly lies, violates others' rights, and shows no remorse most likely has:
o: antisocial personality disorder
Correct: Antisocial personality disorder involves a pervasive pattern of deceit, disregard for others' rights, and lack of remorse.
avoidant personality disorder
Avoidant personality disorder involves social inhibition and fear of rejection.
dependent personality disorder
Dependent personality disorder involves an excessive need to be cared for and submissiveness.
obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder involves perfectionism and rigid control, not rights violations.
questions.x: Antisocial personality disorder involves a pervasive pattern of deceit, disregard for others' rights, and lack of remorse. Trap: Confusing antisocial personality disorder with avoidant or dependent patterns because all are personality disorders.

questions.q: Recurrent unexpected episodes of intense fear with palpitations, sweating, and fear of dying, followed by persistent worry about recurrence, define:
o: specific phobia
Specific phobia is fear triggered by a particular object or situation, not unexpected attacks.
panic disorder
Correct: Panic disorder involves recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by persistent worry about further attacks.
generalized anxiety disorder
Generalized anxiety disorder is persistent diffuse worry without discrete surges of panic.
social anxiety disorder
Social anxiety disorder is fear triggered by social evaluation.
questions.x: Panic disorder involves recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by persistent worry about further attacks. Trap: Confusing panic with generalized anxiety.

questions.q: During a sudden threat, which response is mediated by the sympathetic nervous system?
o: Increased salivation and digestion
Increased salivation and digestion are parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) effects.
Pupil constriction
Pupil constriction is parasympathetic.
Pupil dilation and increased heart rate
Correct: Sympathetic activation prepares fight or flight, producing pupil dilation and increased heart rate.
Slowed heart rate
Slowed heart rate is parasympathetic.
questions.x: Sympathetic activation prepares fight or flight, producing pupil dilation and increased heart rate. Trap: Mixing up sympathetic and parasympathetic effects.

questions.q: A patient understands speech but speaks in halting, effortful, telegraphic sentences. Damage is most likely in the:
o: left superior temporal gyrus
Left superior temporal gyrus damage (Wernicke's area) impairs comprehension and yields fluent nonsensical speech.
angular gyrus
The angular gyrus is involved in reading and writing.
right occipital lobe
The right occipital lobe processes vision.
left inferior frontal gyrus
Correct: Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus mediates speech production, so damage yields effortful, telegraphic speech with preserved comprehension.
questions.x: Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus mediates speech production, so damage yields effortful, telegraphic speech with preserved comprehension. Trap: Confusing Broca's and Wernicke's aphasia.

questions.q: A cyclist rides faster when others watch, and a novice typist makes more errors when watched. Both findings are explained by:
o: social loafing
Social loafing is reduced individual effort in a group, not an audience effect on performance.
social facilitation, in which an audience enhances dominant responses
Correct: An audience raises arousal, which enhances well-learned (dominant) responses like the cyclist's and impairs difficult, novel ones like the novice typist's; this is social facilitation.
groupthink
Groupthink is flawed group consensus that suppresses dissent.
deindividuation
Deindividuation is loss of self-awareness and restraint in anonymous crowds.
questions.x: An audience raises arousal, which enhances well-learned (dominant) responses like the cyclist's and impairs difficult, novel ones like the novice typist's; this is social facilitation. Trap: Assuming an audience always helps performance.

questions.q: Members of a tug-of-war team pull less hard than they do individually when their individual contributions are not identifiable. This is:
o: social facilitation
Social facilitation is an effect of an audience on individual task performance, not reduced effort in pooled work.
group polarization
Group polarization is the strengthening of a group's initial leaning after discussion.
social loafing
Correct: Social loafing is reduced individual effort in a group when contributions are pooled and not individually identifiable.
the bystander effect
The bystander effect is reduced helping in emergencies as the number of witnesses increases.
questions.x: Social loafing is reduced individual effort in a group when contributions are pooled and not individually identifiable. Trap: Confusing loafing with diffusion of responsibility in emergencies.

questions.q: Anonymous members of a masked crowd engage in vandalism they would never commit alone. This best illustrates:
o: informational influence
Informational influence is conforming because others supply accurate information.
cognitive dissonance
Cognitive dissonance is discomfort from inconsistent attitudes and behavior.
self-monitoring
Self-monitoring is adjusting one's behavior to social cues, which does not describe loss of identity.
deindividuation
Correct: Anonymity in a group, like a mask in a crowd, reduces self-awareness and restraint, which is deindividuation.
questions.x: Anonymity in a group, like a mask in a crowd, reduces self-awareness and restraint, which is deindividuation. Trap: Attributing behavior to personality only.

questions.q: A cohesive committee, isolated from outside views and led by a directive chair, suppresses dissent and approves a flawed plan. This is:
o: groupthink
Correct: Groupthink is a drive for consensus, fostered by cohesion, isolation, and a directive leader, that overrides realistic appraisal and suppresses dissent.
group polarization
Group polarization strengthens the group's existing leaning after discussion, without suppressed dissent.
social facilitation
Social facilitation concerns audience effects on performance.
minority influence
Minority influence is a dissenting minority changing the majority, the opposite of suppressed dissent.
questions.x: Groupthink is a drive for consensus, fostered by cohesion, isolation, and a directive leader, that overrides realistic appraisal and suppresses dissent. Trap: Confusing groupthink with polarization.

questions.q: A group of moderately cautious investors becomes much more cautious after discussion. This is:
o: groupthink
Groupthink involves suppressed dissent and flawed decisions, not a shift in initial leaning.
group polarization
Correct: Group polarization is the intensification of the group's initial average leaning after discussion, so moderately cautious members become much more cautious.
conformity to an external norm
Conformity to an external norm involves adopting an outside standard, not intensifying the group's own leaning.
social loafing
Social loafing is reduced effort in groups and does not shift attitudes.
questions.x: Group polarization is the intensification of the group's initial average leaning after discussion, so moderately cautious members become much more cautious. Trap: Assuming groups always move to moderate positions.

questions.q: In Asch's line-judgment studies, participants often gave obviously wrong answers after confederates did. Conformity decreased most when:
o: responses were given publicly
Public responses increase conformity compared with private ones.
the task was made ambiguous
Ambiguity increases reliance on others (informational influence), raising conformity.
one confederate gave the correct answer, breaking unanimity
Correct: In Asch's studies a single confederate giving the correct answer breaks unanimity and greatly reduces conformity.
the confederates were unanimous
A unanimous majority produces the maximum conformity.
questions.x: In Asch's studies a single confederate giving the correct answer breaks unanimity and greatly reduces conformity. Trap: Thinking group size alone is decisive.

questions.q: A tourist copies the behavior of locals in an unfamiliar restaurant because she assumes they know the proper procedure. This is:
o: normative social influence
Normative influence is conforming to gain acceptance or avoid rejection, not to learn the procedure.
compliance via door-in-the-face
Door-in-the-face is a compliance tactic of a large request followed by a smaller one.
reactance
Reactance is resisting perceived pressure to restore freedom, the opposite of copying.
informational social influence
Correct: Following locals because they likely know the correct procedure is informational social influence, conforming to gain accurate information.
questions.x: Following locals because they likely know the correct procedure is informational social influence, conforming to gain accurate information. Trap: Calling all conformity normative.

questions.q: In Milgram's studies, obedience to deliver shocks was lowest when:
o: the experimenter gave orders by phone and was absent
Correct: Milgram found obedience dropped when the authority was physically absent and gave orders by phone, since reduced proximity weakens his influence.
the experimenter was in the same room in a lab coat
An experimenter in the same room in a lab coat is high proximity and authority, which maximizes obedience.
the study took place at a prestigious university
Institutional prestige increased obedience; it fell when the study moved to a rundown office.
the learner was out of sight in another room
A learner out of sight reduces empathy and thus increases obedience.
questions.x: Milgram found obedience dropped when the authority was physically absent and gave orders by phone, since reduced proximity weakens his influence. Trap: Assuming obedience is constant across settings.

questions.q: The Stanford prison experiment is most often cited as evidence for:
o: genetic determinants of aggression
Genetic determinants of aggression were not manipulated or tested in the design.
the power of social roles and situations
Correct: Participants adopted assigned guard and prisoner roles, illustrating the power of social roles and situations on behavior.
classical conditioning of fear
Classical conditioning of fear involves pairing stimuli, which was not the study's method.
cognitive dissonance
Cognitive dissonance concerns attitude-behavior inconsistency, not the role-assignment design.
questions.x: Participants adopted assigned guard and prisoner roles, illustrating the power of social roles and situations on behavior. Trap: Citing it as proof of innate sadism.

questions.q: A person collapses in a crowded station and no one helps. This is best explained by:
o: social facilitation
Social facilitation concerns audience effects on task performance, not helping.
the foot-in-the-door effect
Foot-in-the-door is a compliance tactic starting with a small request.
diffusion of responsibility
Correct: With many bystanders, each person feels less personal responsibility to act, which is diffusion of responsibility.
the cognitive miser effect
The cognitive miser effect is relying on mental shortcuts, which does not explain reduced helping.
questions.x: With many bystanders, each person feels less personal responsibility to act, which is diffusion of responsibility. Trap: Assuming more witnesses guarantee help.

questions.q: Wearing pajamas to a wedding violates a folkway, whereas incest violates a more. Mores differ from folkways because mores:
o: are only informal and unenforced
Informal and unenforced describes folkways, not mores.
are written legal codes
Written legal codes are laws, which are formal norms and not the defining feature of mores.
apply only within small groups
Mores are society-wide, not limited to small groups.
carry strong moral significance and harsher sanctions
Correct: Mores are norms with strong moral significance, and violations draw serious sanctions, unlike casual folkways.
questions.x: Mores are norms with strong moral significance, and violations draw serious sanctions, unlike casual folkways. Trap: Treating all norms as equal in severity.

questions.q: A driver cuts in front of you and you think, 'What a jerk,' overlooking that he might be rushing to a hospital. This is:
o: fundamental attribution error
Correct: Fundamental attribution error overemphasizes dispositional causes ('jerk') and underestimates situational ones (rushing to a hospital) when judging others.
self-serving bias
Self-serving bias concerns explaining one's own successes and failures.
the halo effect
The halo effect generalizes one positive trait to other traits.
the just-world hypothesis
The just-world hypothesis assumes people get what they deserve.
questions.x: Fundamental attribution error overemphasizes dispositional causes ('jerk') and underestimates situational ones (rushing to a hospital) when judging others. Trap: Confusing FAE with self-serving bias.

questions.q: A student attributes her A to her intelligence but her failing grade to an unfair test. This is:
o: fundamental attribution error
Fundamental attribution error concerns judging others' behavior as dispositional.
self-serving bias
Correct: Self-serving bias credits successes to one's own dispositions and blames failures on external situations, as in the unfair test.
the just-world hypothesis
The just-world hypothesis assumes outcomes are deserved, not self-protective attributions.
the halo effect
The halo effect generalizes a positive impression across traits.
questions.x: Self-serving bias credits successes to one's own dispositions and blames failures on external situations, as in the unfair test. Trap: Treating it as fundamental attribution error, which applies to judgments of others rather than oneself.

questions.q: You explain your own lateness with traffic but explain a friend's lateness as laziness. This is the:
o: halo effect
The halo effect generalizes one positive trait to others.
confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is favoring information that supports existing beliefs.
actor-observer bias
Correct: Actor-observer bias is explaining one's own behavior situationally (traffic) but others' behavior dispositionally (laziness).
hindsight bias
Hindsight bias is believing after the fact that an outcome was predictable.
questions.x: Actor-observer bias is explaining one's own behavior situationally (traffic) but others' behavior dispositionally (laziness). Trap: Confusing it with self-serving bias.

questions.q: Believing that a crime victim must have done something to deserve it reflects:
o: the actor-observer bias
Actor-observer bias is an asymmetry between explaining one's own and others' behavior.
confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is favoring information that confirms existing beliefs.
social desirability
Social desirability is answering in ways that look favorable to others.
the just-world hypothesis
Correct: The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve, so a victim must have earned the outcome.
questions.x: The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve, so a victim must have earned the outcome. Trap: Reading it as simple prejudice.

questions.q: Women reminded of the stereotype that women are poor at math perform worse on a math test than those not reminded. This is:
o: stereotype threat
Correct: Stereotype threat is the performance impairment that arises when a negative stereotype about one's group is made salient.
a self-fulfilling prophecy by teachers
A teacher's self-fulfilling prophecy involves another person's expectations altering outcomes, not reminders of a group stereotype.
ingroup favoritism
Ingroup favoritism is preferential treatment of one's own group.
the halo effect
The halo effect generalizes one positive trait to other traits.
questions.x: Stereotype threat is the performance impairment that arises when a negative stereotype about one's group is made salient. Trap: Concluding that the group has lower ability.

questions.q: A teacher expects a student to excel, gives more attention and challenge, and the student improves. This is:
o: stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is impaired performance from anxiety about confirming a negative stereotype.
a self-fulfilling prophecy
Correct: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when expectations lead to behaviors, like more attention and challenge, that bring about the expected outcome.
fundamental attribution error
Fundamental attribution error is overweighting dispositions in judging others.
social loafing
Social loafing is reduced effort in groups.
questions.x: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when expectations lead to behaviors, like more attention and challenge, that bring about the expected outcome. Trap: Thinking the prediction was accurate from the start.

questions.q: Refusing to hire an applicant because of ethnicity is an example of:
o: prejudice, which is a behavior
Prejudice is an attitude, not a behavior.
a stereotype, which is an attitude
A stereotype is a cognitive belief about a group, not an attitude.
discrimination, which is a behavior
Correct: Discrimination is negative behavior toward a group's members, such as refusing to hire based on ethnicity; prejudice is attitude and stereotype is belief.
ethnocentrism, which is a legal norm
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own standards, not a legal norm.
questions.x: Discrimination is negative behavior toward a group's members, such as refusing to hire based on ethnicity; prejudice is attitude and stereotype is belief. Trap: Using prejudice and discrimination interchangeably.

questions.q: Evaluating other cultures' food customs as inferior to one's own is:
o: cultural relativism
Cultural relativism evaluates cultures on their own terms.
assimilation
Assimilation is a minority group adopting the dominant culture.
multiculturalism
Multiculturalism supports preserving and valuing multiple cultures.
ethnocentrism
Correct: Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by one's own standards, here seeing other food customs as inferior.
questions.x: Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by one's own standards, here seeing other food customs as inferior. Trap: Reversing ethnocentrism with relativism.

questions.q: In the Robbers Cave study, hostility between boys' groups decreased after:
o: they worked together on superordinate goals
Correct: Shared superordinate goals that required cooperation reduced intergroup hostility in the Robbers Cave study.
they competed in more contests
More competition escalated the hostility in the study.
they were kept separate
Keeping groups separate leaves stereotypes unchallenged and does not build cooperation.
they were told about stereotypes
Information about stereotypes alone does not create shared goals or reduce conflict.
questions.x: Shared superordinate goals that required cooperation reduced intergroup hostility in the Robbers Cave study. Trap: Believing contact alone is sufficient.

questions.q: Individuals boost self-esteem by viewing their own group more favorably than other groups. This reflects:
o: the contact hypothesis
The contact hypothesis addresses conditions under which intergroup contact reduces prejudice.
social identity theory with ingroup bias
Correct: Social identity theory holds that group membership contributes to self-concept, so people boost self-esteem through ingroup bias, favoring their own group.
the Barnum effect
The Barnum effect is accepting vague, general personality descriptions as personally accurate.
self-perception theory
Self-perception theory says people infer their attitudes from observing their own behavior.
questions.x: Social identity theory holds that group membership contributes to self-concept, so people boost self-esteem through ingroup bias, favoring their own group. Trap: Overlooking that group membership feeds self-esteem.

questions.q: According to Cooley, a person develops a self-concept by:
o: internalizing instinctual drives
Internalizing instinctual drives is Freud's id-based framework, not Cooley's.
comparing to an ideal self only
Comparing to an ideal self only is Rogers's or Higgins's self-discrepancy idea, not social-mirror judgment.
imagining how others perceive and judge them
Correct: Cooley's looking-glass self holds that the self-concept arises from imagining how others perceive and judge us.
observing physiological arousal
Observing one's own physiological arousal relates to emotion theories such as James-Lange or Schachter-Singer.
questions.x: Cooley's looking-glass self holds that the self-concept arises from imagining how others perceive and judge us. Trap: Mixing Cooley's imagined social judgment with Mead's stage-based role-taking theory.

questions.q: In Mead's theory, children learn to take the role of the generalized other during which stage?
o: Preparatory stage
