questions.x: Each person interprets others' inaction as evidence that no emergency exists. Trap: Treating inaction as callousness rather than as people using others' behavior to interpret an ambiguous event.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that high school football games strengthen shared identity and cohesion in a town. Which perspective is she using?
o: Structural functionalism
Correct: Functionalism explains social practices by their contribution to societal stability and solidarity, and shared identity at the town level is exactly that.
Conflict theory
Conflict theory describes power struggles between groups, not cohesion.
Symbolic interactionism
Symbolic interactionism studies meanings negotiated in face-to-face interaction.
Rational choice theory
Rational choice theory explains behavior as individual cost-benefit calculation.
questions.x: Functionalism explains social practices by their contribution to societal stability and solidarity, and shared identity at the town level is exactly that. Trap: Confusing any positive social effect with micro-level meaning-making; cohesion at the societal level signals functionalism.

questions.q: A researcher claims that school funding based on local property taxes perpetuates advantages for wealthy families. This claim most directly reflects which perspective?
o: Functionalism
Functionalism stresses how institutions contribute to stability, not who benefits.
Symbolic interactionism
Symbolic interactionism studies everyday symbols and meanings.
Conflict theory
Correct: Conflict theory emphasizes how institutions such as property-tax school funding preserve inequality and benefit dominant groups.
Dramaturgical analysis
Dramaturgical analysis studies impression management in social performances.
questions.x: Conflict theory emphasizes how institutions such as property-tax school funding preserve inequality and benefit dominant groups. Trap: Choosing functionalism because schools serve a social function, overlooking the focus on who benefits and power.

questions.q: Two students interpret the same handshake differently: one as respect, the other as a challenge. Which theory best emphasizes this variability?
o: Structural functionalism
Structural functionalism is macro-level and looks at how structures sustain society.
Symbolic interactionism
Correct: Symbolic interactionism holds that social reality arises from shared and negotiated meanings of symbols, so one handshake can carry different meanings.
Conflict theory
Conflict theory is macro-level and focuses on power and inequality.
Demographic transition theory
Demographic transition theory describes birth and death rate shifts, not interaction.
questions.x: Symbolic interactionism holds that social reality arises from shared and negotiated meanings of symbols, so one handshake can carry different meanings. Trap: Treating the example as macro-level conflict; the focus on subjective interpretation is the interactionist hallmark.

questions.q: A university's stated purpose for dorm life is to give students housing. An unintended result is that students form lasting friendships and find future spouses. The friendships are best described as a:
o: Manifest function
Manifest function describes intended, recognized effects, like providing housing.
Latent dysfunction
Latent dysfunction would be an unintended harmful consequence, but friendship is beneficial.
Manifest dysfunction
Manifest dysfunction would be an intended or recognized harmful effect, which does not fit.
Latent function
Correct: Latent functions are unintended, unrecognized beneficial consequences, and lasting friendships were not the stated purpose of dorms.
questions.x: Latent functions are unintended, unrecognized beneficial consequences, and lasting friendships were not the stated purpose of dorms. Trap: Calling any beneficial outcome manifest; the key is whether it was intended and recognized.

questions.q: A waiter is polite and formal in the dining room but jokes crudely with coworkers in the kitchen. In Goffman's dramaturgical approach, the kitchen is the:
o: Front stage
Front stage is where the performance occurs before an audience, i.e. the dining room.
Role set
Role set is the array of roles attached to a single status, not a place.
Reference group
Reference group is a standard of comparison for evaluating oneself.
Backstage
Correct: Backstage is where people drop the performance and relax outside the audience's view, as the waiter does in the kitchen.
questions.x: Backstage is where people drop the performance and relax outside the audience's view, as the waiter does in the kitchen. Trap: Thinking the 'real' self appears on front stage; Goffman places relaxed behavior backstage.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects social constructionism?
o: Social categories reflect fixed biological facts that societies merely discover.
This describes biological determinism, treating categories as fixed facts.
Categories such as 'adolescence' gain meaning through shared social agreement and vary across societies.
Correct: Social constructionism holds that categories like adolescence get meaning through collective definitions and vary across societies and eras.
Social order depends mainly on each person's calculation of personal benefit.
This describes rational choice theory, where order stems from individual benefit calculation.
Social change occurs only through class struggle over resources.
This describes a strict conflict-theory view that change comes only from class struggle.
questions.x: Social constructionism holds that categories like adolescence get meaning through collective definitions and vary across societies and eras. Trap: Equating 'constructed' with 'fake'; constructionism says meanings are socially produced, not that they lack real consequences.

questions.q: A neighbor helps a friend move expecting that the friend will help him later. This best illustrates which theory?
o: Exchange theory
Correct: Exchange theory views interaction as the trading of rewards and costs with an expectation of reciprocity, as in helping now for help later.
Labeling theory
Labeling theory addresses how societal tags shape deviance.
Strain theory
Strain theory explains deviance as a gap between goals and legitimate means.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism concerns evaluating cultures on their own terms.
questions.x: Exchange theory views interaction as the trading of rewards and costs with an expectation of reciprocity, as in helping now for help later. Trap: Ascribing altruism; the expectation of return is what marks social exchange.

questions.q: A sociologist studies how household labor expectations disadvantage women in both domestic and paid work. This most closely matches:
o: Functionalism
Functionalism stresses how institutions maintain stability, not gender-based disadvantage.
Social exchange theory
Social exchange theory focuses on individual rewards and costs in interaction.
Feminist theory
Correct: Feminist theory analyzes gender inequality and patriarchal structures across domestic and paid-work institutions.
Ecological theory
Ecological theory concerns spatial patterns of urban populations.
questions.x: Feminist theory analyzes gender inequality and patriarchal structures across domestic and paid-work institutions. Trap: Selecting functionalism because division of labor sounds functional; the focus on gender-based power is feminist.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a secondary group?
o: Coworkers in a large corporation who interact only for tasks
Correct: Secondary groups are large, impersonal, goal-oriented, and often temporary, as coworkers who interact only for tasks are.
A married couple
A married couple is a primary group with intimate, enduring ties.
Close childhood friends
Close childhood friends form a primary group based on emotional bonds.
A multigenerational family
A multigenerational family is the classic primary group.
questions.x: Secondary groups are large, impersonal, goal-oriented, and often temporary, as coworkers who interact only for tasks are. Trap: Assuming any group you see daily is primary; intimacy and emotional bond define primary groups.

questions.q: Tönnies described a society dominated by impersonal, contractual relationships and individual self-interest as:
o: Gemeinschaft
Gemeinschaft is the close, tradition-based community, the opposite type.
Mechanical solidarity
Mechanical solidarity is Durkheim's cohesion from similarity, not Tönnies's term.
Gesellschaft
Correct: Gesellschaft is Tönnies's modern, urban society built on impersonal, contractual ties and self-interest.
Anomie
Anomie is Durkheim's normlessness, not a type of community.
questions.x: Gesellschaft is Tönnies's modern, urban society built on impersonal, contractual ties and self-interest. Trap: Mixing up the German terms; Gemeinschaft means community and Gesellschaft means society.

questions.q: In a small agrarian society, social cohesion arises because members do similar work and share strong beliefs. Durkheim called this:
o: Organic solidarity
Organic solidarity arises from interdependence through specialization in complex societies.
Mechanical solidarity
Correct: Mechanical solidarity is Durkheim's cohesion arising from similar work and shared beliefs in simple societies.
Anomie
Anomie is a state of normlessness, not a source of cohesion.
Bureaucratic rationalization
Bureaucratic rationalization is Weber's idea about formal, efficient organization.
questions.x: Mechanical solidarity is Durkheim's cohesion arising from similar work and shared beliefs in simple societies. Trap: Reversing the terms; 'organic' is associated with specialization and interdependence, not similarity.

questions.q: Durkheim's concept of anomie refers to:
o: Pressure to achieve goals through illegitimate means
This describes Merton's strain: pressure to reach goals by illegitimate means.
Isolation of the individual from a small community
This describes social isolation, not the loss of norms.
The belief that one's culture is superior
This describes ethnocentrism.
A breakdown of social norms leading to a sense of normlessness
Correct: Anomie is a breakdown or weakening of social norms producing normlessness, often during rapid social change.
questions.x: Anomie is a breakdown or weakening of social norms producing normlessness, often during rapid social change. Trap: Merging Durkheim's anomie with Merton's strain theory, which builds on it but is distinct.

questions.q: An individual accepts culturally approved success goals but, lacking legitimate means, turns to selling drugs. In Merton's typology this is:
o: Conformity
Conformity accepts both goals and legitimate means.
Ritualism
Ritualism abandons the goals but keeps following the means.
Retreatism
Retreatism rejects both goals and means.
Innovation
Correct: Innovation in Merton's typology accepts cultural goals while using unapproved means, as selling drugs for success does.
questions.x: Innovation in Merton's typology accepts cultural goals while using unapproved means, as selling drugs for success does. Trap: Choosing retreatism because drug-related; the classification depends on goals and means, not the behavior's content.

questions.q: A teenager begins shoplifting after repeatedly interacting with peers who value and teach theft. Which theory best explains this?
o: Labeling theory
Labeling theory focuses on society's tagging reaction, not peer learning.
Differential association
Correct: Differential association holds deviance is learned through intimate interaction with peers who favor and teach it.
Strain theory
Strain theory focuses on blocked legitimate means to goals.
Broken windows theory
Broken windows theory links visible disorder to further crime.
questions.x: Differential association holds deviance is learned through intimate interaction with peers who favor and teach it. Trap: Picking labeling theory; here the mechanism is learning from peers, not being tagged.

questions.q: A student labeled a 'troublemaker' by teachers begins to act accordingly. This process best reflects:
o: Secondary deviance
Correct: Secondary deviance occurs when a person internalizes a deviant identity after being labeled and then acts accordingly.
Primary deviance
Primary deviance is the initial act with little effect on self-identity.
Social facilitation
Social facilitation is improved performance in the presence of others.
Anomie
Anomie is normlessness in society, not an individual response to a label.
questions.x: Secondary deviance occurs when a person internalizes a deviant identity after being labeled and then acts accordingly. Trap: Reversing primary and secondary; secondary deviance follows from internalizing the label.

questions.q: Which pair correctly ranks norms from least to most strictly enforced?
o: Mores, folkways, taboos
This puts mores before folkways and taboos last in the wrong sequence, starting with a stricter norm.
Taboos, mores, folkways
This is the exact reverse order, from most to least strict.
Folkways, mores, taboos
Correct: Folkways are casual conventions, mores carry moral weight, and taboos are the most strongly prohibited acts, so the order is folkways, mores, taboos.
Folkways, taboos, mores
This places taboos between folkways and mores, though taboos are stricter than mores.
questions.x: Folkways are casual conventions, mores carry moral weight, and taboos are the most strongly prohibited acts, so the order is folkways, mores, taboos. Trap: Thinking mores and taboos are equivalent; taboos are the most extreme.

questions.q: A person is fined for littering, while another is snubbed for chewing loudly. These are respectively:
o: Formal and informal sanctions
Correct: A fine is a formal sanction imposed by an institution, while a snub is an informal sanction from peers.
Informal and formal sanctions
This reverses the labels, calling the fine informal and the snub formal.
Both formal sanctions
The snub is a peer reaction and is not formally administered.
Both informal sanctions
The fine is applied by legal authority and is not informal.
questions.x: A fine is a formal sanction imposed by an institution, while a snub is an informal sanction from peers. Trap: Assuming social disapproval cannot be informal; informal sanctions are just as real.

questions.q: A visitor judges a foreign marriage custom as inferior, by comparing it to his own country's norms. This is:
o: Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism evaluates a practice within its own context, the opposite stance.
Cultural diffusion
Cultural diffusion is the spread of cultural elements between societies.
Ethnocentrism
Correct: Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by the standards of one's own culture, as the visitor does.
Assimilation
Assimilation is adoption of the dominant culture by a minority group.
questions.x: Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by the standards of one's own culture, as the visitor does. Trap: Calling it relativism; relativism withholds judgment based on outside standards.

questions.q: Which is an example of nonmaterial culture?
o: A smartphone
A smartphone is a physical artifact of material culture.
A society's shared beliefs about justice
Correct: Nonmaterial culture comprises ideas, beliefs, values, and norms, such as shared beliefs about justice.
A temple building
A temple building is a physical structure, even if it embodies beliefs.
A traditional garment
A traditional garment is a physical object.
questions.x: Nonmaterial culture comprises ideas, beliefs, values, and norms, such as shared beliefs about justice. Trap: Counting a building as nonmaterial because it embodies a belief; the object itself is material.

questions.q: A group deliberately rejects mainstream values and organizes a lifestyle opposed to them. This group is a:
o: Subculture
A subculture differs from the mainstream but is not defined by opposition.
Reference group
A reference group is a standard of comparison, not defined by rejecting mainstream values.
Primary group
A primary group is defined by intimate, enduring ties, not opposition.
Counterculture
Correct: A counterculture actively opposes dominant cultural norms, while a subculture merely differs and coexists with them.
questions.x: A counterculture actively opposes dominant cultural norms, while a subculture merely differs and coexists with them. Trap: Confusing subculture, which is distinct but not oppositional, with counterculture.

questions.q: A family immigrates and, over generations, gradually abandons its native language and customs in favor of the host society's. This is:
o: Multiculturalism
Multiculturalism preserves multiple distinct cultures side by side.
Segregation
Segregation is the physical or social separation of groups, not cultural absorption.
Cultural lag
Cultural lag is nonmaterial culture adapting slowly to material change.
Assimilation
Correct: Assimilation is gradual absorption into the dominant culture with loss of distinct cultural traits, as with abandoning native language and customs.
questions.x: Assimilation is gradual absorption into the dominant culture with loss of distinct cultural traits, as with abandoning native language and customs. Trap: Treating multiculturalism as the same; there the original culture is preserved.

questions.q: New reproductive technology emerges, but laws and ethical norms about it take years to develop. This reflects:
o: Cultural diffusion
Cultural diffusion is the spread of cultural traits between societies.
Cultural lag
Correct: Cultural lag occurs when nonmaterial culture such as law and ethics adapts more slowly than material culture such as technology.
Anomie
Anomie is normlessness from weakened norms, not a delay between technology and norms.
Cultural capital
Cultural capital is non-financial knowledge and tastes that confer advantage.
questions.x: Cultural lag occurs when nonmaterial culture such as law and ethics adapts more slowly than material culture such as technology. Trap: Choosing anomie; the delay in adapting norms to technology defines lag.

questions.q: A sociologist notes that schools teach punctuality and obedience that prepare students for work discipline. This is best described as the:
o: Hidden curriculum
Correct: The hidden curriculum is the unwritten lessons and values, such as punctuality and obedience, transmitted through schooling.
Manifest curriculum
Manifest curriculum is the formal, stated academic content.
Credentialism
Credentialism is reliance on diplomas as qualifications for jobs.
Tracking
Tracking is sorting students into different academic paths by ability.
questions.x: The hidden curriculum is the unwritten lessons and values, such as punctuality and obedience, transmitted through schooling. Trap: Calling it manifest; these lessons are not formally stated.

questions.q: Sociologists describe the family as the primary agent of:
o: Resocialization
Resocialization replaces old norms and values with new ones, as in institutions.
Anticipatory socialization
Anticipatory socialization prepares a person for a future role.
Primary socialization
Correct: Primary socialization is the early foundational learning of norms and language that the family provides in childhood.
Secondary socialization
Secondary socialization occurs later in settings such as school and work.
questions.x: Primary socialization is the early foundational learning of norms and language that the family provides in childhood. Trap: Choosing secondary because school teaches norms; family comes first.

questions.q: Durkheim argued that religion strengthens society mainly by:
o: Reinforcing shared values and collective identity
Correct: Durkheim saw religion as a source of social cohesion through shared rituals that reinforce collective values and identity.
Providing a rational calculation of salvation
Salvation calculation reflects rational choice thinking, not Durkheim's view.
Legitimizing the dominance of capitalists
Legitimizing capitalist dominance is Marx's critique of religion as the opiate of the masses.
Producing anomie
Durkheim saw religion as reducing normlessness, not producing anomie.
questions.x: Durkheim saw religion as a source of social cohesion through shared rituals that reinforce collective values and identity. Trap: Attributing Marx's critique to Durkheim.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that elite groups use education credentials to preserve their advantages across generations. This best reflects which perspective?
o: Structural functionalism
functionalism stresses institutions' contributions to stability.
Conflict theory
Correct: Conflict theory emphasizes how dominant groups use institutions to maintain power and inequality.
Symbolic interactionism
symbolic interactionism focuses on meanings in everyday interaction.
Rational choice theory
rational choice theory models individual cost-benefit decisions.
questions.x: Conflict theory emphasizes how dominant groups use institutions to maintain power and inequality. Trap: Choosing functionalism because education is an institution; the focus here is on power and reproduced advantage.

questions.q: Michels's 'iron law of oligarchy' states that:
o: Every society goes through stages of population growth
Stages of population growth belong to demographic transition theory.
Large organizations inevitably become dominated by a small elite
Correct: Michels argued that organizational complexity concentrates power in a few leaders, so large organizations inevitably become oligarchies.
Bureaucracies decline when their leaders are charismatic
Michels did not link bureaucratic decline to charismatic leaders; that blends Weber's ideas.
Social mobility rises with organizational size
Michels claimed power concentrates with size, not that mobility rises.
questions.x: Michels argued that organizational complexity concentrates power in a few leaders, so large organizations inevitably become oligarchies. Trap: Associating oligarchy only with governments rather than any large organization.

questions.q: Ritzer's concept of McDonaldization emphasizes which feature of modern society?
o: Spontaneity and emotional expression
Spontaneity and emotional expression contradict the standardization it describes.
Resistance to technological change
Resistance to technology is opposite to the technological control emphasized.
Decline of formal organizations
Rationalization expands formal organizations rather than declining.
Efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control
Correct: McDonaldization extends Weberian rationalization, with efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control, across social institutions.
questions.x: McDonaldization extends Weberian rationalization, with efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control, across social institutions. Trap: Reading it as only about fast food rather than the wider rationalization of society.

questions.q: A job seeker gets an interview through a casual acquaintance. This shows the value of:
o: Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism concerns judging cultures in their own context.
Strain theory
Strain theory explains deviance from goal-means gaps.
Anticipatory socialization
Anticipatory socialization is preparing for a future role, not using network contacts.
Weak ties and social capital
Correct: Granovetter showed that weak ties bridge different networks and supply job information, a form of social capital.
questions.x: Granovetter showed that weak ties bridge different networks and supply job information, a form of social capital. Trap: Believing close friends are always the most useful for jobs; weak ties bridge networks.

questions.q: A physician feels pulled between her roles as a doctor and as a parent. This is:
o: Role strain
Role strain is tension within a single status.
Role conflict
Correct: Role conflict arises from incompatible demands of two or more different statuses, here doctor and parent.
Role exit
Role exit is the process of leaving a role.
Role set
Role set is the array of roles attached to one status, not a tension.
questions.x: Role conflict arises from incompatible demands of two or more different statuses, here doctor and parent. Trap: Choosing role strain; strain is within a single role.

questions.q: Becoming a college professor after years of study is an example of:
o: Achieved status
Correct: Achieved statuses are earned through effort or choice, as becoming a professor after years of study is.
Ascribed status
Ascribed statuses are assigned at birth or involuntarily.
Master status
Master status is a status that dominates a person's identity, not about being earned.
Role exit
Role exit is leaving a role.
questions.x: Achieved statuses are earned through effort or choice, as becoming a professor after years of study is. Trap: Thinking prestigious statuses are always master statuses.

questions.q: A man's identity is overwhelmingly defined by others as 'ex-convict' in every social setting. This is a:
o: Ascribed status
Ascribed status is assigned at birth and the label here is not defined by that.
Role set
Role set is the roles attached to a single status.
Master status
Correct: A master status overrides other statuses and shapes how a person is perceived in every setting, like 'ex-convict'.
Reference group
Reference group is a standard for self-comparison.
questions.x: A master status overrides other statuses and shapes how a person is perceived in every setting, like 'ex-convict'. Trap: Equating master status with ascribed status; it can be achieved.

questions.q: If people define situations as real, they are real in their consequences. This is the:
o: Thomas theorem
Correct: The Thomas theorem states that situations defined as real are real in their consequences, highlighting subjective definitions in interactionism.
Looking-glass self
Looking-glass self concerns forming self-image from others' perceived reactions.
Self-fulfilling attribution
Self-fulfilling attribution is not the named theorem for this statement.
Iron law
The iron law refers to Michels's oligarchy claim.
questions.x: The Thomas theorem states that situations defined as real are real in their consequences, highlighting subjective definitions in interactionism. Trap: Mistaking it for the looking-glass self, which is about identity.

questions.q: A new associate compares her salary to that of colleagues at a rival firm in order to judge her own success. The rival colleagues are her:
o: In-group
An in-group is one to which a person belongs, and she is not a rival-firm member.
Primary group
A primary group is defined by intimate, enduring ties, which colleagues at a rival firm lack.
Reference group
Correct: A reference group is a standard for evaluating oneself, and membership is not required.
Peer group
A peer group consists of similar-status members one interacts with, which does not fit.
questions.x: A reference group is a standard for evaluating oneself, and membership is not required. Trap: Assuming one must belong to one's reference group.

questions.q: Fans of one team strongly favor their own members and dislike rival fans. This demonstrates:
o: Anomie
Anomie is normlessness, not group boundaries.
In-group/out-group distinction
Correct: In-groups generate loyalty among members while out-groups are viewed with antagonism, as with rival fans.
Gemeinschaft
Gemeinschaft is a close, tradition-based community type.
Cultural capital
Cultural capital is non-financial knowledge conferring advantage.
questions.x: In-groups generate loyalty among members while out-groups are viewed with antagonism, as with rival fans. Trap: Thinking this requires direct conflict; boundaries alone can produce bias.

questions.q: A child who learns to appreciate classical music and sophisticated language at home gains advantages at school. Bourdieu called these assets:
o: Social capital
Social capital is resources from networks and relationships.
Human capital
Human capital is skills and training valued in the labor market.
Material culture
Material culture is physical artifacts, not tastes and knowledge.
Cultural capital
Correct: Cultural capital is non-financial knowledge, tastes, and language that confer advantage in school and society.
questions.x: Cultural capital is non-financial knowledge, tastes, and language that confer advantage in school and society. Trap: Confusing cultural capital with social capital.

questions.q: A committee suppresses doubts and agrees quickly to preserve harmony, resulting in a poor decision. This is:
o: Social loafing
Social loafing is reduced individual effort in groups.
Deindividuation
Deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in groups or crowds.
Role strain
Role strain is tension within a single role.
Groupthink
Correct: Groupthink is faulty decision-making caused by pressure for conformity and harmony in cohesive groups.
questions.x: Groupthink is faulty decision-making caused by pressure for conformity and harmony in cohesive groups. Trap: Calling it social loafing, which concerns effort rather than decision quality.

questions.q: Parsons's 'sick role' states that an ill person is:
o: Permanently exempt from obligations
Permanent exemption is not part of the sick role, which is temporary.
Temporarily exempt from normal duties but expected to seek treatment
Correct: Parsons's sick role grants temporary exemption from normal duties but obliges the person to seek treatment and get well.
Responsible for causing the illness
The sick role holds that the ill person is not blamed for the illness.
Expected to avoid medical help
The sick role obliges the person to seek competent help, not avoid it.
questions.x: Parsons's sick role grants temporary exemption from normal duties but obliges the person to seek treatment and get well. Trap: Assuming the sick role excuses someone from seeking help.

questions.q: A conflict theorist would most likely interpret the criminal justice system as:
o: Reflecting and reinforcing the interests of powerful groups
Correct: Conflict theory sees laws and institutions like criminal justice as tools reflecting and reinforcing the interests of dominant groups.
Maintaining equilibrium through shared values
Maintaining equilibrium through shared values is the functionalist view.
Producing meaning through symbols alone
Producing meaning through symbols is the interactionist view.
Operating by individual cost-benefit analyses only
Individual cost-benefit analysis is the rational choice view.
questions.x: Conflict theory sees laws and institutions like criminal justice as tools reflecting and reinforcing the interests of dominant groups. Trap: Selecting functionalism because law serves order.

questions.q: Which concept describes the shift of a society from tradition toward the use of efficiency-focused rules and calculation?
o: Anomie
Anomie is normlessness, not a shift toward formal rules.
Differentiation
Differentiation is the increasing specialization of institutions.
Rationalization
Correct: Weber's rationalization is the replacement of tradition with efficiency, calculation, and formal rules.
Resocialization
Resocialization is replacing an individual's old norms with new ones.
questions.x: Weber's rationalization is the replacement of tradition with efficiency, calculation, and formal rules. Trap: Linking it to Durkheim's anomie.

questions.q: The crude birth rate is defined as the number of:
o: Live births per 1,000 people per year
Correct: Crude birth rate is live births per 1,000 people in the total population per year, with total population as the denominator.
Births per 1,000 women of childbearing age
Births per 1,000 women of childbearing age is the general fertility rate.
Deaths per 1,000 live births
Deaths per 1,000 live births is the infant mortality rate.
Children per woman over her lifetime
Children per woman over her lifetime is the total fertility rate.
questions.x: Crude birth rate is live births per 1,000 people in the total population per year, with total population as the denominator. Trap: Confusing crude birth rate with the fertility rate, which uses women as the denominator.

questions.q: The total fertility rate describes:
o: The number of births per 1,000 people
Births per 1,000 people is the crude birth rate.
The proportion of women aged 15-49
The proportion of women aged 15-49 describes age structure, not fertility.
The average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime
Correct: Total fertility rate estimates the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime given current age-specific fertility rates.
The number of infants who die before age one
Infants dying before age one describes infant mortality.
questions.x: Total fertility rate estimates the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime given current age-specific fertility rates. Trap: Treating TFR as a count of births per population.

questions.q: In a low-mortality country, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 is described as:
o: Zero population growth immediately
Zero growth does not follow immediately because age-structure momentum keeps the population growing for decades.
Replacement-level fertility
Correct: A TFR of about 2.1 replaces two parents, with a small allowance for children who die before reproducing.
Demographic dividend
Demographic dividend is an economic boost from a large working-age share, not a fertility level.
Natural decrease
Natural decrease means deaths exceed births, which TFR 2.1 would not cause.
questions.x: A TFR of about 2.1 replaces two parents, with a small allowance for children who die before reproducing. Trap: Assuming TFR of exactly 2.0 is replacement.

questions.q: In Stage 1 of the demographic transition model, a population has:
o: High birth rates and falling death rates
High births with falling deaths describes Stage 2.
Falling birth rates and low death rates
Falling births with low deaths describes Stage 3.
Low birth and low death rates
Low birth and low death rates describe Stage 4.
High birth and high death rates with slow growth
Correct: Stage 1 is pre-industrial, with high birth and high death rates balancing out so growth is slow.
questions.x: Stage 1 is pre-industrial, with high birth and high death rates balancing out so growth is slow. Trap: Thinking Stage 1 has fast growth because birth rates are high.

questions.q: Rapid population growth in Stage 2 of the demographic transition occurs because:
o: Birth rates fall faster than death rates
Birth rates falling faster than deaths would slow growth, not speed it.
Immigration increases sharply
Immigration is not what defines Stage 2 growth, which is natural increase.
Fertility drops to below replacement
Below-replacement fertility belongs to later stages and would slow growth.
Death rates fall while birth rates remain high
Correct: Improved sanitation, food, and medicine lower death rates before birth rates decline, so births exceed deaths and growth is rapid.
questions.x: Improved sanitation, food, and medicine lower death rates before birth rates decline, so births exceed deaths and growth is rapid. Trap: Attributing growth to rising birth rates.

questions.q: A country with low birth rate, low death rate, and nearly stable population is in which stage?
o: Stage 1
Stage 1 has high birth and death rates.
Stage 4
Correct: Stage 4 has low birth and low death rates and a nearly stable population.
Stage 2
Stage 2 has falling death rates with high births and rapid growth.
Stage 3
Stage 3 has falling birth rates with continued growth, not yet stable.
questions.x: Stage 4 has low birth and low death rates and a nearly stable population. Trap: Mixing up stages 1 and 4, both with slow growth.

questions.q: A population pyramid with a very wide base and narrow top indicates:
o: A young population with high fertility
Correct: A wide base means many children relative to older adults, indicating a young population with high fertility.
An aging population
An aging population shows a wide top and narrower base.
A declining population with low fertility
A declining population with low fertility shows a narrow base.
A stable age distribution
A stable age distribution gives a more column-like shape, not a steep triangle.
questions.x: A wide base means many children relative to older adults, indicating a young population with high fertility. Trap: Reading the pyramid as indicating total population size rather than age structure.

questions.q: A country has a narrow base and a growing proportion of people over 65. Which is the most likely consequence?
o: Decreasing median age
Median age rises, not falls, as the proportion of older people grows.
Rapid natural increase
Rapid natural increase is unlikely given a narrow base reflecting low births.
Increasing old-age dependency ratio
Correct: An aging population has more elderly per working-age person, raising the old-age dependency ratio.
Greater proportion of children
A narrow base means fewer children, not a greater proportion.
questions.x: An aging population has more elderly per working-age person, raising the old-age dependency ratio. Trap: Assuming fewer children immediately means more output per person while ignoring the rising elderly dependency burden.

questions.q: The dependency ratio compares the number of:
o: Dependents (young and old) to working-age people
Correct: The dependency ratio is dependents under 15 and over 64 divided by working-age people 15-64.
Men to women
Men to women is the sex ratio.
Urban to rural residents
Urban to rural residents is an urbanization measure.
Immigrants to natives
Immigrants to natives describes migrant composition, not age dependency.
questions.x: The dependency ratio is dependents under 15 and over 64 divided by working-age people 15-64. Trap: Counting only the elderly as dependents.

questions.q: Life expectancy at birth is strongly influenced by:
o: Total migration only
Migration alone does not change deaths per birth cohort in a strong way.
The sex ratio at birth
Sex ratio at birth affects composition, not average survival.
Infant and child mortality
Correct: High infant and child mortality pulls down average life expectancy at birth because early deaths weigh heavily in the average.
Median age of marriage
Median age of marriage does not directly determine mortality.
questions.x: High infant and child mortality pulls down average life expectancy at birth because early deaths weigh heavily in the average. Trap: Assuming life expectancy refers to the age at which most people die.

questions.q: Morbidity refers to:
o: The rate of death in a population
Rate of death in a population is mortality.
The rate of disease in a population
Correct: Morbidity is the rate of disease or illness in a population, measured as incidence or prevalence.
The rate of births
Rate of births is fertility or birth rate.
The rate of migration
Rate of migration is movement between places, not disease.
questions.x: Morbidity is the rate of disease or illness in a population, measured as incidence or prevalence. Trap: Mixing up mortality and morbidity.

questions.q: Infant mortality rate is the number of:
o: Deaths under age five per 1,000 people
Deaths under five per 1,000 people uses the wrong age range and denominator.
Stillbirths per 1,000 women
Stillbirths per 1,000 women is not the infant mortality definition.
Deaths at birth per 100,000 people
Deaths at birth per 100,000 people uses the wrong denominator and scale.
Deaths of infants under one year per 1,000 live births
Correct: Infant mortality rate is deaths of infants under one year per 1,000 live births.
questions.x: Infant mortality rate is deaths of infants under one year per 1,000 live births. Trap: Using total population as the denominator.

questions.q: Natural increase equals:
o: Birth rate plus immigration
Birth rate plus immigration mixes births with migration.
Immigration minus emigration
Immigration minus emigration is net migration.
Death rate minus migration
Death rate minus migration mixes mortality with migration.
Birth rate minus death rate
Correct: Natural increase is births minus deaths (birth rate minus death rate), excluding migration.
questions.x: Natural increase is births minus deaths (birth rate minus death rate), excluding migration. Trap: Including migration in natural increase.

questions.q: A country records 500,000 immigrants and 350,000 emigrants in a year. Its net migration is:
o: -150,000 subtracts in the wrong order.
Correct: Net migration = immigrants minus emigrants = 500,000 - 350,000 = +150,000.
+850,000 adds the two flows.
+350,000 reports only the emigrant count.
questions.x: Net migration = immigrants minus emigrants = 500,000 - 350,000 = +150,000. Trap: Adding immigrants and emigrants.

questions.q: A farmer leaves a drought-stricken region for a city with factory jobs. The drought and the jobs are, respectively:
o: Push and pull factors
Correct: Push factors like drought drive people out of an origin, while pull factors like factory jobs attract them to a destination.
Pull and push factors
This reverses the roles, calling drought a pull and jobs a push.
Both push factors
Jobs attract the farmer, so they are not a push factor.
Both pull factors
Drought drives the farmer away, so it is not a pull factor.
questions.x: Push factors like drought drive people out of an origin, while pull factors like factory jobs attract them to a destination. Trap: Reversing push (drives people away) and pull (attracts them to a destination).

questions.q: A person leaving Country A to live permanently in Country B is described as an:
o: Immigrant to A and emigrant from B
This reverses the terms for both countries.
Immigrant in both
The person is not an immigrant to A because they are leaving it.
Emigrant from A and immigrant to B
Correct: Emigration is exiting a country and immigration is entering one, so the person emigrates from A and immigrates to B.
Emigrant from both
The person is not an emigrant from B because they are entering it.
questions.x: Emigration is exiting a country and immigration is entering one, so the person emigrates from A and immigrates to B. Trap: Viewing the term as describing a person, not perspective of the country.

questions.q: The loss of highly educated professionals from a country to wealthier countries is:
o: Brain drain
Correct: Brain drain is the emigration of highly educated, skilled workers to wealthier countries.
Demographic dividend
Demographic dividend is an economic boost from a large working-age share.
Gentrification
Gentrification is wealthier residents moving into a poor neighborhood.
Urban sprawl
Urban sprawl is uncontrolled outward spread of cities.
questions.x: Brain drain is the emigration of highly educated, skilled workers to wealthier countries. Trap: Calling it a demographic dividend.

questions.q: A refugee differs from a typical economic migrant in that a refugee:
o: Moves for better wages
Moving for better wages describes an economic migrant.
Moves within the same country
Moving within the same country describes an internally displaced person.
Flees due to a well-founded fear of persecution
Correct: A refugee crosses a border to flee a well-founded fear of persecution or violence, unlike economic migrants seeking opportunity.
Is not subject to border crossing
Refugees do cross borders, so avoiding border crossing is wrong.
questions.x: A refugee crosses a border to flee a well-founded fear of persecution or violence, unlike economic migrants seeking opportunity. Trap: Calling anyone who flees across a border a refugee.

questions.q: Malthus predicted that:
o: Food supply outpaces population
Food outpacing population contradicts his theory.
Population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically
Correct: Malthus predicted population grows geometrically while food supply grows only arithmetically, so population outstrips food unless checked.
Population remains stable
Malthus did not predict a stable population without checks.
Fertility always falls with industrialization
Fertility falling with industrialization is demographic transition thinking, not Malthus.
questions.x: Malthus predicted population grows geometrically while food supply grows only arithmetically, so population outstrips food unless checked. Trap: Reversing geometric and arithmetic growth.

questions.q: The increasing proportion of a population living in cities is called:
o: Suburbanization
Suburbanization is movement to suburbs.
Gentrification
Gentrification is wealthier residents moving into poorer neighborhoods.
Deindustrialization
Deindustrialization is the decline of manufacturing.
Urbanization
Correct: Urbanization is the increasing proportion of a population living in cities.
questions.x: Urbanization is the increasing proportion of a population living in cities. Trap: Mixing urbanization with gentrification.

questions.q: Higher-income residents move into a low-income neighborhood, renovate housing, and rents rise, displacing longtime residents. This is:
o: Urban decay
Urban decay is deterioration of an area, not renovation.
Suburbanization
Suburbanization is movement of population to suburbs.
White flight
White flight is movement of white residents out of racially diversifying urban areas.
Gentrification
Correct: Gentrification is an influx of affluent residents who renovate housing, raising rents and displacing lower-income residents.
questions.x: Gentrification is an influx of affluent residents who renovate housing, raising rents and displacing lower-income residents. Trap: Interpreting gentrification as neighborhood improvement without displacement.

questions.q: Post-World War II expansion of highways and mortgage programs encouraged:
o: Ruralization
Ruralization is a shift toward rural living, not the move to suburbs near cities.
Suburbanization
Correct: Postwar highway building and mortgage programs made car-based residential living outside city centers affordable, driving suburbanization.
Urban concentration only
Urban concentration only ignores the outflow from cities to suburbs.
Counter-urbanization only
Counter-urbanization only describes movement to rural areas and was not the main postwar pattern.
questions.x: Postwar highway building and mortgage programs made car-based residential living outside city centers affordable, driving suburbanization. Trap: Choosing urban concentration because cities were growing, while missing that policy pushed residents outward.

questions.q: A once-thriving district experiences property abandonment, declining tax base, and disinvestment. This is:
o: Urban decay
Correct: Urban decay is deterioration of urban areas through disinvestment, abandonment, and declining tax base.
Gentrification
Gentrification is the opposite: wealthier residents and reinvestment arrive.
Urban sprawl
Urban sprawl is outward expansion of development, not deterioration.
Rural flight
Rural flight is out-migration from the countryside to cities.
questions.x: Urban decay is deterioration of urban areas through disinvestment, abandonment, and declining tax base. Trap: Treating decay as caused by residents' behavior rather than disinvestment and structural economic forces.

questions.q: Relative deprivation theory says movements arise when:
o: Absolute poverty reaches its worst level
Absolute poverty is not required; relative comparison drives the theory.
Elites create organizations
Elites creating organizations is the resource mobilization emphasis.
People feel worse off than expected compared with a reference standard
Correct: Relative deprivation theory holds that perceived gaps between expectations and reality, judged against a reference standard, motivate collective action.
Resources are plentiful
Plentiful resources do not generate the felt deprivation the theory requires.
questions.x: Relative deprivation theory holds that perceived gaps between expectations and reality, judged against a reference standard, motivate collective action. Trap: Equating deprivation with absolute poverty.

questions.q: Resource mobilization theory proposes that social movements succeed mainly because of:
o: Access to organization, funding, and leadership
Correct: Resource mobilization theory emphasizes organization, funding, and leadership as the keys to movement success, more than grievances.
Widespread grievances alone
Widespread grievances alone are exactly what the theory says are insufficient.
Random events
Random events are not the explanatory focus of the theory.
Individual personalities only
Individual personalities only ignores the organizational resources it stresses.
questions.x: Resource mobilization theory emphasizes organization, funding, and leadership as the keys to movement success, more than grievances. Trap: Thinking grievances alone cause movements.

questions.q: Globalization most directly refers to:
o: Population growth in cities
Population growth in cities describes urbanization.
Decline of international trade
Decline of international trade is the opposite of globalization.
Increasing worldwide interconnectedness of economies and cultures
Correct: Globalization is the growing worldwide interconnectedness of economies, cultures, people, and ideas across borders.
Homogeneity within nations
Homogeneity within nations is not what globalization means.
questions.x: Globalization is the growing worldwide interconnectedness of economies, cultures, people, and ideas across borders. Trap: Equating globalization with economic trade only, ignoring cultural and population flows.

questions.q: A sex ratio of 105 at birth means:
o: 105 females born per 100 males
105 females per 100 males reverses the ratio.
105 males born per 100 females
Correct: Sex ratio is conventionally males per 100 females, so 105 means 105 males born per 100 females.
105 births per 1,000 people
105 births per 1,000 people confuses it with crude birth rate.
105% increase in male births
105% increase in male births is a growth change, not a ratio.
questions.x: Sex ratio is conventionally males per 100 females, so 105 means 105 males born per 100 females. Trap: Reversing the ratio so that females per 100 males is reported instead.

questions.q: A population growing at about 2 percent per year will double in approximately:
o: 70 years
70 years forgets to divide by the rate.
10 years
10 years divides by 7 rather than 2.
100 years
100 years has no basis in the rule.
35 years
Correct: Rule of 70: doubling time is about 70 / growth rate = 70/2 = 35 years.
questions.x: Rule of 70: doubling time is about 70 / growth rate = 70/2 = 35 years. Trap: Forgetting to divide 70 by the percentage.

questions.q: Members of a generation experiencing the Great Depression share distinct attitudes about money throughout life. This is best explained by:
o: Period effect
Period effects affect all age groups at one time, not a birth cohort over life.
Age effect
Age effects are tied to life stage rather than a historical generation.
Selection effect
Selection effect refers to biased sample composition, not generational influence.
Cohort effect
Correct: A cohort effect is a lasting influence shared by people born in the same period, as the Great Depression generation's attitudes toward money.
questions.x: A cohort effect is a lasting influence shared by people born in the same period, as the Great Depression generation's attitudes toward money. Trap: Confusing cohort with period effects.

questions.q: Sociologists define race as:
o: A biological classification into subspecies
Biological subspecies classification is not supported by genetics.
A socially constructed category based on perceived physical traits
Correct: Sociologists define race as a socially constructed category based on perceived physical traits, not biology.
Shared cultural heritage
Shared cultural heritage describes ethnicity.
Nationality
Nationality refers to legal citizenship or national origin.
questions.x: Sociologists define race as a socially constructed category based on perceived physical traits, not biology. Trap: Thinking race refers to cultural traits.

questions.q: Ethnicity primarily involves:
o: Shared culture, ancestry, and language
Correct: Ethnicity is a cultural identity based on shared culture, ancestry, and language.
Skin color
Skin color is a trait associated with race, not ethnicity.
Social class
Social class is economic and status position.
Citizenship
Citizenship is legal membership in a state.
questions.x: Ethnicity is a cultural identity based on shared culture, ancestry, and language. Trap: Using ethnicity and race as synonyms.

questions.q: Residential segregation is best defined as:
o: Voluntary migration of cultures
Voluntary migration of cultures does not describe separation.
Cultural blending
Cultural blending describes amalgamation.
The physical separation of groups across neighborhoods
Correct: Residential segregation is the physical separation of groups across neighborhoods.
Shared institutions
Shared institutions describes integration or pluralism.
questions.x: Residential segregation is the physical separation of groups across neighborhoods. Trap: Assuming only legally enforced segregation counts, when neighborhood separation also arises from markets and choices.

questions.q: A society in which distinct ethnic groups coexist while maintaining their cultural identities is practicing:
o: Pluralism
Correct: Pluralism is the coexistence of multiple groups that maintain distinct cultural identities.
Assimilation
Assimilation absorbs minority groups into the dominant culture.
Genocide
Genocide is deliberate destruction of a group.
Segregation
Segregation separates groups rather than letting them coexist as equals.
questions.x: Pluralism is the coexistence of multiple groups that maintain distinct cultural identities. Trap: Confusing pluralism with segregation.

questions.q: The deliberate and systematic destruction of a racial, ethnic, or national group is:
o: Expulsion
Expulsion forces a group to leave without necessarily destroying it.
Segregation
Segregation physically separates groups.
Genocide
Correct: Genocide is the deliberate and systematic destruction of a racial, ethnic, or national group.
Amalgamation
Amalgamation blends groups into a new one.
questions.x: Genocide is the deliberate and systematic destruction of a racial, ethnic, or national group. Trap: Mixing expulsion with genocide.

questions.q: When different groups combine to form a new cultural group, this is:
o: Assimilation
Assimilation is a group joining and adopting the dominant culture, not forming a new one.
Amalgamation
Correct: Amalgamation is the blending of different groups into a new cultural group.
Segregation
Segregation separates groups.
Pluralism
Pluralism keeps groups distinct.
questions.x: Amalgamation is the blending of different groups into a new cultural group. Trap: Treating blending into a new culture as one group being absorbed by the dominant one.

questions.q: Which factor is most consistently associated with declining fertility in developing countries?
o: Reduced contraception
Reduced contraception would raise fertility.
Increased infant mortality
Increased infant mortality tends to sustain high fertility as families replace lost children.
Greater agricultural labor demand
Greater agricultural labor demand raises the value of children as workers.
Increased female education and workforce participation
Correct: Greater female education and workforce participation raise the opportunity cost of children and expand contraception use, lowering fertility.
questions.x: Greater female education and workforce participation raise the opportunity cost of children and expand contraception use, lowering fertility. Trap: Assuming rising income alone drives fertility down, when women's education and work are more consistent factors.

questions.q: A 'demographic dividend' occurs when a country has:
o: A large elderly population
A large elderly population raises dependency, not a dividend.
A high fertility rate
High fertility produces many young dependents first, not a dividend.
High infant mortality
High infant mortality reflects poor health, not an economic boost.
A large working-age share relative to dependents
Correct: A demographic dividend occurs when a large working-age share relative to dependents boosts economic growth.
questions.x: A demographic dividend occurs when a large working-age share relative to dependents boosts economic growth. Trap: Thinking any large population produces a dividend.

questions.q: In Stage 3 of the demographic transition, population growth slows primarily because:
o: Death rates rise again
Death rates do not rise again in Stage 3.
Birth rates decline while death rates remain low
Correct: In Stage 3, urbanization, contraception, and education reduce birth rates while death rates stay low, narrowing the gap and slowing growth.
Emigration surges
Emigration surges are not what defines the stage.
Fertility returns to pre-industrial levels
Fertility returning to pre-industrial levels would raise growth.
questions.x: In Stage 3, urbanization, contraception, and education reduce birth rates while death rates stay low, narrowing the gap and slowing growth. Trap: Thinking growth slows because death rates rise.

questions.q: A sudden recession causes people of all ages to delay marriage and childbearing in the same years. This is best described as a:
o: Period effect
Correct: A period effect is a historical-event influence that affects all age groups at the same time, as a recession delaying marriage.
Cohort effect
Cohort effects are specific to people born in a certain era.
Age effect
Age effects arise from life stage, not from a shared event.
Generation gap
Generation gap describes differences between generations, not a time-specific influence.
questions.x: A period effect is a historical-event influence that affects all age groups at the same time, as a recession delaying marriage. Trap: Calling it a cohort effect because the event is historical; cohort effects depend on birth year.

questions.q: A country has a birth rate of 15 and a death rate of 9 per 1,000, with net migration of -2 per 1,000. Its annual growth rate per 1,000 is:
o: 6 ignores net migration.
8 adds migration with the wrong sign.
Correct: Growth equals natural increase (15 - 9 = 6) plus net migration (-2), giving 4 per 1,000.
11 does not follow from the data, as it adds the death rate and migration magnitude.
questions.x: Growth equals natural increase (15 - 9 = 6) plus net migration (-2), giving 4 per 1,000. Trap: Forgetting to include net migration in total growth.

questions.q: Five reaction times (ms) are 4, 6, 6, 8, and 40. Which statement about the data is correct?
o: The median (6) is less affected by the extreme value than the mean (12.8)
Correct: The mean is 64/5 = 12.8, pulled upward by 40, whereas the median is 6; the median is resistant to outliers.
The mean (6) is less affected than the median (12.8)
This reverses the two values; the median is 6 and the mean is 12.8.
The mean and median are both 12.8
The median is the middle value, 6.
The mode (4) best represents the data
The mode is 6, the most frequent value, not 4.
questions.x: The mean is 64/5 = 12.8, pulled upward by 40, whereas the median is 6; the median is resistant to outliers. Trap: Assuming the mean is always the best summary of a data set.

questions.q: A diagnostic test is applied to 300 people: 80 true positives, 20 false negatives, 30 false positives, and 170 true negatives. What is the specificity?
o: 80/100 is the sensitivity, TP/(TP + FN).
80/110 is the positive predictive value, TP/(TP + FP).
Correct: Specificity = TN/(TN + FP) = 170/200 = 85%.
170/190 is the negative predictive value, TN/(TN + FN).
questions.x: Specificity = TN/(TN + FP) = 170/200 = 85%. Trap: Mixing up specificity with sensitivity or predictive values.

questions.q: In a cohort study, 30 of 100 exposed people and 10 of 100 unexposed people develop the disease. What is the relative risk?
o: This inverts the ratio of the risks.
Twenty percentage points is the absolute risk difference, not a ratio.
This is the relative excess risk, (0.30 - 0.10)/0.10, not the relative risk.
questions.x: RR = (30/100)/(10/100) = 3.0. Trap: Reporting the risk difference as if it were the risk ratio.

questions.q: In a case-control study, 40 of 100 cases and 20 of 100 controls were exposed. What is the odds ratio for exposure?
o: This compares only the exposed counts, 40/20, and ignores the unexposed.
This is the reciprocal of the odds ratio.
This is 60/40 and ignores the controls entirely.
Correct: Odds in cases are 40/60 and in controls 20/80, so OR = (40 x 80)/(60 x 20) = 3200/1200 = 2.67.
questions.x: Odds in cases are 40/60 and in controls 20/80, so OR = (40 x 80)/(60 x 20) = 3200/1200 = 2.67. Trap: Dividing exposed counts instead of cross-multiplying the 2 x 2 table.

questions.q: In a 200-person study, 50 people received a drug and 40 people improved overall. If drug and improvement were independent, how many drug recipients would be expected to improve?
o: This assumes half of the improvers received the drug.
This assumes half of the drug group improves.
This is the total number who improved, ignoring group size.
Correct: Expected = (row total x column total)/grand total = 50 x 40/200 = 10.
questions.x: Expected = (row total x column total)/grand total = 50 x 40/200 = 10. Trap: Using observed counts or marginal totals instead of expected counts.

questions.q: A researcher performs 20 independent hypothesis tests at alpha = 0.05 when no real effects exist. About how many false positives are expected?
o: This would require 100 tests at alpha = 0.05.
Correct: Expected false positives = 20 x 0.05 = 1.
Each test carries a 5% chance of Type I error even when the null is true.
This would be the case only if every test were significant.
questions.x: Expected false positives = 20 x 0.05 = 1. Trap: Believing alpha applies only to the whole set rather than to each test.

questions.q: A study reports p = 0.03 for the difference between a drug and placebo. Which interpretation is correct?
o: There is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true
The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
There is a 97% chance that the drug works
This misreads p as the probability that the effect is real.
If the null hypothesis were true, results at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
Correct: The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme given the null hypothesis.
The effect is large
The p-value does not measure effect size.
questions.x: The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme given the null hypothesis. Trap: Interpreting p as the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

questions.q: Which change would increase the statistical power of a study?
o: Increasing the sample size
Correct: A larger sample reduces standard error, making a true effect easier to detect.
Decreasing alpha from 0.05 to 0.01
A stricter alpha lowers power.
Increasing the variability in the outcome
More variability lowers power.
Studying a smaller true effect size
Smaller effects are harder to detect.
questions.x: A larger sample reduces standard error, making a true effect easier to detect. Trap: Thinking that a smaller alpha always makes a study stronger.

questions.q: A sample of 100 participants has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the population mean?
o: Correct: SE = 10/sqrt(100) = 1, so the interval is about 50 +/- 2.
This uses 1 SD of the data rather than the standard error.
This is about +/- 1 SE, roughly a 68% interval.
This is about +/- 2 SD of the data, an interval for individuals rather than the mean.
questions.x: SE = 10/sqrt(100) = 1, so the interval is about 50 +/- 2. Trap: Using the standard deviation instead of the standard error.

questions.q: A sample of 25 has a standard deviation of 20. If the sample size is increased to 100 with the same SD, the standard error will:
o: drop from 4 to 1
This assumes SE falls in proportion to n.
remain at 4
SE depends on n.
drop from 4 to 2
Correct: SE = 20/5 = 4 at n = 25 and 20/10 = 2 at n = 100.
rise from 4 to 8
More data cannot increase SE.
questions.x: SE = 20/5 = 4 at n = 25 and 20/10 = 2 at n = 100. Trap: Believing SE falls in direct proportion to n rather than sqrt(n).

questions.q: Two variables are correlated with r = -0.6. What fraction of variance in one variable is explained by the other?
o: This treats r itself as the variance explained.
Correct: r squared = 0.36.
Variance explained cannot be negative.
This is 1 - r squared, the variance left unexplained.
questions.x: r squared = 0.36. Trap: Treating r as the proportion of variance explained.

questions.q: A study finds that coffee drinkers have more lung cancer, but many coffee drinkers also smoke. In this study, smoking is a:
o: dependent variable
The dependent variable is lung cancer.
placebo
A placebo is an inert treatment.
control group
A control group is a comparison group, not a variable associated with both.
confounding variable
Correct: Smoking is associated with both coffee drinking and lung cancer, creating a spurious association.
questions.x: Smoking is associated with both coffee drinking and lung cancer, creating a spurious association. Trap: Calling the confounder the outcome variable. Key distinction missed: Smoking is associated with both coffee drinking and lung cancer, creating a spurious association.

questions.q: A survey on exercise habits is posted online and answered only by volunteers. The greatest threat to the study is:
o: observer expectancy limiting internal validity
Expectancy refers to experimenter influence.
regression to the mean
This arises in repeated measures with extreme scores.
low statistical power from a large sample
Large samples do not reduce power.
selection bias limiting external validity
Correct: Volunteers may differ from the target population, so results may not generalize.
questions.x: Volunteers may differ from the target population, so results may not generalize. Trap: Confusing generalizability with internal validity.

questions.q: Mean systolic blood pressure is compared across three independent treatment groups. The most appropriate test is:
o: paired t-test
This is for dependent samples.
one-way ANOVA
Correct: ANOVA compares means across more than two groups.
chi-square test
This is for categorical frequencies.
Pearson correlation
This measures association between two continuous variables.
questions.x: ANOVA compares means across more than two groups. Trap: Running multiple t-tests instead of ANOVA. Key distinction missed: ANOVA compares means across more than two groups.

questions.q: To compare the proportions of smokers in two groups, the most appropriate test is the:
o: ANOVA
ANOVA compares means.
independent t-test
A t-test compares means of continuous data.
chi-square test
Correct: Chi-square compares frequencies of categorical outcomes.
linear regression
Linear regression predicts a continuous outcome.
questions.x: Chi-square compares frequencies of categorical outcomes. Trap: Using a t-test for categorical data. Key distinction missed: Chi-square compares frequencies of categorical outcomes.

questions.q: The primary purpose of double blinding in a clinical trial is to:
o: reduce bias from participant and researcher expectations
Correct: Neither participants nor investigators know assignments, limiting expectation effects.
increase the sample size
Blinding does not alter sample size.
ensure random assignment
Randomization is a separate procedure.
improve external validity
Blinding addresses internal validity.
questions.x: Neither participants nor investigators know assignments, limiting expectation effects. Trap: Confusing blinding with randomization. Key distinction missed: Neither participants nor investigators know assignments, limiting expectation effects.

questions.q: Which design is the most efficient for studying risk factors for a very rare disease?
o: Case-control
Correct: It starts with cases and compares them with controls.
Prospective cohort
A cohort would need a huge sample to accrue cases.
Cross-sectional survey
Rare cases would be missed.
Randomized controlled trial
Assigning risk factors may be unethical and inefficient.
questions.x: It starts with cases and compares them with controls. Trap: Choosing a cohort design for rare outcomes. Key distinction missed: It starts with cases and compares them with controls.

questions.q: Patients selected for extremely high blood pressure show lower readings at follow-up even without treatment. This is most likely due to:
o: a placebo effect only
Placebo does not explain a change in untreated people.
a history effect
No outside event is described.
regression to the mean
Correct: Extreme values tend to move toward the average on remeasurement.
observer bias
Not suggested.
questions.x: Extreme values tend to move toward the average on remeasurement. Trap: Attributing a change to a treatment. Key distinction missed: Extreme values tend to move toward the average on remeasurement.

questions.q: In a randomized trial, many participants who experience side effects drop out of the treatment arm only. This primarily threatens:
o: external validity only
It affects comparisons within the study.
internal validity
Correct: Differential dropout makes the groups no longer comparable.
test-retest reliability
The issue is not measurement consistency.
face validity
Face validity is about apparent measure relevance.
questions.x: Differential dropout makes the groups no longer comparable. Trap: Treating dropout as only a loss of sample size.

questions.q: IQ scores are normally distributed with mean 100 and SD 15. About what percentage of people score above 130?
o: This is the percentage above 1 SD.
This is the two-tailed total beyond 2 SD.
This is the percentage above 3 SD.
Correct: 130 is 2 SD above the mean; roughly 2.5% lie above that point.
questions.x: 130 is 2 SD above the mean; roughly 2.5% lie above that point. Trap: Counting both tails when only one is asked. Key distinction missed: 130 is 2 SD above the mean; roughly 2.5% lie above that point.

questions.q: The same 30 patients' pain scores are measured before and after treatment. The most appropriate test of the mean change is:
o: independent samples t-test
This assumes separate groups.
chi-square test
This is for categorical data.
one-way ANOVA with three groups
There are only two measurements and the data are paired.
paired t-test
Correct: The measurements are dependent because they come from the same people.
questions.x: The measurements are dependent because they come from the same people. Trap: Treating repeated measures as independent groups.
